Television shows, such as David Lynch and Mark Frost's ''[[Twin Peaks]]'' and Dennis Potter's ''[[The Singing Detective]]'', also have "a loosening of causality, a greater emphasis on psychological or anecdotal realism, violations of classical clarity of space and time, explicit authorial comment, and ambiguity".<ref>{{cite book|first=Kristin|last=Thompson|title=''Storytelling in Film and Television''|publisher=Harvard University Press|location=Cambridge, Massachusetts|year=2003}}</ref>

As with much of Lynch's other work (notably the film ''[[Blue Velvet (film)|Blue Velvet]]''), ''Twin Peaks'' explores the gulf between the veneer of small-town respectability and the seedier layers of life lurking beneath its surface. The show is difficult to place in a defined television genre; stylistically, it borrows the unsettling tone and supernatural premises of horror films and simultaneously offers a bizarrely comical parody of American soap operas with a [[Camp (style)|campy]], melodramatic presentation of the morally dubious activities of its quirky characters. The show represents an earnest moral inquiry distinguished by both [[Surreal humor|weird humor]] and a deep vein of [[surrealism]], incorporating highly stylised vignettes, surrealist and often inaccessible artistic images alongside the otherwise comprehensible narrative of events.

[[HBO]]'s ''[[The Wire]]'' might also qualify as "artistic television", as it has garnered a greater amount of critical attention from academics than most television shows receive. For example, the [[film theory]] journal ''[[Film Quarterly]]'' has featured the show on its cover.<ref>{{cite web|first=D.|last=Driscoll|url=http://machines.pomona.edu/152-2009/2009/11/02/the-wire-being-taught-at-harvard/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110720033154/http://machines.pomona.edu/152-2009/2009/11/02/the-wire-being-taught-at-harvard/|archive-date=20 July 2011 |title=''The Wire'' Being Taught at Harvard |publisher=Machines.pomona.edu |date=2 November 2009|access-date=6 October 2010}}</ref>

==In popular media==
Art films have been part of popular culture from animated sitcoms like ''[[The Simpsons]]''<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.imdb.com/title/tt1225549/|title=Any Given Sundance|publisher= IMDb}}</ref> and ''[[Clone High]]'' spoofing and satirizing them<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.imdb.com/title/tt0542907/|title=Film Fest: Tears of a Clone|publisher= IMDb}}</ref> to even the comedic film review webseries ''Brows Held High'' (hosted by Kyle Kallgren).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.geek.com/movies/real-good-you-guys-kyle-kallgren-and-brows-held-high-1721593/ |title=Real Good You Guys: Kyle Kallgren and Brows Held High|date=7 November 2017|access-date=12 September 2019 |archive-date=15 August 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180815041155/https://www.geek.com/movies/real-good-you-guys-kyle-kallgren-and-brows-held-high-1721593/ |url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://the-avocado.org/2018/06/03/brows-held-high-night-thread/ |title=Brows Held High Night Thread |work= The Avocado|first = Sam|last = Aronow|date = 3 June 2018}}</ref><ref name="top15essayistsonyoutube">{{Cite web|url=https://raindance.org/top-15-video-essayists-youtube/|title=Top 15 Video Essayists on Youtube|first=Bruno Savill De|last=Jong|date=27 June 2017}}</ref><ref name="essaysof2017">{{Cite web |last1=Lee |first1=Kevin B. |last2=Verdeure |first2=David |date=2010-01-10 |title=The best video essays of 2017 |url=https://www2.bfi.org.uk/news-opinion/sight-sound-magazine/polls-surveys/annual-round-ups/best-video-essays-2017 |access-date=2020-12-24 |website=[[British Film Institute]] |language=en}}</ref>

The '''cinema of China''' is the [[filmmaking]] and [[film industry]] of [[mainland China]], one of three distinct historical threads of [[Chinese languages|Chinese-language]] cinema together with the [[cinema of Hong Kong]] and the [[cinema of Taiwan]]. China is the home of the largest movie and drama production complex and film studios in the world, the [[Oriental Movie Metropolis]]<ref>{{Cite web |last=Brzeski |first=Patrick |date=2016-11-02 |title=Breathtaking Photos From Inside the China Studio Luring Hollywood East |url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/general-news/qingdao-china-movie-metropolis-easts-massive-wanda-studios-943117/ |access-date=2025-04-17 |website=The Hollywood Reporter |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Galuppo |first=Mia |date=2016-10-17 |title=Wanda Unveils Plans for $8 Billion 'Movie Metropolis,' Reveals Details About Film Incentives |url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/general-news/wanda-unveils-plans-8-billion-939003/ |access-date=2025-04-17 |website=The Hollywood Reporter |language=en-US}}</ref> and [[Hengdian World Studios]]. In 2012 the country became the second-largest market in the world by box office receipts behind only the [[United States]]. In 2016 the gross box office in China was {{CNY|45.71 billion}} ({{USD|6.58 billion}}). China has also become a major hub of business for Hollywood studios.

== History ==
{{Main|History of cinema of China}}

== Beginnings ==
While early accounts traditionally date the introduction of cinema to China to an anonymous variety show in August 1896 at Shanghai's Xu Garden teahouse, archival newspaper research by Dr Yongchun Fu demonstrates that this event was a magic lantern exhibition projecting still glass slides (yingxi). The historical record confirms that the first true motion picture exhibition in China occurred on May 22, 1897, when itinerant showman Harry Welby Cook projected celluloid film strips using Edison's Animatoscope at the Astor House Hotel in Shanghai. Later that summer, Cook also produced China's earliest localized actualities by filming local bicycle riders and swimming baths, before expanding his commercial film circuit north to Tianjin and Beijing.
Chinese-made short melodrama and comedy films began emerging in 1913.<ref name=":Qian">{{Cite book |last=Qian |first=Ying |title=Revolutionary Becomings: Documentary Media in Twentieth-Century China |date=2024 |publisher=[[Columbia University Press]] |isbn=9780231204477 |location=New York, NY}}</ref>{{Rp|page=48}} In 1913, the first independent Chinese screenplay, ''[[The Difficult Couple]]'', was filmed in Shanghai by [[Zheng Zhengqiu]] and [[Zhang Shichuan]].<ref name="carter">{{cite book |author=David Carter |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Nydlzbe2LhEC&pg=PA1945 |title=East Asian Cinema |publisher=Kamera Books |year=2010 |isbn=978-1-84243-380-5}}</ref>  Zhang Shichuan then set up the first Chinese-owned film production company in 1916. The first full-length feature film was ''[[Yan Ruisheng]]'' (閻瑞生) released in 1921, which was a docudrama about the [[Murder of Wang Lianying|killing of a Shanghai courtesan]].<ref name=":03">{{Cite book |last=Ye, Tan |title=Historical dictionary of Chinese cinema |date=2012 |publisher=The Scarecrow Press, Inc |others=Zhu, Yun, 1979- |isbn=978-0-8108-6779-6 |location=Lanham |oclc=764377427}}</ref>

Chinese film production developed significantly in the 1920s.<ref name=":Qian" />{{Rp|page=48}} During the 1920s film technicians from the United States trained Chinese technicians in Shanghai, and American influence continued to be felt there for the next two decades.<ref name="carter" /> Since film was still in its earliest stages of development, most Chinese silent films at this time were only comic skits or operatic shorts, and training was minimal at a technical aspect due to this being a period of experimental film.<ref name=":03"/> Throughout the 1920s and 1930s, filmmaking in China was largely done by film studios and there was comparatively little small scale filmmaking.<ref name=":Qian" />{{Rp|page=62}}

Upscale movie theaters in China had contracts which required them to exclusively show Hollywood films, and thus as of the later 1920s, Hollywood films accounted for 90% of screen time in Chinese theaters.<ref name=":Qian" />{{Rp|page=64}}

After trial and error, China was able to draw inspiration from its traditional values and began producing [[martial arts]] films, with the first being ''[[The Burning of the Red Lotus Temple|Burning of Red Lotus Temple]]'' (1928). ''Burning of Red Lotus Temple'' was so successful at the box office, the [[Mingxing|Star Motion Pictures]] (Mingxing) production later filmed 18 sequels, marking the beginning of China's esteemed martial arts films.<ref name=":03"/> Many imitators followed, including U. Lien (Youlian) Studio's ''Red Heroine'' (1929), which is still extant.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Rea |first=Christopher |date=1929-02-24 |title=Red Heroine 紅俠 (1929) |url=https://chinesefilmclassics.org/red-heroine-1929/ |access-date=2025-04-17 |website=Chinese Film Classics |language=en-US}}</ref> It was during this period that some of the more important production companies first came into being, notably [[Mingxing Film Company|Mingxing]] and the Shaw brothers' Tianyi ("Unique"). Mingxing, founded by Zheng Zhengqiu and Zhang Shichuan in 1922, initially focused on comic shorts, including the oldest surviving complete Chinese film, ''[[Laborer's Love]]'' (1922).<ref name="Centennial">{{cite web |author=Zhang Yingjin |date=2003-10-10 |title=A Centennial Review of Chinese Cinema |url=http://chinesecinema.ucsd.edu/essay_ccwlc.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080907160026/http://chinesecinema.ucsd.edu/essay_ccwlc.html |archive-date=2008-09-07 |access-date=2007-04-26 |publisher=University of California-San Diego}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=A Brief History of Chinese Film |url=http://people.cohums.ohio-state.edu/denton2/courses/c505/temp/history/chapter2.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140410062249/http://people.cohums.ohio-state.edu/denton2/courses/c505/temp/history/chapter2.html |archive-date=2014-04-10 |access-date=2007-04-24 |publisher=Ohio State University}}</ref><ref>Berry, Chris. "China Before 1949", in ''The Oxford History of World Cinema'', edited by Geoffrey Nowell-Smith (1997). Oxford: Oxford University Press, pp. 409–410.</ref> This soon shifted, however, to feature-length films and family dramas including ''[[Orphan Rescues Grandfather]]'' (1923).<ref name="Centennial" /> Meanwhile, Tianyi shifted their model towards folklore dramas and also pushed into foreign markets; their film ''[[Legend of the White Snake (film)|White Snake]]'' (1926){{efn|Bai She Zhuan (1926) 白蛇传 : ''Legend of the White Snake''<ref name="White-Snake:Mirror">{{cite web|title=《Legend of the White Snake》(1926)|url=http://www.chinesemirror.com/index/2012/03/legend-of-the-white-snake-1926.html|publisher=The Chinese Mirror|access-date=23 January 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130319032519/http://www.chinesemirror.com/index/2012/03/legend-of-the-white-snake-1926.html|archive-date=19 March 2013}}</ref> Adaptation of ''[[Legend of the White Snake]]''}} proved a typical example of their success in the Chinese communities of Southeast Asia.<ref name="Centennial" /> In 1931, the first Chinese [[sound film]] ''[[Sing-Song Girl Red Peony]]'' was made, the product of a cooperation between the Mingxing Film Company's image production and [[Pathé Frères]]'s sound technology. However, the sound was [[Sound-on-disc|disc-recorded]], which was then played in the theater in-sync with the action on the screen. The first [[sound-on-film]] [[talkie]] made in China was either ''Spring on Stage'' (歌場春色) by Tianyi, or ''Clear Sky After Storm'' by Great China Studio and Jinan Studio.<ref>{{cite book |author=Yingjin Zhang |title=A Companion to Chinese Cinema |publisher=Wiley-Blackwell |year=2012 |isbn=978-1-4443-3029-8 |page=456 |chapter=Chapter 24 - Chinese Cinema and Technology |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gDRxR-wb-fsC&pg=PT262}}</ref> Musical films, such as ''[[Song at Midnight]]'' (1937)<ref>{{Cite web |last=Rea |first=Christopher |date=1937-02-21 |title=Song at Midnight 夜半歌聲 (1937) |url=https://chinesefilmclassics.org/song-at-midnight-1937/ |access-date=2025-04-17 |website=Chinese Film Classics |language=en-US}}</ref> and ''Street Angels'' (1937),<ref>{{Cite web |last=Rea |first=Christopher |date=1937-07-22 |title=Street Angels 馬路天使 (1937) |url=https://chinesefilmclassics.org/street-angels-1937/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231001111044/https://chinesefilmclassics.org/street-angels-1937/ |archive-date=Oct 1, 2023 |access-date=2025-04-17 |website=Chinese Film Classics |language=en-US}}</ref> starring Zhou Xuan,<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Rea |first1=Christopher |title=Zhou Xuan 周璇 |url=https://chinesefilmclassics.org/zhou-xuan-%E5%91%A8%E7%92%87/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230721224217/https://chinesefilmclassics.org/zhou-xuan-%E5%91%A8%E7%92%87/ |archive-date=21 Jul 2023 |website=Chinese Film Classics}}</ref> became one of the most popular film genres in China.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Rea |first=Christopher |title=Chinese Film Classics, 1922-1949 |publisher=Columbia University Press |year=2021 |isbn=978-0-231-18813-5 |location=New York |pages=chs. 7–8}}</ref>

In the late 1920s, the [[Censorship in the Republic of China (1912–1949)|ROC banned]] the adaptation of martial arts novels into films.<ref name=":122">{{Cite book |last=Ni|first=Zhange|title=Uncanny Beliefs: Superstition in Modern Chinese History|date=2026|publisher=[[Harvard University Asia Center]]|isbn=978-0-674-30340-9|editor-last=Baum|editor-first=Emily|series=Harvard Contemporary China series|volume=22|location=Cambridge (Massachusetts) London|chapter=Reimagining Superstition in the Digital Age: Fantasy Novels, Media Corporations, and the Chinese State|jstor=jj.45767069|editor-last2=Wu|editor-first2=Albert}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=289}} The Nationalist government contended that the masses were superstitious and would take the fantastical elements of these narratives as factual.<ref name=":122" />{{Reference page|page=289}}

News films increased in importance following the Japanese air raid on Shanghai in 1932.<ref name=":Qian" />{{Rp|page=66}} The bombing also destroyed significant amounts of the Chinese film industry and resulted in the loss of many early films.<ref name=":Qian" />{{Rp|page=66}}

=== Leftist movement ===
[[File:LoveandDuty.jpg|left|thumb|20-year-old [[Ruan Lingyu]], a superstar during the silent film era, in ''[[Love and Duty (1931 film)|Love and Duty]]'' (1931)<ref>{{Cite web |date=24 February 1931 |title=Love and Duty 戀愛與義務 (1931) |url=https://chinesefilmclassics.org/love-and-duty-1931/}}</ref>]]
Many important Chinese films were produced beginning in the 1930s with the advent of the "progressive" or "left-wing" movement, including [[Cheng Bugao]]'s ''[[Spring Silkworms (film)|Spring Silkworms]]'' (1933),<ref>{{Cite web |last=Cheng |first=Bugao |date=1933-03-08 |title=Spring Silkworms 春蠶 (1933) |url=https://chinesefilmclassics.org/spring-silkworms-1933/ |access-date=2023-03-23 |website=Chinese Film Classics |language=en-US}}</ref> [[Wu Yonggang]]'s ''[[The Goddess (1934 film)|The Goddess]]'' (1934),<ref>{{Cite web |title=Module 3: Goddess (1934) |url=https://chinesefilmclassics.org/course/module-3-goddess-1934/ |access-date=2025-04-17 |website=Chinese Film Classics |language=en-US}}</ref> and [[Sun Yu (director)|Sun Yu]]'s ''The Great Road'', also known as ''[[The Big Road]]'' (1934).<ref>{{Cite web |title=Module 4: The Great Road (1934) |url=https://chinesefilmclassics.org/course/module-4-the-great-road-1934/ |access-date=2023-03-23 |website=Chinese Film Classics |language=en-US}}</ref> These films were noted for their emphasis on class struggle and external threats (i.e. Japanese aggression), as well as on their focus on common people, such as a family of silk farmers in ''Spring Silkworms'' and a prostitute in ''The Goddess''.<ref name="Geiselmann">{{cite web |author=Martin Geiselmann |year=2006 |title=Chinese Film History - A Short Introduction |url=http://www.univie.ac.at/Sinologie/repository/ueLK110_ChinFilmgesch/filmgeschichteSkript.pdf |access-date=2007-07-25 |publisher=The University of Vienna- Sinologie Program}}</ref> In part due to the success of these kinds of films, this post-1930 era is now often referred to as the first "golden period" of Chinese cinema.<ref name="Geiselmann" /> The Leftist cinematic movement often revolved around the Western-influenced Shanghai, where filmmakers portrayed the struggling lower class of an overpopulated city.<ref>Laikwan Pang, ''Building a New China in Cinema'' (Rowman and Littlefield Productions, Oxford, 2002)</ref>

As part of their strategy to use art as a medium for its political messages, the [[Chinese Communist Party]] (CCP) became active in Shanghai's film industry.'''<ref name=":05">{{Cite book |last=Pan |first=Yihong |title=Not Just a Man's War: Chinese Women's Memories of the War of Resistance Against Japan, 1931-45 |publisher=[[University of British Columbia Press]] |year=2025 |isbn=9780774870368}}</ref>'''{{Reference page|page=11}} Films with themes of women's liberation that were produced as a result of this strategy included the 1935 film ''[[Children of Troubled Times]]'', the theme song of which (''[[March of the Volunteers|The March of the Volunteers]]'') became the PRC's national anthem.<ref name=":05" />{{Reference page|page=11}}

Three [[Production company|production companies]] dominated the market in the early to mid-1930s: the newly formed [[Lianhua Film Company|Lianhua]] ("United China"),{{efn|Lianhua's original English name is "United Photoplay Service"}} the older and larger Mingxing and Tianyi.<ref>{{cite web |author=Kraicer, Shelly |date=2005-12-06 |title=Timeline |url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/thr/international/feature_display.jsp?vnu_content_id=1001614559 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100802065514/http://www.hollywoodreporter.com/hr/search/article_display.jsp?vnu_content_id=1001614559 |archive-date=2010-08-02 |access-date=2006-05-08 |work=The Hollywood Reporter}}</ref> Both Mingxing and Lianhua leaned left (Lianhua's management perhaps more so),<ref name="Geiselmann" /> while Tianyi continued to make less socially conscious fare.{{citation needed|date=December 2025}}
[[File:JinYan2.jpg|thumb|[[Jin Yan]], a Korean-born Chinese actor featured in ''[[The Big Road]]'' (1935), who gained fame during China's golden age of cinema]]
The period also produced the first big Chinese movie stars, such as Hu Die, Ruan Lingyu,<ref>{{Cite web |date=8 March 2021 |title=Ruan Lingyu 阮玲玉 |url=https://chinesefilmclassics.org/ruan-lingyu/}}</ref> [[Li Lili]],<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Rea |first1=Christopher |title=Li Lili 黎莉莉 |url=https://chinesefilmclassics.org/li-lili-%e9%bb%8e%e8%8e%89%e8%8e%89/ |website=Chinese Film Classics}}</ref> [[Chen Yanyan]],<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Rea |first1=Christopher |title=Chen Yanyan 陳燕燕 |url=https://chinesefilmclassics.org/chen-yanyan-%e9%99%b3%e7%87%95%e7%87%95/ |website=Chinese Film Classics}}</ref> [[Zhou Xuan]], [[Zhao Dan]] and [[Jin Yan]]. Other major films of the period include ''[[Love and Duty (1931 film)|Love and Duty]]'' (1931), ''[[Little Toys]]'' (1933), ''[[New Women]]'' (1934),<ref>{{Cite web |date=4 February 1935 |title=New Women 新女性 (1935) |url=https://chinesefilmclassics.org/new-women-1935/}}</ref> ''[[Song of the Fishermen]]'' (1934),<ref>{{Cite web |date=14 June 1934 |title=Song of the Fishermen 漁光曲 (1934) |url=https://chinesefilmclassics.org/song-of-the-fishermen-1934/}}</ref> ''[[Plunder of Peach and Plum]]'' (1934), ''[[Crossroads (1937 film)|Crossroads]]'' (1937), and ''[[Street Angel (1937 film)|Street Angel]]'' (1937).<ref name="auto1">{{Cite web |date=22 July 1937 |title=Street Angels 馬路天使 (1937) |url=https://chinesefilmclassics.org/street-angels-1937/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231001111044/https://chinesefilmclassics.org/street-angels-1937/ |archive-date=Oct 1, 2023 |website=Chinese Film Classics}}</ref> Throughout the 1930s, the [[Kuomintang|Nationalists]] and the CCP struggled for power and control over the major studios; their influence can be seen in the films the studios produced during this period.{{citation needed|date=December 2025}}

=== Japanese occupation and World War II ===
[[File:ZhouXuan1.jpg|thumb|231x231px|[[Zhou Xuan]], an iconic Chinese singer and film actress]]
The start of the [[Second Sino-Japanese War]] in 1937, in particular the [[Battle of Shanghai]], ended this golden run in Chinese cinema. All production companies except [[Xinhua Film Company]] ("New China") closed shop. A large number filmmakers left to join the War of Resistance, with many going to the Nationalist-controlled hinterlands to join the Nationalist film studios Central Motion Picture Studio or China Motion Picture Studio.<ref name=":Qian" />{{Rp|page=102}} A smaller number went to [[Yan'an]] or Hong Kong.<ref name=":Qian" />{{Rp|pages=102–103}}

The Shanghai film industry, though severely curtailed, did not stop however, thus leading to the "[[Solitary Island]]" period (also known as the "Sole Island" or "Orphan Island"), with Shanghai's foreign concessions serving as an "island" of production in the "sea" of Japanese-occupied territory. It was during this period that artists and directors who remained in the city had to walk a fine line between staying true to their leftist and nationalist beliefs and Japanese pressures. Director [[Bu Wancang]]'s ''Hua Mu Lan'', also known as ''[[Mulan Joins the Army (1939 film)|Mulan Joins the Army]]'' (1939),<ref>{{Cite web |date=17 February 1939 |title=Hua Mu Lan 木蘭從軍 (1939) |url=https://chinesefilmclassics.org/hua-mu-lan-1939/}}</ref> with its story of a young Chinese peasant fighting against a foreign invasion, was a particularly good example of Shanghai's continued film-production in the midst of war.<ref name="Centennial" /><ref>{{cite web |author=Ministry of Culture Staff |year=2003 |title=Sole Island Movies |url=http://www.chinaculture.org/gb/en_artqa/2003-09/24/content_38559.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060826094341/http://www.chinaculture.org/gb/en_artqa/2003-09/24/content_38559.htm |archive-date=2006-08-26 |access-date=2006-08-18 |publisher=ChinaCulture.org}}</ref> This period ended when Japan declared war on the Western allies on 7 December 1941; the solitary island was finally engulfed by the sea of the Japanese occupation. With the Shanghai industry firmly in Japanese control, films like the [[Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere]]-promoting ''[[Eternity (1943 film)|Eternity]]'' (1943) were produced.<ref name="Centennial" />

By the 1930s and 1940s, both the [[Nationalist government]] and the CCP used documentary films as a form of propaganda.<ref name=":32">{{Cite journal |last=Kendall |first=Paul |date=2024-10-09 |title=Third Front as Method: Mao, Market and the Present in CCTV Documentaries |journal=[[The China Quarterly]] |volume=260 |pages=872–886 |doi=10.1017/s0305741024000912 |issn=0305-7410 |doi-access=free}}</ref>{{Rp|pages=874}}

During the 1930 and 1940s, both the Nationalist government and the Japanese occupation authorities sent mobile projectionist units into areas under their control to show propaganda films.<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Li |first=Jie |title=Cinematic Guerillas: Propaganda, Projectionists, and Audiences in Socialist China |publisher=[[Columbia University Press]] |year=2023 |doi=10.7312/li--20626 |isbn=9780231206273 |jstor=10.7312/li--20626}}</ref>{{Rp|page=69}}

In the [[Yan'an Soviet]] during September 1938, the [[Eighth Route Army]] established its first film group.<ref name=":1" />{{Rp|page=69}} In 1943, the CCP released its first campaign film, ''Nanniwan'', which sought to develop relationships between its forces and local people in the Yan'an area by showcasing the army's production campaign to alleviate material shortages.<ref name=":Qian" />{{Rp|page=16}}

Following Japan's unconditional surrender in August 1945, the [[Red Army|Soviet Red Army]] helped the CCP to take over the Japanese colonial film establishment in Manchuria, the [[Manchukuo Film Association|Manchukuo Film Association (Man-ei)]].<ref name=":Qian" />{{Rp|page=132}} Man-ei had state-of-the-art film production equipment and supplies.<ref name=":Qian" />{{Rp|page=132}} The former colonial studio was relocated to [[Hegang]], where it was established as [[Northeast Film Studio|Northeastern Film Studio]], the CCP's first full-capacity film studio.<ref name=":Qian" />{{Rp|page=132}} [[Yuan Muzhi]] was its director and [[Chen Bo'er]] was its party secretary.<ref name=":Qian" />{{Rp|page=132}} Northeastern Film Studio began production in early 1947, focusing on news and documentary films, as well as some fiction, educational film for children, and animation.<ref name=":Qian" />{{Rp|pages=132–133}}

During the later phase of the [[Chinese Civil War]], filmmakers trained in Yan'an and Northeastern Film Studio documented all the major battles leading to the CCP's defeat of the Nationalists.<ref name=":Qian" />{{Rp|page=134}}

== Second golden age ==
[[File:New_Fisherman's_Song.jpg|left|thumb|[[Wang Danfeng]] in the film ''New Fisherman's Song'' (1942)]]
The film industry continued to develop after 1945. Production in Shanghai once again resumed as a new crop of studios took the place that Lianhua and Mingxing studios had occupied in the previous decade. In 1945, [[Cai Chusheng]] returned to Shanghai to revive the Lianhua name as the "Lianhua Film Society with Shi Dongshan, Meng Junmou, and Zheng Junli."<ref>{{cite web |author=Zhang Yingjin |date=2007-01-01 |title=Chinese Cinema - Cai Chusheng |url=http://chinesecinema.ucsd.edu/directors_ccwlc.html#cai |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070307193958/http://chinesecinema.ucsd.edu/directors_ccwlc.html |archive-date=7 March 2007 |access-date=2007-04-25 |publisher=University of California-San Diego}}</ref> This in turn became [[Kunlun Film Company|Kunlun Studios]], which would go on to become one of the most important studios of the era (Kunlun Studios merged with seven other studios to form Shanghai film studio in 1949), putting out the classics ''[[The Spring River Flows East]]'' (1947),<ref>{{Cite web |date=10 October 1947 |title=Spring River Flows East 一江春水向東流 (1947) |url=https://chinesefilmclassics.org/spring-river-flows-east-1947/}}</ref> ''[[Myriad of Lights]]'' (1948), ''[[Crows and Sparrows]]'' (1949),<ref>{{Cite web |date=14 January 1950 |title=Crows and Sparrows 烏鴉與麻雀 (1949) |url=https://chinesefilmclassics.org/crows-and-sparrows-1949/}}</ref> and ''Wanderings of Three-Hairs the Orphan'', also known as ''[[San Mao, The Little Vagabond]]'' (1949).<ref>{{Cite web |date=31 October 1949 |title=Wanderings of Three Hairs the Orphan 三毛流浪記 (1949) |url=https://chinesefilmclassics.org/wanderings-of-three-hairs-the-orphan-1949/}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |year=2004 |title=Kunlun Film Company |url=http://ftvdb.bfi.org.uk/sift/organisation/13907 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080122023815/http://ftvdb.bfi.org.uk/sift/organisation/13907 |archive-date=2008-01-22 |access-date=2007-04-25 |publisher=British Film Institute}}</ref> Many of these films showed the disillusionment with the oppressive rule of [[Chiang Kai-shek]]'s Nationalist Party and the struggling oppression of nation by war. ''The Spring River Flows East'', a three-hour-long two-parter directed by Cai Chusheng and [[Zheng Junli]], was a particularly strong success. Its depiction of the struggles of ordinary Chinese during the Second Sino-Japanese war, replete with biting social and political commentary, struck a chord with audiences of the time.

Meanwhile, companies like the [[Wenhua Film Company]] ("Culture Films"), moved away from the leftist tradition and explored the evolution and development of other dramatic genres. Wenhua treated postwar problems in universalistic and humanistic ways, avoiding the family narrative and melodramatic formulae. Excellent examples of Wenhua's fare are its first two postwar features, ''[[Unending Emotions|Love Everlasting]]'' (''Bu liaoqing'', 1947)<ref>{{Cite web |last=Rea |first=Christopher |date=1947-02-14 |title=Love Everlasting 不了情 (1947) |url=https://chinesefilmclassics.org/love-everlasting-1947/ |access-date=2023-03-23 |website=Chinese Film Classics |language=en-US}}</ref> and ''[[Fake Bride, Phony Bridegroom]]'' (1947).<ref>Pickowicz, Paul G. "Chinese Film-making on the Eve of the Communist Revolution", in ''The Chinese Cinema Book'', edited by Song Hwee Lim and Julian Ward (2011). BFI: Palgrave Macmillan, p. 80–81.</ref> Another memorable Wenhua film is ''[[Long Live the Missus]]'' (1947),<ref>{{Cite web |title=Module 8: Long Live the Missus! (1947) |url=https://chinesefilmclassics.org/course/module-8-long-live-the-missus-1947/ |access-date=2023-03-23 |website=Chinese Film Classics |language=en-US}}</ref> like ''Love Everlasting'' with an original screenplay by writer [[Eileen Chang]]. Wenhua's romantic drama, ''[[Spring in a Small Town]]'' (1948),<ref>{{Cite web |date=26 September 1948 |title=Spring in a Small Town 小城之春 (1948) |url=https://chinesefilmclassics.org/spring-in-a-small-town-1948/}}</ref> directed by [[Fei Mu]]<ref>{{Cite web |last=Rea |first=Christopher |date=22 April 2021 |title=Fei Mu 費穆 |url=https://chinesefilmclassics.org/fei-mu-%E8%B2%BB%E7%A9%86/ |accessdate=30 December 2023 |website=Chinese Film Classics}}</ref> shortly prior to the revolution, is often regarded by Chinese film critics as one of the most important films in the history of Chinese cinema, in 2005, Hong Kong film awards it as the best 100 years of film.<ref>{{cite web |year=2004 |title=Welcome to the Hong Kong Film Awards |url=http://www.hkfaa.com/news/100films.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191022211054/http://www.hkfaa.com/news/100films.html |archive-date=22 October 2019 |access-date=2007-04-04}}</ref> Ironically, it was precisely its artistic quality and apparent lack of "political grounding" that led to its labeling by the CCP as rightist or reactionary, and the film was quickly forgotten by those on the mainland following the CCP's victory in 1949.<ref>Zhang Yingjin, "Introduction" in ''Cinema and Urban Culture in Shanghai, 1922–1943'', ed. Yingjin Zhang (Stanford: Stanford University Press, 1999), p. 8.</ref> However, with the China Film Archive's re-opening after the [[Cultural Revolution]], a new print was struck from the original negative, allowing ''Spring of the Small Town'' to find a new and admiring audience and to influence an entire new generation of filmmakers. Indeed, an acclaimed [[Springtime in a Small Town|remake]] was made in 2002 by [[Tian Zhuangzhuang]]. A Chinese Peking opera film, ''[[A Wedding in the Dream]]'' (1948), by the same director (Fei Mu), was the first Chinese [[Color motion picture film|color film]].{{citation needed|date=December 2025}}

== Early People's Republic of China ==

=== Film infrastructure ===
At the founding of the People's Republic of China (PRC) in 1949, there were fewer than 600 movie theaters in the country.<ref name=":12">{{Cite book |last=Li |first=Jie |title=Material Contradictions in Mao's China |date=2022 |publisher=[[University of Washington Press]] |isbn=978-0-295-75085-9 |editor-last=Altehenger |editor-first=Jennifer |location=Seattle |chapter=Mobile Projectionists and the Things They Carried |doi=10.7312/li--20626-004 |editor-last2=Ho |editor-first2=Denise Y.}}</ref>{{Rp|page=102}} The PRC government solved the problem of a lack of film theaters by building mobile projection units which could tour the remote regions of China, ensuring that even the poorest could have access to films. The vast majority of China's people lived in rural areas, and most people in China had not seen a film until mobile projectionists brought them.<ref name=":1" />{{Rp|page=148}}

Yuan Muzhi was important in developing the government's theories and practices of rural film exhibition.<ref name=":1" />{{Rp|page=46}} Yuan and Chen Bo'er transformed the post-Second Sino-Japanese War remnants of the Manchurian Motion Picture Association into the Northeast Film Studio and when Yuan became Film Bureau chief in 1949, he applied its model to help institute a film exhibition network around the country.<ref name=":1" />{{Rp|page=46}} The Northeast Film Studio also trained the first generation of communist Chinese documentary filmmakers.<ref name=":Qian" />{{Rp|page=103}} In 1950, 1,800 projectionists from around the country traveled to Nanjing for a training program.<ref name=":1" />{{Rp|page=71}} These projectionists replicated the training program in their own home provinces to create more projectionists.<ref name=":1" />{{Rp|page=71}} Nanjing was later termed a "Cradle of People's Cinema."<ref name=":1" />{{Rp|page=71}}

The PRC sought to recruit [[Women in China|women]] and [[Ethnic minorities in China|ethnic minority]] projectionists in an effort to more effectively reach marginalized communities.<ref name=":1" />{{Rp|page=72}} Rural mobile projectionist teams and urban movie theaters were generally managed through the PRC's cultural bureaucracy.<ref name=":1" />{{Rp|page=47}}  Mobile projection teams during the Mao era typically included three to four workers who physically transported film infrastructure through a large geographic area mostly not covered by any electrical grid.<ref name=":12" />{{Rp|page=102}} Trade Unions and PLA propaganda departments also operated film exhibition networks.<ref name=":1" />{{Rp|page=47}} Work as a mobile projectionist was physically and technically demanding.<ref name=":12" />{{Rp|page=104}} As a result, women projectionists and all-women mobile projection teams were promoted in Chinese media as examples of advancing gender equality under socialism.<ref name=":12" />{{Rp|pages=104–105}}

Until the profusion of mobile projectionist teams in the 1950s, most rural people had not seen a film.<ref name=":12" />{{Rp|page=103}} The number of movie-viewers hence increased sharply, partly bolstered by the fact that film tickets were given out to work units and attendance was compulsory,<ref name="Ward, Julian 2011 p. 88" /> with admissions rising from 47 million in 1949 to 4.15 billion in 1959.<ref name="Bordwell and Thompson 2010 371">{{cite book |last=Bordwell and Thompson |title=Film History: An Introduction |publisher=McGraw-Hill Companies, Inc |year=2010 |isbn=978-0-07-338613-3 |edition=Third |location=New York |page=371}}</ref> By 1965 there were around 20,393 mobile film units.<ref name="Yau, Esther 1997 p. 694" /> During the course of the Mao era, the majority of films were shown by such units, with only a minority watched in theaters.<ref name=":12" />{{Rp|page=103}}

In the 1950s and the 1960s, the CCP built cinemas (among other cultural buildings) in industrial districts on urban peripheries.<ref name=":1" />{{Rp|page=148}} These structures were influenced by Soviet architecture and were intended to be vivacious but not "palatial."<ref name=":1" />{{Rp|pages=148–149}}

In 1953, the non-state film industry was nationalized.<ref name=":22222">{{Cite book |last=Pickowicz |first=Paul G. |title=Revolutionary Natures: Grassroots Environmental Histories of China's Mao Era |publisher=[[University of Washington Press]] |year=2026 |isbn=9780295754383 |editor-last=Muscolino |editor-first=Micah S. |chapter=Independent Visualizations of China's Environmental Crisis}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=287}}

=== Film themes and content ===
The government saw motion pictures as an important artform and tool for mass [[Propaganda in China|propaganda]]. The Soviet-led collaborations ''Victory of the Chinese People'' (1950) and ''[[The New China|Liberated China]]'' (1951) were among the biggest film events in the PRC's early years.<ref name=":Qian" />{{Rp|page=17}} ''Victory of the Chinese People'' depicted re-enactments of four of the CCP's major military victories and was filmed using real ammunition with the participation of the [[People's Liberation Army]].<ref name=":Qian" />{{Rp|page=15}}

From the founding of the PRC through the 1970s, scientific education films were a major genre.<ref name=":1222">{{Cite book |last=Mi |first=You |title=Machine Decision Is Not Final: China and the History and Future of Artificial Intelligence |publisher=Urbanomic, [[MIT Press]] |year=2025 |isbn=9781913029999 |editor-last=Bratton |editor-first=Benjamin |chapter=A Different Endpoint: Qian Xuesen and Cosmotechnics |editor-last2=Greenspan |editor-first2=Anna |editor-last3=Ireland |editor-first3=Amy |editor-last4=Konior |editor-first4=Bogna}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=107}} Addressing topics like hygiene, modern production methods, communal organisation, and agricultural methods, these films were intended to advance modernisation while conveying a sense of collective progress.<ref name=":1222" />{{Reference page|page=107}}

The private studios in Shanghai, including Kunming, Wenhua, Guotai, and Datong, were at first encouraged to make new films. They made approximately 47 films during the next two years but soon ran into trouble, owing to the furor over the Kunlun-produced drama ''[[The Life of Wu Xun]]'' (1950), directed by Sun Yu and starring veteran Zhao Dan. In an anonymous article in ''[[People's Daily]]'' in May 1951, the feature was accused of spreading feudal ideas. After the article was revealed to be penned by [[Mao Zedong]], the film was banned, the Film Steering Committee was formed to "re-educate" the film industry, and the private studios were all incorporated into the state-run [[Shanghai Film Studio]].<ref name="Yau, Esther 1997 p. 694">Yau, Esther. "China After the Revolution", in ''The Oxford History of World Cinema'', edited by Geoffrey Nowell-Smith (1997). Oxford: Oxford University Press, p. 694.</ref><ref name="Ward, Julian 2011 p. 88">Ward, Julian. "The Remodelling of a National Cinema: Chinese Films of the Seventeen Years (1949–66)", in ''The Chinese Cinema Book'', edited by Song Hwee Lim and Julian Ward (2011). BFI: Palgrave Macmillan, p. 88.</ref>

After the establishment of the PRC, China's cultural bureaucracy described American films as screen-opium and began criticizing American film alongside anti-drug campaigns.<ref name=":1" />{{Rp|pages=225–226}} The Chinese Communist Party (CCP) sought to tighten control over mass media, producing instead movies centering on peasants, soldiers, and workers, such as ''[[Bridge (1949 film)|Bridge]]'' (1949) and ''[[The White-Haired Girl]]'' (1950).<ref name="Yau, Esther 1997 p. 694" /> One of the production bases in the middle of all the transition was the [[Changchun Film Studio]]. American films were banned as part of the [[Korean War]] effort.<ref name=":1" />{{Rp|pages=225–226}}

In 1950s China, a common view of film was that it served as "socialist distance horizon education".<ref name=":1" />{{Rp|page=24}} For example, films promoted [[People's commune|rural collectivization]].<ref name=":1" />{{Rp|page=24}} Cinema also sought to develop the [[Proletariat|proletarian]] [[class consciousness]] of rural workers, encouraging the industrialization and militarization of their labor.<ref name=":1" />{{Rp|page=50}} Film projection teams operating in rural China were asked to incorporate [[Magic lantern|lantern slides]] into their work to introduce national policies and political campaigns.<ref name=":1" />{{Rp|page=82}}

Between 1949 and 1957, China imported more than 1,300 films, two-thirds of them from the Soviet Union.<ref name=":022">{{Cite book |last=Healy|first=Gavin|title=A Guide to Mao's China: Showing the Nation to Foreign Guests|date=2026|publisher=[[Cornell University Press]]|isbn=9781501785900|location=Ithaca and London|series=Histories and Cultures of Tourism series}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=83}}

In the 17 years between the founding of the [[People's Republic of China]] and the Cultural Revolution, 603 feature films and 8,342 reels of documentaries and [[newsreel]]s were produced, sponsored mostly as CCP propaganda by the government, according to the state-run [[China Internet Information Center]].<ref>{{cite web |author=Li Xiao |date=2004-01-17 |title=Film Industry in China |url=http://www.china.org.cn/english/features/film/84966.htm |access-date=2007-02-27 |website=[[China Internet Information Center]] |publisher=}}</ref> For example, in ''[[Guerrilla on the Railroad]]'' (铁道游击队), dated 1956, the Chinese Communist Party was depicted as the primary resistance force against the Second Sino-Japanese War.<ref>{{Citation |chapter=4 The Purloined Lantern: Maoist Semiotics and Public Discourse in Early PRC Film and Drama |date=2003-05-12 |title=Witness Against History |pages=106–128 |publisher=[[Stanford University Press]] |doi=10.1515/9781503624146-009 |isbn=978-1-5036-2414-6}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=111}} Chinese filmmakers were sent to [[Moscow]] to study the [[Soviet Union|Soviet]] [[socialist realism]] style of filmmaking.<ref name="Bordwell and Thompson 2010 371" /> The [[Beijing Film Academy]] was established in 1950 and officially opened in 1956. One important film of this era is ''[[This Life of Mine (1950 film)|This Life of Mine]]'' (1950), directed by Shi Hu, which follows an old beggar reflecting on his past life as a policeman working for the various regimes since 1911.<ref>{{cite book |last=Bordwell and Thompson |title=Film History: An Introduction |publisher=McGraw-Hill Companies, Inc |year=2010 |isbn=978-0-07-338613-3 |edition=Third |location=New York |pages=371–372}}</ref><ref>Ward, Julian. "The Remodelling of a National Cinema: Chinese Films of the Seventeen Years (1949–66)", in ''The Chinese Cinema Book'', edited by Song Hwee Lim and Julian Ward (2011). BFI: Palgrave Macmillan, p. 90.</ref> The first [[widescreen]] Chinese film was produced in 1960. [[Animations|Animated films]] using a variety of [[Chinese folk art|folk arts]], such as [[Chinese paper art|papercuts]], [[Shadow theatre|shadow plays]], [[Glove puppetry|puppetry]], and [[Chinese painting|traditional paintings]], also were very popular for entertaining and educating children. The most famous of these, the classic ''[[Havoc in Heaven]]'' (two parts, 1961, 4), was made by [[Wan Laiming]] of the [[Wan Brothers]] and won the Outstanding Film award at the [[London International Film Festival]].

Films such as ''The White-Haired Girl'' and ''Serf'' were part of a genre of redemptive melodramas, which sought to encourage audiences to "speak bitterness".<ref name=":1" />{{Rp|page=183}}

After the [[China–United Kingdom relations|United Kingdom and the PRC]] established diplomatic relations, cultural exchanges between the two countries gradually resumed, including British moves being made available in China.<ref name=":Gao">{{Cite book |last=Gao |first=Yunxiang |title=Arise, Africa! Roar, China! Black and Chinese Citizens of the World in the Twentieth Century |date=2021 |publisher=[[University of North Carolina Press]] |isbn=9781469664606 |location=Chapel Hill, NC}}</ref>{{Rp|page=107}}

The thawing of censorship in 1956–57 (known as the [[Hundred Flowers Campaign]]) and in the early 1960s led to more indigenous Chinese films being made, which were less reliant on their Soviet counterparts.<ref>{{cite book |last=Bordwell and Thompson |title=Film History: An Introduction |publisher=McGraw-Hill Companies, Inc |year=2010 |isbn=978-0-07-338613-3 |edition=Third |location=New York |page=373}}</ref> During this campaign the sharpest criticisms came from the satirical comedies of [[Lü Ban]]. ''[[Before the New Director Arrives]]'' exposes the hierarchical relationships occurring between the cadres, while his next film, ''[[The Unfinished Comedy]]'' (1957), was labeled as a "poisonous weed" during the [[Anti-Rightist Movement]], and Lü was banned from directing for life.<ref>Yau, Esther. "China After the Revolution", in ''The Oxford History of World Cinema'', edited by Geoffrey Nowell-Smith (1997). Oxford: Oxford University Press, p. 695.</ref><ref>Ward, Julian. "The Remodelling of a National Cinema: Chinese Films of the Seventeen Years (1949–66)", in ''The Chinese Cinema Book'', edited by Song Hwee Lim and Julian Ward (2011). BFI: Palgrave Macmillan, pp. 92–93.</ref> Other noteworthy films produced during this period were adaptations of literary classics, such as [[Sang Hu]]'s ''[[The New Year's Sacrifice]]'' (1956, adapted from a [[Lu Xun]] story) and [[Shui Hua]]'s ''[[The Lin Family Shop]]'' (1959, adapted from a [[Mao Dun]] story). The most prominent filmmaker of this era was [[Xie Jin]], whose three films in particular, ''[[Woman Basketball Player No. 5]]'' (1957), ''[[The Red Detachment of Women (1961 film)|The Red Detachment of Women]]'' (1961), and ''[[Two Stage Sisters]]'' (1964), exemplify China's increased expertise in filmmaking. Films made during this period are polished, exhibiting high production value and elaborate sets.<ref>{{cite book |last=Bordwell and Thompson |title=Film History: An Introduction |publisher=McGraw-Hill Companies, Inc |year=2010 |isbn=978-0-07-338613-3 |edition=Third |location=New York |pages=372–373}}</ref> While Beijing and Shanghai remained the main centers of production, between 1957 and 1960 the government built regional studios in [[Guangzhou]], [[Xi'an]], and [[Chengdu]] to encourage representation of ethnic minorities in films. Chinese cinema began to directly address the issue of such ethnic minorities during the late 1950s and early 1960s in films like ''[[Five Golden Flowers]]'' (1959), ''[[Third Sister Liu]]'' (1960), ''[[Serfs (1963 film)|Serfs]]'' (1963), and ''[[Ashima (poem)|Ashima]]'' (1964).<ref>{{cite book |last=Bordwell and Thompson |title=Film History: An Introduction |publisher=McGraw-Hill Companies, Inc |year=2010 |isbn=978-0-07-338613-3 |edition=Third |location=New York |pages=370–373}}</ref><ref>Yau, Esther. "China After the Revolution", in ''The Oxford History of World Cinema'', edited by Geoffrey Nowell-Smith (1997). Oxford: Oxford University Press, p. 696.</ref>

On 9 March 1958, the [[Ministry of Culture (China)|Ministry of Culture]] held a meeting to introduce a Great Leap Forward in cinema.<ref name=":Qian" />{{Rp|pages=149–150}} During the Great Leap Forward, the film industry rapidly expanded, with documentary films being the genre that experienced the greatest growth.<ref name=":Qian" />{{Rp|page=150}} Trends in documentary film included "artistic documentaries," in which actors and non-actors reenacted events.<ref name=":Qian" />{{Rp|page=15}}  Film venues also expanded rapidly, including both urban cinemas and mobile projection units.<ref name=":Qian" />{{Rp|page=150}}

As part of the [[Socialist Education Movement]], mobile film projectionist units showed films and slideshows that emphasized class struggle and encouraged audience members to discuss bitter experiences onstage.<ref name=":1" />{{Rp|page=184}} New films termed "emphasis films" were released to coincide with the campaign, and the film version of ''The White-Haired Girl'' was re-released.<ref name=":1" />{{Rp|page=185}}

In 1965, China launched the Resist America, Aid Vietnam campaign in response to the [[Vietnam War|U.S. bombing of North Vietnam]].<ref name=":Minami2">{{Cite book |last=Minami |first=Kazushi |title=People's Diplomacy: How Americans and Chinese Transformed US-China Relations during the Cold War |date=2024 |publisher=[[Cornell University Press]] |isbn=9781501774157 |location=Ithaca, NY}}</ref>{{Rp|page=29}} To promote campaign themes denouncing U.S. imperialism and promoted Vietnamese resistance, the CCP used film exhibitions and other cultural media.<ref name=":Minami2" />{{Rp|page=29}}

== Films of the Cultural Revolution ==
During the Cultural Revolution, the film industry was severely restricted. Almost all previous films were banned, and only a few new ones were produced, the [[revolutionary model opera]]s. The most notable of these was a [[ballet]] version of the revolutionary opera ''[[The Red Detachment of Women (1970 film)|The Red Detachment of Women]]'', directed by Pan Wenzhan and Fu Jie in 1970.

The release of filmed versions of the revolutionary model operas resulted in a re-organization and expansion of China's film exhibition network.<ref name=":1" />{{Rp|page=73}} From 1965 to 1976, the number of film projection units in China quadrupled, total film audiences nearly tripled, and the national film attendance rate doubled.<ref name=":1" />{{Rp|page=133}} The [[Cultural Revolution Group]] drastically reduced ticket prices which, in its view, would allow film to better serve the needs of workers and of socialism.<ref name=":1" />{{Rp|page=133}}

In addition to films deemed laudatory, from the middle of 1966 to 1968, the expanding film distribution network screened films characterized as "poisonous weeds" to hundreds of millions of audience members for the purpose of criticizing the films.<ref name=":1" />{{Rp|page=232}} These criticism screenings were sometimes accompanied by [[struggle session]]s.<ref name=":1" />{{Rp|page=233}}

[[Sent-down youth]] were a major subset of China's rural projectionists during the Cultural Revolution period.<ref name=":1" />{{Rp|page=75}}

Feature film production came almost to a standstill in the early years from 1967 to 1972. Movie production revived after 1972 under the strict jurisdiction of the [[Gang of Four]] until 1976, when they were overthrown. The few films that were produced during this period, such as 1975's ''[[Breaking with Old Ideas]]'', were highly regulated in terms of plot and characterization.<ref>Zhang, Yingjin & Xiao, Zhiwei. "Breaking with Old Ideas" in ''Encyclopedia of Chinese Film''. Taylor & Francis (1998), p. 101. {{ISBN|0-415-15168-6}}.</ref>

In 1972, Chinese officials invited [[Michelangelo Antonioni]] to China to film the achievements of the Cultural Revolution.<ref name=":02">{{Cite book |last=Sorace |first=Christian |title=Afterlives of Chinese Communism: Political Concepts from Mao to Xi |date=2019 |publisher=[[Australian National University Press]] |isbn=9781760462499 |location=Acton, Australia |chapter=Aesthetics}}</ref>{{Rp|page=13}} Antonioni made the documentary ''[[Chung Kuo, Cina]]''.<ref name=":02" />{{Rp|page=13}} When it was released in 1974, CCP leadership in China interpreted the film as [[reactionary]] and anti-Chinese.<ref name=":02" />{{Rp|page=13}} Viewing art through the principles of the [[Yan'an Forum|Yan'an Talks]], particularly the concept that there is no such thing as art-for-art's-sake, party leadership construed Antonioni's aesthetic choices as politically motivated and banned the film.<ref name=":02" />{{Rp|page=14}} [[Jiang Qing]] criticized Premier [[Zhou Enlai]]'s role in Antonioni's invitation to China as not only a failure but also treasonous.<ref name=":Minami2" />{{Rp|page=121}} Since its 2004 release in China, the film has been well-regarded by Chinese audiences, especially for its beautiful depictions of a more simple time.<ref name=":02" />{{Rp|page=14}}

Because China rejection of most foreign film importation, comparatively minor cinema like [[Cinema of Albania|Albanian cinema]] and [[Cinema of North Korea|North Korean cinema]] developed mass audiences in China.<ref name=":1" />{{Rp|page=207}} Through Albanian films screened during this period, many Chinese audience members were introduced to [[avant-garde]] and modernist storytelling techniques and aesthetics.<ref name=":1" />{{Rp|page=206–207}}

== Post-Cultural Revolution ==

=== Box office boom after the Cultural Revolution ===
In the years immediately following the Cultural Revolution, the film industry again flourished as a medium of popular entertainment. Production rose steadily, from 19 features in 1977 to 125 in 1986.<ref>{{cite book |last=Bordwell and Thompson |title=Film History: An Introduction |publisher=McGraw-Hill Companies, Inc |year=2010 |isbn=978-0-07-338613-3 |edition=Third |location=New York |page=638}}</ref> Domestically produced films played to large audiences, and tickets for foreign [[film festival]]s sold quickly. The industry tried to revive crowds by making more innovative and "exploratory" films like their counterparts in the West.{{citation needed|date=November 2021}}

Chinese cinema grew significantly in the late 1970s. In 1979, annual box office admissions reached a peak of {{nowrap|29.3 billion}} tickets sold, equivalent to an average of {{nowrap|30 films}} per person. Chinese cinema continued to prosper into the early 1980s. In 1980, annual box office admissions stood at {{nowrap|23.4 billion}} tickets sold, equivalent to an average of {{nowrap|29 films}} per person.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Zhang |first1=Rui |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xUXqAQAAQBAJ&pg=PA22 |title=The Cinema of Feng Xiaogang: Commercialization and Censorship in Chinese Cinema after 1989 |date=1 September 2008 |publisher=[[Hong Kong University Press]] |isbn=978-962-209-885-5 |page=22}}</ref> In terms of [[List of films by box office admissions|box office admissions]], this period represented the peak ticket sales in the history of the Chinese box office.<ref>{{Cite book |author=赵子忠 (Zhào Zizhōng) |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7Be2AAAAIAAJ |title=中国影视投融资的产业透视 |date=2006 |publisher=中国传媒大学出版社 ([[Communication University of China|Communication University of China Press]]) |isbn=978-7-81085-720-8 |page=179 |language=zh |trans-title=An Industry Perspective of China's Film and Television Investment and Financing |quote=1979 年中国大陆生产的影片只有 50 多部,但观众人次达到了 279 亿,平均每天有 7 千万人次的观众看电影,创造了中国电影票房史上 |trans-quote=In 1979, there were only more than {{nowrap|50 films}} produced in mainland China, but the number of viewers reached {{nowrap|27.9 billion}}, and an average of {{nowrap|70 million}} viewers watched films every day, creating history at the box office in China}}</ref> High ticket sales were driven by low ticket prices, with a cinema ticket typically costing between [[Renminbi|¥]]0.1 ({{US$|{{To USD|0.1|CHN|year=1979}}|long=no}}) and ¥0.3 ({{US$|{{To USD|0.3|CHN|year=1979}}|long=no}}) at the time.<ref name="Link">{{cite book |last1=Link |first1=Perry |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qhBYxOitb-MC&pg=PA204 |title=The Uses of Literature: Life in the Socialist Chinese Literary System |date=2000 |publisher=[[Princeton University Press]] |isbn=978-0-691-00198-2 |page=204}}</ref>

By the early 1980s, there were 162,000 projection units in China, primarily composed of mobile movie teams which showed films outdoors in both rural and urban areas.<ref name=":12" />{{Rp|page=102}}

A number of films during this period drew box office admissions in the hundreds of millions. [[List of highest-grossing films in China|China's highest-grossing film]] in box office admissions was ''[[List of media adaptations of the Legend of the White Snake|Legend of the White Snake]]'' (1980) with an estimated {{nowrap|700 million}} admissions,<ref name=":9">{{Cite journal |year=1985 |title=Fujian xi ju: Fujianxiju |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3HIxAAAAMAAJ |journal=福建省戯劇年鑑 (Fujian Drama Yearbook) |language=zh |location=[[Fujian]] |publisher=中国戏剧家协会福建分会 (Fujian Branch of China Dramatists Association) |issue=1–6 |page=11 |quote=近年拍摄的戏曲片《白蛇传》观众人数最多,达七亿人次、《七品芝麻官》五亿人次。 |trans-quote=In recent years, the opera film "Legend of the White Snake" has the largest audience, reaching {{nowrap|700 million}} people, and "Sesame Official" with {{nowrap|500 million}} people.}}</ref><ref name=":8">{{Cite news |date=2014-12-29 |script-title=zh:回望中国电影20年 从5亿人看《少林寺》到票房1日破亿 |trans-title=Looking back at Chinese movies over 20 years, from 500 million people watching |language=zh}}</ref> followed by {{Interlanguage link|In-Laws (Full House of Joy)|lt=''In-Laws'' (''Full House of Joy'')|zh|喜盈門}} (1981) and ''The Undaunted Wudang'' (1983) with more than {{nowrap|600 |page=161 |language=zh |trans-title=China Film Yearbook |quote=近四年来城乡观众人次超过 1 亿的影片有:《喜盈门》 6 亿 5 千万,《武当》 6 亿 1 千万,《少林弟子》 5 亿 2 千万,《武林志》 5 亿,《从奴隶到将军》 4 亿 7 千万,《西安事变》 4 亿 5 千万,《吉鸿昌》 3 亿 8 千万,《开枪,为他送行》 3
