==== Early 20th century ====
[[File:Thedarose.jpg|thumb|Actress Theda Bara, in the 1915 film ''[[A Fool There Was (1915 film)|A Fool There Was]]'']]
[[Mrs Patrick Campbell]], [[George Bernard Shaw]]'s "second famed platonic love affair", (she published some of his letters)<ref>{{cite book|last1=Campbell|first1=Mrs Patrick|title=My Life and Some Letters|date=1922|publisher=Dodd, Mead and Company|location=New York|url=https://archive.org/details/mylifesomeletter00camp|access-date=9 October 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine|title=Shaw's Vampire|date=April 22, 1940|magazine=[[Time (magazine)|Time]]|url=http://www.time.com/time/magazine/article/0,9171,763873,00.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090321043453/http://www.time.com/time/magazine/article/0,9171,763873,00.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=March 21, 2009|access-date=August 9, 2008}}<!-- https://darkclassics.blogspot.com/2011/01/philip-burne-jones-vampire.html --></ref> and [[Philip Burne-Jones]]'s lover and subject of his 1897 painting, ''The Vampire'', inspired Burne-Jones's cousin [[Rudyard Kipling]] to write his poem "The Vampire", in the year [[Dracula]] was published.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://poets.org/poem/vampire-0|title = The Vampire by Rudyard Kipling – Poems &#124; Academy of American Poets}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.bl.uk/collection-items/first-edition-of-dracula|title=British Library|access-date=2021-07-25|archive-date=2021-07-25|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210725191816/https://www.bl.uk/collection-items/first-edition-of-dracula|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://artmagick.com/pictures/picture.aspx?id=7427&name=the-vampire |title=Archived copy |website=artmagick.com |access-date=17 January 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100207235200/http://artmagick.com/pictures/picture.aspx?id=7427&name=the-vampire |archive-date=7 February 2010 |url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|url=https://muse.jhu.edu/article/479931/summary |title=Project MUSE - Rudyard Kipling, The Vampire, and the Actress |journal=English Literature in Transition, 1880-1920|date=2012 |volume=55 |issue=3 |pages=303–314 |last1=Mitchell |first1=J. Lawrence }}</ref> <!--Rudyard Kipling, The Vampire, and the Actress J. Lawrence Mitchell English Literature in Transition, 1880–1920 ELT Press Volume 55, Number 3, 2012 pp. 303–314 -->The poem, which began: "A fool there was&nbsp;...",<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Vampire_(Kipling)|title=The Vampire|first=Rudyard|last=Kipling|via=Wikisource}}</ref> inspired [[Porter Emerson Browne]] to write the play, ''A Fool There Was''.

The poem was adapted to become a 1909 [[Broadway theatre|Broadway]] production. This was followed by The 1913 film ''[[The Vampire (1913 film)|The Vampire]]'' by [[Robert Vignola]], containing a "vamp" dance.<ref>John T. Soister, ''American Silent Horror, Science Fiction and Fantasy Feature Films, 1913–1929'', McFarland, 2012, p. 41</ref> Protagonist [[Alice Hollister]] was publicised as "the original vampire".<ref name=Kalem>{{cite book |title=Kalem Films The Lotus Woman|url=https://archive.org/details/moviewor28chal/page/n445?q=%22the+vampire%22+%22alice+hollister%22|publisher=[[Moving Picture World]]|year=1916|page=1074}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |title=Greenroom Jottings|url=https://archive.org/details/motionpicture191712chic|publisher=[[Motion Picture Story Magazine]]|date=1914|page=[https://archive.org/details/motionpicture191712chic/page/136 136]}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |title=Who's who in pictures|url=https://archive.org/details/motionpicturemag152moti|publisher=[[Motion Picture Magazine]]|date=1918|pages=[https://archive.org/details/motionpicturemag152moti/page/51 51]}}</ref> The 1915 film, [[A Fool There Was (1915 film)|''A Fool There Was'']], starring [[Theda Bara]], as "The Vamp" followed.<ref name="SilentEra">{{cite web|url=http://www.silentera.com/PSFL/data/F/FoolThereWas1915.html|title=Progressive Silent Film List: ''A Fool There Was'' |website=www.silentera.com}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.jewishvirtuallibrary.org/theda-bara|title=Theda Bara (1885–1955)|publisher=Jewish Virtual Library|access-date=April 21, 2021}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite book|title=Mondo Exotica: Sounds, Visions, Obsessions of the Cocktail Generation|last=Adinolfi|first=Francesco|date=2008|publisher=Duke University Press|location=Durham|page=24|oclc=179838406|isbn=9780822341321|translator-last=Pinkus|translator-first=Karen|translator-last2=Vivrette|translator-first2=Jason}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.vaultofthoughts.com/2014/05/31/vamping-it-up/|title = Vamping It up: Rudyard Kipling, Theda Bara & the 20th Century Femme Fatale|date = 31 May 2014}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.qbbooks.com/pages/books/52956/rudyard-kipling/the-vampire|title=The Vampire by Rudyard Kipling on Quill & Brush, Inc|access-date=2021-07-25|archive-date=2021-07-25|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210725191824/https://www.qbbooks.com/pages/books/52956/rudyard-kipling/the-vampire|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://onlinebooks.library.upenn.edu/webbin/book/lookupid?key=ha010824184|title = The vampire : A poem : Written for a picture by Philip Burne-Jones exhibited at the New Gallery in London, 1897 /, by Rudyard Kipling &#124; the Online Books Page}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nrMrAQAAMAAJ|title=The Vampire: A Poem : Written for a Picture by Philip Burne-Jones Exhibited at the New Gallery in London, 1897|last1=Kipling|first1=Rudyard|year=1898}}</ref> The short poem may have been used in the publicity for the 1915 film.{{citation needed|date=September 2019}} 1910s [[American English|American]] [[slang]] for ''femme fatale'' was  ''vamp'', for ''vampire''.<ref>Per the Oxford English Dictionary, ''vamp'' is originally English, used first by [[G. K. Chesterton]], but popularized in the American silent film ''The Vamp'', starring [[Enid Bennett]]</ref><ref>[http://www.oed.com/search?searchType=dictionary&q=Vamp&_searchBtn=Search "Vamp", Oxford English Dictionary]; retrieved 30 December 2016</ref><ref name=":1" />

Another icon of the time was Margaretha Geertruida Zelle. While working as an exotic dancer, she took the stage name [[Mata Hari]]. She was accused of German espionage during [[World War I]] and was put to death by a French firing squad. After her death she became the subject of many sensational films and books, including, but not limited to: [[Mata Hari (1927 film)|Mata Hari]] (1927), [[Dishonored (film)|Dishonored]] (1931), [[Up the Front]] (1972).<ref>{{Cite web |title=Mata Hari {{!}} History {{!}} Research Starters {{!}} EBSCO Research |url=https://www.ebsco.com/ |access-date=2026-07-12 |website=EBSCO |language=en}}</ref>

''Femmes fatales'' appear widely in [[detective fiction]], especially in its 'hard-boiled' sub-genre, which largely originated with the crime stories of [[Dashiell Hammett]] in the 1920s.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Sexton |first=Megan |title='The stuff dreams are made of' |url=https://www.sc.edu/uofsc/posts/2015/05_dashiell_hammett_collection_unveiled_at_uofsc_libraries.php |access-date=2026-07-12 |website=University of South Carolina |language=en}}</ref> A tone that carried through to the 1930's in which one fictional French-Canadian villainess, Marie de Sabrevois, gave a contemporary edge to "one of America's most Popular historical novelists<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title='At the nadir of 'discouragement': The Story Of Dartmouth's Kenneth Roberts Collection |url=https://www.dartmouth.edu/library/Library_Bulletin/Apr1990/LB-A90-Bales.html |access-date=2026-07-12 |website=www.dartmouth.edu}}</ref>", [[Kenneth Roberts (author)|Kenneth Roberts]], set during the [[American Revolution]].<ref name=":2" />

A [[Jazz Age]] vamp (also known as a "baby vamp") was defined by [[F. Scott Fitzgerald]] in reference to one of his "careless" [[flapper]] characters, as a [[siren (mythology)|siren]] - 'a picker up and thrower away of men, an unscrupulous and fundamentally unmoved toyer with affections.'<ref>{{Cite book | last = Fitzgerald | first = F. Scott | author-link = F. Scott Fitzgerald | title = The Beautiful and Damned | year = 1922 | publisher = [[Charles Scribner's Sons]] | location = New York | url = https://archive.org/details/beautifuldamned00fitzrich_202012 | url-access = registration | via = Internet Archive}}, Collins Classic Paperback 2013, pp. 27 & 88.</ref> [[Greta Garbo]] and [[Marlene Dietrich]] were considered femme fatales in the late 1920s and early 1930s. A vamp, "was exotic, luxurious, and escapist, epitomizing the excess of the Roaring Twenties."<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |date=2017-04-06 |title=Silent Film Actresses and Their Most Popular Characters |url=https://www.womenshistory.org/articles/silent-film-actresses-and-their-most-popular-characters |access-date=2026-07-13 |website=National Women's History Museum |language=en}}</ref>

Film villainesses of this vamp variety often appeared foreign, mostly of Eastern European or Asian ancestry. They were a contrast to the wholesome, and virginal personas of actresses such as [[Lillian Gish]] and [[Mary Pickford]]. Notable silent-cinema vamps include [[Theda Bara]] and [[Anna May Wong]].<ref name=":3" />

==== Classic film noir era ====
[[File:Double-Indemnity-LIFE-1944-2.jpg|thumb|300px|left|''Femme fatale'' [[Phyllis Dietrichson]], played by [[Barbara Stanwyck]], in the classic film noir ''[[Double Indemnity]]'' ]]
During the era of classic [[film-noir]]s of the 1940s and 1950s, the ''femme fatale'' flourished in American cinema. The archetypal ''femme fatale'' is [[Phyllis Dietrichson]], played by [[Barbara Stanwyck]] (who was nominated for the [[Academy Award for Best Actress]] for this role) in the 1944 film ''[[Double Indemnity]]''. This character is considered one of the best ''femme fatale'' roles in film noir history.<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=Y04MQEgHbZsC&dq=phyllis+dietrichson+iconic+character&pg=PA130 History of American Cinema] accessed 1-4-2016</ref> The character was ranked as the #8 film villain of the first 100 years of American cinema by the [[American Film Institute]] in the [[AFI's 100 Years... 100 Heroes and Villains]].<ref name="AFI List">[http://www.afi.com/100Years/handv.aspx AFI List] accessed 1-4-2016</ref> In a classical film noir trope, she manipulates a man into killing her husband for financial gain.

Other examples of ''femme fatale'' include the [[Dorothy Dandridge]] as the titular character in ''[[Carmen Jones (film)|Carmen Jones]]'', Brigid O'Shaughnessy, portrayed by [[Mary Astor]], who murders Sam Spade's partner in ''[[The Maltese Falcon (1941 film)|The Maltese Falcon]]'' ([[1941 in film|1941]]); manipulative narcissistic daughter Veda (portrayed by [[Ann Blyth]]) in [[Mildred Pierce (1945 film)|''Mildred Pierce'']] who exploits her indulgent mother Mildred (portrayed by [[Joan Crawford]]) and fatally destroys her mother's remarriage to stepfather Monte Barragon (portrayed by [[Zachary Scott]]); [[Gene Tierney]] as Ellen Brent Harland in ''[[Leave Her to Heaven]]'' ([[1945 in film|1945]]), and the cabaret singer portrayed by [[Rita Hayworth]] in ''[[Gilda (film)|Gilda]]'' ([[1946 in film|1946]]),<ref name="Independent">{{cite news|last=Johnston |first=Sheila |title=Whatever happened to the femme fatale? |work=The Independent |date=27 February 2009 |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/films/features/whatever-happened-to-the-femme-fatale-1633088.html |access-date=27 February 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090228103849/http://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/films/features/whatever-happened-to-the-femme-fatale-1633088.html |archive-date=February 28, 2009 }}</ref> narcissistic wives who manipulate their husbands; [[Ava Gardner]] in ''[[The Killers (1946 film)|The Killers]]'' and Cora ([[Lana Turner]]) in ''[[The Postman Always Rings Twice (1946 film)|The Postman Always Rings Twice]]'', based on novels by [[Ernest Hemingway]] and [[James M. Cain]] respectively, manipulate men into killing their husbands.<ref name="Independent" />

In the [[Alfred Hitchcock|Hitchcock]] film ''[[The Paradine Case]]'' (1947), [[Alida Valli]]'s character causes the deaths of two men and the near destruction of another. Another frequently cited example is the character Jane played by [[Lizabeth Scott]] in ''[[Too Late for Tears]]'' (1949): during her quest to keep some dirty money from its rightful recipient and her husband, she uses poison, lies, sexual teasing and a gun to keep men wrapped around her finger. [[Jane Greer]] is notable as a murderous ''femme fatale'' using her wiles on [[Robert Mitchum]] in ''[[Out of the Past]]'' (1947). In ''[[Gun Crazy]]'' (1950), the ''femme fatale'' lures a man into a life of crime. In Hitchcock's [[Rebecca (1940 film)|1940 film]] and Daphne du Maurier's [[Rebecca (novel)|1938 novel]] ''Rebecca'', the eponymous ''femme fatale'' completely dominates the plot, even though she is already dead and we never see an image of her.

==== Since the 1980s ====
{{More citations needed section|date=January 2026}}
{{quote box|width=30%|align=right|quote=The femme fatale is one of the most mesmerizing of sexual personae. She is not a fiction but an extrapolation of biologic realities in women that remain constant.|source=''[[Sexual Personae]]'' (1990) by [[Camille Paglia]]<ref>{{cite book |author=Paglia, Camille |author-link=Camille Paglia |title=Sexual Personae: Art and Decadence from Nefertiti to Emily Dickinson |publisher=Yale University Press |location=London |year=1990 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/sexualpersonaear00pagl_1/page/16 16] |isbn=978-0-300-04396-9 |url=https://archive.org/details/sexualpersonaear00pagl_1/page/1}}</ref>}}
The ''femme fatale'' character has continued in films such as ''[[Body Heat]]'' (1981) and ''[[Prizzi's Honor]]'' (1985) – both with [[Kathleen Turner]], ''[[Blade Runner]]'' (1982) with [[Sean Young]], ''[[The Fourth Man (1983 film)|The Fourth Man]]'' (1983) with [[Renée Soutendijk]], ''[[The Hunger (1983 film)|The Hunger]]'' (1983) with [[Catherine Deneuve]], ''[[Blue Velvet (film)|Blue Velvet]]'' (1986) with [[Isabella Rossellini]], ''[[Fatal Attraction]]'' (1987) with [[Glenn Close]], ''[[Basic Instinct]]'' (1992) with [[Sharon Stone]], ''[[Damage (1992 film)|Damage]]'' (1992) with [[Juliette Binoche]], ''[[Final Analysis]]'' (1992) with [[Kim Basinger]], ''[[Dream Lover (1993 film)|Dream Lover]]'' (1993) with [[Mädchen Amick]], ''[[The Crush (1993 film)|The Crush]]'' (1993) with [[Alicia Silverstone]], ''[[Pulp Fiction]]'' (1994) with [[Uma Thurman]], ''[[The Last Seduction]]'' (1994) with [[Linda Fiorentino]], ''[[To Die For]]'' (1995) with [[Nicole Kidman]], ''[[Lost Highway (film)|Lost Highway]]'' (1997) with [[Patricia Arquette]], ''[[Devil in the Flesh (1998 film)|Devil in the Flesh]]'' (1998) and ''[[Jawbreaker (film)|Jawbreaker]]'' (1999), both with [[Rose McGowan]], ''[[Cruel Intentions]]'' (1999) with [[Sarah Michelle Gellar]], ''[[Original Sin (2001 film)|Original Sin]]'' (2001) with [[Angelina Jolie]], ''[[Femme Fatale (2002 film)|Femme Fatale]]'' (2002) with [[Rebecca Romijn]], ''[[Sherlock Holmes (2009 film)|Sherlock Holmes]]'' (2009) with [[Rachel McAdams]], and ''[[Jennifer's Body]]'' (2009) with [[Megan Fox]]. In 2013, [[Tania Raymonde]] played the [[Jodi Arias|title role]] in ''[[Jodi Arias: Dirty Little Secret]]''. In 2014, [[Eva Green]] portrayed a ''[[Ava Lord|femme fatale]]'' in ''[[Sin City: A Dame to Kill For]]'' and [[Rosamund Pike]] starred in ''[[Gone Girl (film)|Gone Girl]]''. In ''[[Babylon (2022 film)|Babylon]]'' (2022), [[Margot Robbie]] plays a character with ''femme fatale'' tendencies.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Le Roy |first=Félix |date=2023-01-31 |title=" Babylon " : Hollywood et ses fantômes |url=https://laregledujeu.org/2023/01/31/39037/babylon-hollywood-et-ses-fantomes/ |access-date=2023-04-03 |website=La Règle du Jeu |quote=Margot Robbie […] in the role of the incendiary blonde Nellie LaRoy, dancing like Salomé, plays a femme fatale who dreams of seeing her name rise, in letters of fire, at the top of the bill.}}</ref> [[Mia Goth]] has portrayed manipulative female antagonists in ''[[Pearl (2022 film)|Pearl]]'' (2022) and ''[[Infinity Pool (film)|Infinity Pool]]'' (2023). In 2026, [[Inde Navarrette]] starred as a crazed, obsessed character in ''[[Obsession (2025 film)|Obsession]]''.

Academy Award-winning actress [[Marion Cotillard]] has frequently played ''femmes fatales'', in such films as ''[[A Private Affair (2002 film)|A Private Affair]]'' (2002), ''[[A Very Long Engagement]]'', ''[[La Boîte noire|The Black Box]]'', ''[[Inception]]'', ''[[Midnight in Paris]]'', ''[[The Dark Knight Rises]]'' and ''[[Macbeth (2015 film)|Macbeth]]''. In addition to her role in ''To Die For'', Nicole Kidman has played ''femmes fatales'' in films such as ''[[Malice (1993 film)|Malice]]'', ''[[Moulin Rouge!]]'', ''[[The Paperboy (2012 film)|The Paperboy]]'', and ''[[The Northman]]''. Eva Green has also played a ''femme fatale'' witch in ''[[Dark Shadows (film)|Dark Shadows]]'' (2012).

The archetype is also abundant in American television. One of the most famous ''femmes fatales'' of American television is [[Sherilyn Fenn]]'s [[Audrey Horne]] in the [[David Lynch]] cult series ''[[Twin Peaks]]''. The horror anthology series ''[[American Horror Story]]'' has featured various cunning ''femme fatales'' played by [[Jessica Lange]]. The [[Showtime (TV network)|Showtime]] TV series ''[[Dexter (TV series)|Dexter]]'' included two major menacing female love interests of the [[Dexter Morgan|title character]]: [[Lila West]] and [[Hannah McKay]], played by [[Jaime Murray]] and [[Yvonne Strahovski]] respetively. In the TV series ''[[Femme Fatales (TV series)|Femme Fatales]]'', actress [[Tanit Phoenix]] played [[Lilith]], the host who introduced each episode [[Rod Serling]]-style and occasionally appeared within the narrative. In the [[Netflix]] TV series ''[[Orange Is the New Black]]'', actress [[Laura Prepon]] played [[Alex Vause]], a modern ''femme fatale'', who led both men and women to their destruction.

''Femmes fatales'' appear frequently in [[comic book]]s. Notable examples include [[Batman]]'s long-time nemesis [[Catwoman]], who first appeared in comics in 1940; various adversaries of [[The Spirit (character)|The Spirit]], such as [[P'Gell]];{{citation needed|date=August 2025}} and [[Tomie Kawakami]] the titular character of the horror manga ''[[Tomie]]''.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Yi |first=Lynn |date=2024-10-23 |title=Junji Ito’s Grotesquely Beautiful Femme Fatale|url=https://www.34st.com/article/2024/10/tomie-manga-junji-ito-anime-beauty-groteque-femme-fatale |access-date=2026-08-17 |website=34st Street |language=en-US}}</ref>

This stock character is also often found in the genres of opera and [[musical theatre]], where she will traditionally have a [[Mezzo-soprano|mezzo]], [[alto]] or [[contralto]] range, opposed to the [[ingénue]]'s [[soprano]], to symbolize the masculinity and lack of feminine purity.{{Citation needed|date=October 2022}} An example is Hélène from ''[[Natasha, Pierre and the Great Comet of 1812]]''.

In more recent years, ''femmes fatales'' have been incorporated into video games, an example of which being [[Ada Wong]] in the ''[[Resident Evil]]'' video game series.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Chan |first=Harri |date=2023-04-20 |title=Resident Evil's Ada Wong goes head-to-head with sexpionage stereotypes |url=https://www.polygon.com/23679586/resident-evil-4-re4-remake-ada-wong-stereotypes |access-date=2025-06-30 |website=Polygon |language=en-US}}</ref>

==Use in criminal trials==
The term has been used by the media in connection with highly publicised criminal trials, such as the trials of [[Amanda Knox]]<ref>{{Cite news|title = Amanda Knox is no femme fatale, defence lawyer says|work = BBC News|date = 27 September 2011|url = https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-15076916|access-date =30 April 2015}}</ref> and [[Murder of Travis Alexander|Jodi Arias]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.nydailynews.com/news/crime/jurors-hear-conflicting-persona-jodi-arias-trial-article-1.1237319|title = Jodi Arias: Femme fatale or woman of faith? Jurors hear conflicting persona in murder trial as prosecutors play phone calls of Arias lying|last = Ortiz|first = Erik}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title = Jodi Arias Trial Update: Lawyer Reveals Femme Fatale Was Terrified During Sentencing|date=15 April 2015 |url=http://www.newseveryday.com/articles/13812/20150415/jodi-arias-scared-death-lawyer-reveals.htm|access-date =30 April 2015}}</ref> Arias received the nickname "{{lang|fr|La Tueuse au visage d'ange}}" ("The Angel-Faced Killer") from the [[Mass media in France|French media]] during her high-profile 2013 trial.<ref>{{Cite web |date=6 June 2023 |title=Jodi Arias : 10 ans après son procès, que devient « la tueuse au visage d'ange » ? |url=https://www.parismatch.com/actu/faits-divers/jodi-arias-10-ans-apres-son-proces-mediatique-que-devient-la-tueuse-au-visage-dange-225929 |access-date=22 July 2026 |website=parismatch.com |language=fr}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=14 April 2015 |title=Prison à vie pour l'énigmatique tueuse - Fin du procès Jodi Arias |url=https://www.parismatch.com/actu/faits-divers/prison-vie-pour-lenigmatique-tueuse-fin-du-proces-jodi-arias-140243 |access-date=22 July 2026 |website=parismatch.com |language=fr}}</ref>

* Julie Grossman (2009) ''Rethinking the Femme Fatale in film noir: Ready for her close-up'', {{ISBN|9781349313341}}. Tries to bring about a more nuanced and sympathetic reading of the "femme fatale" in film criticism and popular culture commentary.
