sometimes known interchangeably as the broader '''classical''' or '''classical-industrial period''' (Spanish: ''período clásico-industrial''),<ref name="historiografia"/><ref name="trabajadores"/> is an era in the history of the [[cinema of Argentina]] that began in the 1930s and lasted until the 1940s or 1950s, depending on the definition,{{refn|group=note|name=date|It is generally agreed that the advent of the [[sound era]] in 1933 constituted the opening to industrialization in Argentine cinema.{{sfn|España|2000|p=23}} Film historian {{ill|Domingo Di Núbila|es|Domingo Di Núbila}}—who introduced the concept of the Golden Age—<ref name="manzano">{{cite journal|url=http://www.publicacions.ub.edu/bibliotecadigital/cinema/filmhistoria/2001/Cineargentino.htm#2b|language=es|last=Manzano|first=Valeria|accessdate=11 November 2022|title=Cine argentino y peronismo: cultura política y propaganda, 1946–1955|year=2001|volume=XI|issue=3|journal=Filmhistoria|issn=2014-668X|location=Barcelona|publisher=[[Universitat de Barcelona]]|archive-date=11 November 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221111190136/http://www.publicacions.ub.edu/bibliotecadigital/cinema/filmhistoria/2001/Cineargentino.htm#2b|url-status=live}}</ref> places the period between 1933 and 1942, the years of release of the films ''[[¡Tango!]]'' and ''[[La guerra gaucha]]'' respectively.{{sfn|Di Núbila|1998|p=71}}{{sfn|Di Núbila|1998|p=391}} Writers that equate the Golden Age to the so-called "classical" or "classical-industrial" period, like {{ill|Claudio España|es|Claudio España}} and his collaborators,{{sfn|España|2000|p=23}} date its end in 1956, with the crisis and decline of the [[studio system]].<ref name="edad">{{cite web|url=https://www.pagina12.com.ar/2001/suple/Radar/01-11/01-11-18/NOTA4.HTM|work=Radar. [[Página/12]]|accessdate=14 November 2022|title=Made in Argentina|language=es|date=18 November 2001|first=Mariano|last=Kairuz|archive-date=6 November 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221106224045/https://www.pagina12.com.ar/2001/suple/Radar/01-11/01-11-18/NOTA4.HTM|url-status=live}}</ref> According to {{ill|Fernando Martín Peña|es|Fernando Martín Peña}}, the Argentine film industry was consolidated as such around 1938 and ceased to exist around 1948,{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Introducción}} although he also wrote that the Golden Age ended definitively in 1956 with the crisis triggered by the [[Revolución Libertadora|new dictatorship]].{{sfn|Peña|2024|p=251}} Other authors, like Peter H. Rist and Jorge Finkielman, narrow the Golden Age between 1937 and 1942, the years of greatest production and international dominance.{{sfn|Rist|2014|p=4}}{{sfn|Finkielman|2004|p=213}}}} during which national [[Film industry|film production]] underwent a process of [[industrialization]] and [[standardization]] that involved the emergence of [[mass production]], the establishment of the [[Studio system|studio]], [[Film genre|genre]] and [[Star system (filmmaking)|star systems]], and the adoption of the [[institutional mode of representation]] (MRI) that was mainly—though not exclusively—spread by [[Cinema of the United States|Hollywood]],<ref name="trabajadores">{{cite journal |last=Alvira |first=Pablo |year=2014 |title=Representaciones de trabajadores/as en el cine clásico-industrial argentino: los mensúes, entre la denuncia y la tragedia |trans-title=Representations of workers in Argentine classic-industrial cinema: the mensúes, between denunciation and tragedy |url=https://revistapaginas.unr.edu.ar/index.php/RevPaginas/article/view/41/41 |journal=Páginas |language=es |location=Rosario |publisher=Escuela de Historia. Facultad de Humanidades y Artes. [[Universidad Nacional de Rosario]] |volume=6 |issue=10 |pages=53–82 |doi=10.35305/rp.v6i10.41 |hdl=2133/15923 |issn=1851-992X |doi-access=free |hdl-access=free |accessdate=14 November 2022 |archive-date=14 November 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221114041046/https://revistapaginas.unr.edu.ar/index.php/RevPaginas/article/view/41/41 |url-status=live }}</ref>{{sfn|Manetti|Rodríguez Riva|2014|p=44}} quickly becoming one of the most popular film industries across [[Latin America]] and the [[Spanish-speaking world]].{{sfn|Schumann|1987|p=19}}

Argentine industrial cinema arose in 1933 with the creation of its first and most prominent [[film studio]]s, [[Argentina Sono Film]] and [[Lumiton]], which released ''[[¡Tango!]]'' (1933) and ''[[Los tres berretines]]'' (1933), respectively, two foundational films that ushered in the [[sound-on-film]] era.{{sfn|Manetti|Rodríguez Riva|2014|p=24}}{{sfn|Mahieu|1966|p=15}} Although they were not national productions, the 1931–1935 films made by [[Paramount Pictures]] with tango star [[Carlos Gardel]] were a decisive influence on the emergence and popularization of Argentine cinema.{{sfn|Finkielman|2004|p=199}}{{sfn|Di Núbila|1998|p=108}} The nascent film industry grew steadily, accompanied by the appearance of other studios such as {{ill|Sociedad Impresora de Discos Electrofónicos|lt=SIDE|es|Sociedad Impresora de Discos Electrofónicos}}, {{ill|Estudios Río de la Plata|es|Estudios Río de la Plata}}, {{ill|Establecimientos Filmadores Argentinos|lt=EFA|es|Establecimientos Filmadores Argentinos}}, [[Pampa Film]] and [[Estudios San Miguel]], among others, which developed a continuous production and [[distribution chain]].{{sfn|Manetti|Rodríguez Riva|2014|p=44}} The number of films shot in the country grew 25-fold between 1932 and 1939, more than any other Spanish-speaking country.{{sfn|Getino|2005|p=17}} By 1939, Argentina established itself as the world's leading producer of films in Spanish, a position that it maintained until 1942, the year in which film production reached its peak for the decade.{{sfn|Rist|2014|p=4}}

In classical Argentine cinema, [[film genres]] were almost always configured as hybrids,{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Introducción}} with [[melodrama film|melodrama]] emerging as the reigning mode of the period.{{sfn|Karush|2012|p=85}}{{sfn|Manetti|Rodríguez Riva|2014|p=30}}<ref name="criterion">{{cite web|url=https://www.criterion.com/current/posts/7938-prisioneros-de-la-tierra-tropical-oppression?srsltid=AfmBOoq_xWkuA1uxAy6FYjmQ0p4PGNRue7O9cO_8SFk1fbQEHAuPowdW|title=Prisioneros de la tierra: Tropical Oppression|accessdate=13 March 2025|work=Current|publisher=[[Criterion Collection]]|date=28 September 2022|last=Karush|first=Matthew B.|archive-date=31 May 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250531140705/https://www.criterion.com/current/posts/7938-prisioneros-de-la-tierra-tropical-oppression?srsltid=AfmBOoq_xWkuA1uxAy6FYjmQ0p4PGNRue7O9cO_8SFk1fbQEHAuPowdW|url-status=live}}</ref> Its early audience were the urban [[working class]]es, so its content was strongly rooted in [[Working-class culture|their culture]],{{sfn|Di Núbila|1998|p=94}}<ref name="tesis">{{cite thesis |last=Kelly Hopfenblatt |first=Alejandro |title=La formulación de un modelo de representación en el cine clásico argentino: desarrollo, cambios y continuidades de la comedia burguesa (1939–1951) |accessdate=4 November 2022 |type=Doctoral thesis |publisher=Facultad de Filosofía y Letras. [[Universidad de Buenos Aires]] |url=http://repositorio.filo.uba.ar/xmlui/bitstream/handle/filodigital/6109/uba_ffyl_t_2016_se_Hopfenblatt.pdf?sequence=2&isAllowed=y |language=es |trans-title=The formulation of a representation model in classical Argentine cinema: development, changes and continuities of bourgeois comedy (1939–1951) |location=Buenos Aires |year=2016 |archive-date=4 November 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221104212956/http://repositorio.filo.uba.ar/xmlui/bitstream/handle/filodigital/6109/uba_ffyl_t_2016_se_Hopfenblatt.pdf?sequence=2&isAllowed=y |url-status=live }}</ref> most notably [[tango music]] and dance, [[radio drama]]s, and popular theatrical genres like [[sainete]]{{sfn|Di Núbila|1998|p=87}} or the ''[[revista porteña]]'' (local revue).{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Introducción}}{{sfn|Manetti|Rodríguez Riva|2014|p=45}} These forms of [[popular culture]] became the main roots of the film industry, from which many of its main performers, directors and screenwriters came.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Introducción}}{{sfn|Manetti|Rodríguez Riva|2014|p=45}} Much of the themes that defined the Argentine sound cinema in its beginnings were inherited from the [[Silent film|silent period]], including the opposition between the countryside and the city, and the interest in representing the world of tango.{{sfn|Manetti|Rodríguez Riva|2014|p=26}} As the industry's prosperity increased in the late 1930s, [[bourgeois]] characters shifted from [[villain]]s to protagonists, in an attempt to appeal to the [[middle class]]es and their aspirations.<ref name="tesis"/> Starting in the mid-1940s, Argentine cinema adopted an "internationalist" style that minimized national references, including the disuse of [[Rioplatense Spanish|local dialect]] and a greater interest in adapting works of [[world literature]].{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=El afán internacional}}

Beginning in 1943, as a response to [[Argentina during World War II|Argentina's neutrality]] in the context of [[World War II]], the United States imposed a boycott on sales of film stock to the country, causing [[Mexican cinema]] to displace Argentina as the market leader in Spanish.{{sfn|Schumann|1987|p=19}} During the presidency of [[Juan Perón]] (1946–1955), [[protectionist]] measures were adopted,{{sfn|Getino|2005|p=17}} which managed to revitalize Argentine film production.{{sfn|Rist|2014|p=5}} However, financial fragility of the industry led to its paralysis once Perón was [[Revolución Libertadora|overthrown in 1955]] and his stimulus measures ended.{{sfn|Getino|2005|p=24}}{{sfn|Schumann|1987|p=22}} With the studio system entering its definitive crisis, the classical era came to an end as new criteria for funding and shooting films emerged,{{sfn|Lusnich|2007|p=21}} including the irruption of [[Modernist film|modernism]] and [[Auteur|''auteur'' films]],<ref name="trabajadores"/> and a greater prominence of [[Independent film|independent cinema]].{{sfn|Schumann|1987|p=23}} The creation of the National Film Institute in 1957 and the innovative work of figures such as [[Leopoldo Torre Nilsson]] gave rise to a new wave of filmmakers in the 1960s,<ref name="ibermedia">{{cite book|chapter-url=http://ibermediadigital.com/ibermedia-television/contexto-historico/historia-del-cine-argentino-4/|accessdate=19 November 2022|pages=420–442|chapter=Argentina|language=es|title=Diccionario del Cine Iberoamericano|issue=Tomo 1|year=2011|last=García Oliveri|first=Ricardo|publisher=[[Sociedad General de Autores y Editores|SGAE]]|isbn=978-848-048-822-8|via=Ibermedia Digital|location=Madrid|archive-date=7 November 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221107054540/https://ibermediadigital.com/ibermedia-television/contexto-historico/historia-del-cine-argentino-4/|url-status=live}}</ref> who opposed "commercial" cinema and experimented with new [[cinematic techniques]].<ref name="cossalter">{{cite journal|last=Cossalter|first=Javier|title=El cine experimental de cortometraje en la Argentina de los años sesenta y setenta: apropiaciones y vinculaciones transnacionales|url=http://www.eras.utad.pt/docs/DEZ%20VISUAIS%202014.pdf|volume=5|issue=4|year=2014|pages=32–49|issn=1647-3558|accessdate=20 November 2022|journal=European Review of Artistic Studies|location=Vila Real|publisher=[[Universidade de Trás-os-Montes e Alto Douro]]|doi=10.37334/eras.v5i4.125|language=es}}{{Dead link|date=June 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref><ref name="manzano14">{{cite book|pages=36–43|last=Manzano|first=Valeria|title=The Age of Youth in Argentina: Culture, Politics & Sexuality from Perón to Videla|isbn=978-146-961-161-7|year=2014|publisher=[[The University of North Carolina Press]]|location=Chapel Hill}}</ref>

==History==
===Background (1896–1933)===
====1896–1929: The Argentine silent era====
[[File:Eugenio Py.jpg|thumb|upright|French immigrant [[Eugène Py|Eugenio Py]] is generally considered to have made the first films of the country in the 1890s.|alt=Eugenio Py, a pioneer of Argentine filmmaking, stands full-body in a black-and-white photo, next to a vintage camera]]

[[Thomas Edison]]'s first [[kinetoscope]]s arrived in [[Buenos Aires]] in 1894, but public film projection onto a screen became possible only with the [[Lumière brothers]]' [[cinematograph]], with which a series of presentations were made on 18 July 1896 at the [[Teatro Odeón]].{{sfn|Schumann|1987|p=16}}{{sfn|Mahieu|1966|p=5}} In 1897, the first projectors and cameras—from the Lumière and Gaumont firms—reached the country through Enrique Lepage's photography store, Casa Lepage.{{sfn|Mahieu|1966|p=5}} Their technician, the French [[Eugène Py|Eugenio Py]], became the first person to systematically film in Argentina;{{sfn|Mahieu|1966|p=5}} he shot the short ''[[La bandera argentina]]'' (1897), a register of the [[Flag of Argentina|national flag]] which is generally considered the country's first film.{{sfn|Schumann|1987|p=16}} Other authors believe that the first films were made by the German filmmaker Federico Fignero, who shot different views with a [[vitascope]] in 1896, with camera operator José Steimberg.{{sfn|Maranghello|2005|p=14}} In addition to Lepage and Py, the third figure who dominated film production at this time was the Austrian [[Max Glücksmann]], who was initially an employee of Casa Lepage and later acquired the firm in 1908.{{sfn|Schumann|1987|p=17}}{{sfn|Mahieu|1966|p=6}} The works of these early years of Argentine cinema correspond to [[actuality film]]s.{{sfn|Schumann|1987|p=17}} As noted by historian {{ill|José Agustín Mahieu|es|José Agustín Mahieu}}, this stage of national cinema "naively discovers the magic of movement, the direct capture of the landscape, of the event. The camera is still a primary eye planted in front of the facts. Over any other concern (artistic or cultural) prevails the technical curiosity, the exploration of a tool that is just beginning to be known."{{sfn|Mahieu|1966|p=6}} Thus, a small-scale commercial exploitation began, with the Casa Lepage offering projectors and films to restaurants, cafes or other entertainment venues.{{sfn|Mahieu|1966|p=6}} The company dominated the country's film production for a decade, dedicated to filming curiosities and current events such as official state visits, festivities and tourist sights.{{sfn|Schumann|1987|p=16}} In 1900, the first movie theater, the Salón Nacional, was inaugurated, and soon more venues dedicated to the projection of films were opened.{{sfn|Mahieu|1966|p=6}}

[[File:La revolución de mayo- fragmento.jpg|thumb|left|A frame from [[Mario Gallo (director)|Mario Gallo]]'s ''[[La Revolución de Mayo]]'' (1909), regarded as the first [[narrative film]] of the country.|alt=Still from ''La Revolución de Mayo'' (1909), directed by Mario Gallo, depicting men in 19th-century costumes; Argentina's first narrative film]]
At the end of the 1900s, Argentine cinema made significant progress with the appearance of the first [[narrative film]]s, which stimulated production and distribution.{{sfn|Schumann|1987|p=16}} [[Mario Gallo (director)|Mario Gallo]], an Italian who had arrived in Buenos Aires a few years before as part of an opera company, started producing narrative films.{{sfn|Di Núbila|1998|p=12}} There is confusion as to which was the first narrative film in the country: those who date its release in 1908 consider it to be ''[[El fusilamiento de Dorrego]]'',{{sfn|Mahieu|1966|p=6}} while more recent researchers point out that this film is actually from 1910 and the first one was really ''[[La Revolución de Mayo]]'', released in 1909.{{sfn|Di Núbila|1998|p=13}} For this reason, May 23 is considered National Film Day in the country, in commemoration of the release date of the latter film.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cultura.gob.ar/celebramos-el-dia-del-cine-nacional-9022/|language=es|title=23 de mayo: Día del Cine Nacional|date=15 May 2020|accessdate=13 October 2023|location=Buenos Aires|publisher=[[Ministry of Culture (Argentina)|Ministerio de Cultura]]|archive-date=19 October 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231019122121/https://www.cultura.gob.ar/celebramos-el-dia-del-cine-nacional-9022/|url-status=live}}</ref> In the manner of the French ''[[film d'art]]'' trend, Gallo's films were closer to photographed theatre, almost always on historical topics.{{sfn|Mahieu|1966|p=6}} In 1914, Glücksmann produced the oldest surviving feature film, ''[[Amalia (1914 film)|Amalia]]'', very similar in style to Gallo's films.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Comienzos de la ficción}} The film was an initiative of the Buenos Aires [[Aristocracy (class)|aristocracy]], and premiered at the prestigious [[Teatro Colón]] with the attendance of President [[Victorino de la Plaza]].{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Comienzos de la ficción}} European film production declined due to the outbreak of [[World War I]] in 1914, which resulted in an abundance of Argentine production in the following years.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=El caso de ''Juan Sin Ropa''}}

[[File:Nobleza Gaucha- poster.jpg|thumb|upright|The unprecedented commercial success of ''[[Nobleza gaucha (1915 film)|Nobleza gaucha]]'' (1915) inaugurated a new boom period for Argentine [[silent cinema]].|alt=Poster for the 1915 film ''Nobleza Gaucha'', an illustration of a gaucho riding a horse and swinging a lasso in the air]]

Before the arrival of sound films, Argentina experienced a "golden age" of silent films and led their production in Spanish, with more than 100 feature films being made between 1915 and 1924, equal to the combined total of those made in Mexico and Spain.{{sfn|Rist|2014|p=3}}{{sfn|Rist|2014|p=4}} During the first three decades of the 20th century, more than 200 feature films were produced in the country, in addition to a large number of documentaries, [[newsreels]] and shorter fictional works.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.pagina12.com.ar/diario/suplementos/radar/9-5474-2009-08-09.html|language=es|work=Radar. [[Página/12]]|accessdate=10 November 2022|title=Los muchachos de antes no usaban sonido|date=9 August 2009|last=Kairuz|first=Mariano|archive-date=10 November 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221110230438/https://www.pagina12.com.ar/diario/suplementos/radar/9-5474-2009-08-09.html|url-status=live}}</ref>  The release of the 1915 film ''[[Nobleza gaucha (1915 film)|Nobleza gaucha]]'' was a turning point in Argentine film history,{{sfn|Getino|2005|p=13}} opening new artistic and economic paths.{{sfn|Schumann|1987|p=17}} Nicknamed "the goldmine" by distributors and exhibitors, ''Nobleza gaucha'' was an unexpected massive commercial success which remained in theaters for more than two decades,{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=''Nobleza gaucha'', o "la mina de oro"}} and was also released in Spain and several Latin American countries.{{sfn|Mahieu|1966|p=10}} The artistic and commercial possibilities that the success of this film signaled translated into a growth of film activity in the country, with new producers and directors following its path; however, none were able to reach the initial success of ''Nobleza gaucha''.{{sfn|Mahieu|1966|p=10}} Another notable production of the era was ''[[Juan Sin Ropa]]'' (1919), produced by a partnership between the prestigious actors [[Camila Quiroga|Camila]] and Héctor Quiroga and the French filmmakers [[Paul Capellani]] and [[Georges Benoît]].{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=El caso de ''Juan Sin Ropa''}} This period is also significant for the emergence of the country's first [[women film directors|women filmmakers]],{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Mujeres cineastas}} the production of numerous newsreels and documentaries,{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Noticieros y documentales, espejo del mundo}} and the first animated feature films in cinema history by [[Quirino Cristiani]].{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Dibujo animado y sátira política}} Reflecting on the Argentine silent era, {{ill|Fernando Martín Peña|es|Fernando Martín Peña}} wrote:
<blockquote>
If anything characterizes {{ill|Argentine silent cinema|es|Cine mudo argentino}}, even during its most prolific period, it is its dispersion and diversity. Instead of being concentrated in large companies, production appears atomized in dozens of independent enterprises, technically assisted by a relatively small number of specialists and laboratories (or ''"talleres"'' [workshops], in the terms of the time). This phenomenon explains its wide thematic variety and its singularities: in this mode of production, opposed by definition to the mass production favored by the big studios, the exception was the rule.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Mujeres cineastas}}
</blockquote>

[[File:Perdón, viejita - María Turgenova and Ermete Meliante.jpg|thumb|left|[[María Turgenova]] and {{ill|Ermete Meliante|es|Ermete Meliante}} in ''[[Perdón, viejita]]'' (1927), one of the many [[Tango music|tango]]-based films by [[José A. Ferreyra]], of great influence for later cinema.]]

In the early 1920s, Argentine silent cinema entered a crisis caused by the recovery of European industry after the end of the war and the ascent of [[Cinema of the United States|Hollywood cinema]] to a position of unparalleled international dominance.{{sfn|Karush|2012|p=73}} The 1920s was marked by the activity of four main directors: [[José A. Ferreyra]], [[Nelo Cosimi]], {{ill|Edmo Cominetti|es|Edmo Cominetti}} and [[Julio Irigoyen]].{{sfn|Mahieu|1966|p=12}} In this decade, the first model of [[Tango music|tango]]-based films was systematized, despite the absence of sound, with titles including {{ill|Milonguita (film)|lt=''Milonguita''|es|Milonguita (película)}} ({{ill|José Bustamante y Ballivián|es|José Bustamante y Ballivián}}, 1922), {{ill|La cieguita de la avenida Alvear (1924 film)|lt=''La cieguita de la avenida Alvear''|es|La cieguita de la Avenida Alvear (película de 1924)}} (Julio Irigoyen, 1924), {{ill|La borrachera del tango|lt=''La borrachera del tango''|es|La borrachera del tango}} (Edmo Cominetti, 1928) and {{ill|La vendedora de Harrods|lt=''La vendedora de Harrods''|es|La vendedora de Harrods}} ({{ill|Francisco Defilippis Novoa|es|Francisco Defilippis Novoa}}, 1921).{{sfn|Manetti|Rodríguez Riva|2014|p=25}} These silent films laid the groundwork for the tango [[Melodrama (film genre)|melodramas]] that defined the Argentine cinema of the early classical period in the following decade.{{sfn|Manetti|Rodríguez Riva|2014|p=27}}

The most complete form of the silent "tango melodrama" model was the work of [[José A. Ferreyra]],{{sfn|Manetti|Rodríguez Riva|2014|p=26}} who began his career in the mid-1910s and stands out as the most important Argentine filmmaker of the 1920s,{{sfn|Getino|2005|p=14}} and would continue to be a central figure during the transition to sound and later in the classical-industrial period.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Cine nacional versus cine extranjero}} Considered a precursor of [[Italian neorealism|neorealism]], Ferreyra's influential style was characterized by its profoundly local identity, with characters and situations linked to the world of tango lyrics and the urban working classes of Buenos Aires, in whose streets he filmed with low resources and often starring non-actors.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Cine nacional versus cine extranjero}}{{sfn|Getino|2005|p=15}} Many of Ferreyra's titles point to a connection with the mythology of the city and its music: ''[[La muchacha del arrabal]]'' (1922), ''[[Buenos Aires, ciudad de ensueño]]'' (1922), {{ill|My Last Tango (1925 film)|lt=''Mi último tango''|es|Mi último tango}} (1925), {{ill|El organito de la tarde|lt=''El organito de la tarde''|es|El organito de la tarde}} (1925), {{ill|Muchachita de Chiclana|lt=''Muchachita de Chiclana''|es|Muchachita de Chiclana}} (1926), {{ill|La vuelta al bulín|lt=''La vuelta al bulín''|es|La vuelta al bulín}} (1926) and ''[[Perdón, viejita]]'' (1927), among others.{{sfn|Manetti|Rodríguez Riva|2014|p=26}} Some of these films were based on specific tangos while others inspired the composition of new tangos, and also incorporated other elements of popular culture such as [[sainete]] and [[Serial (literature)|serial]] novels.{{sfn|Karush|2012|p=106}} Historian {{ill|Jorge Miguel Couselo|es|Jorge Miguel Couselo}} noted Ferreyra's total identification with tango and his adherence to Buenos Aires, particularly its working-class neighborhoods.{{sfn|Manetti|Rodríguez Riva|2014|p=26}}

====1929–1933: Transition to sound films====
[[File:Muñequita porteña.jpg|thumb|María Turgenova in José A. Ferreyra's ''[[Muñequitas porteñas]]'' (1931), one of the first sound films in the country, which used the [[sound-on-disc]] technique.]]
Around 1929, the inventor {{ill|Alfredo Murúa|es|Alfredo Pablo Murúa}}—founder of {{ill|Sociedad Impresora de Discos Electrofónicos|es|Sociedad Impresora de Discos Electrofónicos}} (SIDE)—became a partner of the Ariel production company, and produced the short film ''Mosaico criollo'' (1929), with his own [[sound-on-disc]] system.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Hacia el sonoro}} ''Mosaico criollo'', the first instalment of an intended series, does not have any spoken dialogue and is instead a filmed "musical [[revue]]".{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Hacia el sonoro}} Murúa was responsible for the sound of most of the Argentine sound films made between 1931 and 1933, always using the sound-on-disc technique.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Hacia el sonoro}} The most important was ''[[Muñequitas porteñas]]'' (1931) by Ferreyra, for its pioneering use of spoken dialogue, although there were several others that used it partially, such as ''Amanecer de una raza'' (1931) by Cominetti, ''[[The Singer of My City|El cantar de mi ciudad]]'' (1930) by Ferreyra or ''[[La vía de oro]]'' (1931) by Cominetti; or that used sound to record only music and sound effects, among them ''[[Goodbye Argentina|¡Adiós Argentina!]]'' (1930) by {{ill|Mario Parpagnoli|es|Mario Parpagnoli}}, {{ill|La canción del gaucho|lt=''La canción del gaucho''|es|La canción del gaucho}} (1930) by Ferreyra or {{ill|Dios y la patria|lt=''Dios y la patria''|es|Dios y la patria}} (1931) by Cosimi.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Hacia el sonoro}} Films that were originally silent were re-released with new sound added, as in the case of ''Nobleza gaucha'' and ''Perdón, viejita'', among others.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Hacia el sonoro}} Fernando Martín Peña noted that Argentina's transition from silent to sound films was similar to the United States and Europe.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Hacia el sonoro}}

[[File:Carlos Gardel en Luces de Buenos Aires.jpg|thumb|left|upright|[[Carlos Gardel]] in ''[[Luces de Buenos Aires]]'' (1931), the first in a series of films produced by [[Paramount Pictures]] featuring the tango star that were decisively influential on the incipient local producers.]]

The arrival of sound films reduced the international dominance of American cinema due to the language barrier.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Hacia el sonoro}} This situation was analogous to the one that occurred during World War I, when the European film crisis benefited Argentine producers.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Hacia el sonoro}} Hollywood tried to deal with these difficulties with attempts at [[dubbing]] that ended up failing and also with various forms of [[subtitling]], although this still required technical development and also excluded illiterate audiences.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Hacia el sonoro}} Eventually, the U.S. industry reacted by making little accepted Spanish-language versions of its most important productions, although they found the greatest success once they began to produce original Spanish-language films made to showcase Latin American stars.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Hacia el sonoro}} Among them, the 1931–1935 films made by [[Paramount Pictures]] starring [[Carlos Gardel]] stood out, and became a major influence on the emergence of an Argentine film industry.{{sfn|Finkielman|2004|p=199}}{{sfn|Di Núbila|1998|p=108}} Before being hired by Paramount, Gardel—the most popular performer in the history of tango—had starred in a series of short films using optical sound between 1930 and 1931, which were directed by [[Eduardo Morera]] and produced by {{ill|Federico Valle|es|Federico Valle}}.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Hacia el sonoro}} The first of Gardel's feature films produced by Paramount was ''[[Luces de Buenos Aires]]'', released in September 1931 to great success.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Hacia el sonoro}}{{sfn|Karush|2012|p=76}} By this time optical sound had demonstrated its advantage over disc systems, so the equipment was progressively replaced in a process that lasted throughout 1932.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Hacia el sonoro}}

Despite being foreign productions, Gardel's films may be considered part of the history of Argentine cinema, as they were conceived by the singer himself together with other Argentine artists (like his lyricist [[Alfredo Le Pera]] or revue producer [[Manuel Romero (director)|Manuel Romero]]), and their model corresponded to that of the tango dramas directed by Ferreyra during the silent era, resulting in a strong Argentine identity.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Hacia el sonoro}} In addition, their commercial success demonstrated the viability of Argentine cinema for the incipient local producers that would inaugurate the Golden Age period in 1933.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Hacia el sonoro}}{{sfn|Karush|2012|p=76}} Paradoxically, Hollywood's attempt to dominate the local market resulted in the birth of the national industry, which took Gardel's films as a model to be replicated.{{sfn|Karush|2012|p=76}} According to Peña, the success of Gardel's films was "in fact the success of Ferreyra's and [[Leopoldo Torres Ríos|Torres Ríos]]' ideas taken up by a popular idol and legitimized for the local culture because of their 'foreign' condition".{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Hacia el sonoro}} In an interview, Argentine film historian Clara Kriger felt that: "... we [Argentine film historians] always say 'in 1933 the industry was born in Argentina', and the truth is that I would say that until Gardel appeared in films, Argentine cinema practically did not exist on billboards; very little Argentine cinema was being seen."<ref name="kriger">{{cite web|location=Buenos Aires|language=es|accessdate=1 October 2023|title=Clara Kriger: 'Hasta hace algunos años, los libros de historia del cine le dedicaban solo tres páginas a la época del peronismo'|first1=Álvaro|last1=Bretal|first2=Agustín|last2=Durruty|date=21 February 2022|publisher=Taipei|url=https://taipeirevista.com/index.php/2022/02/21/hasta-hace-algunos-anos-los-libros-de-historia-del-cine-le-dedicaban-solo-tres-paginas-a-la-epoca-del-peronismo/|archive-date=1 December 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231201201606/https://taipeirevista.com/index.php/2022/02/21/hasta-hace-algunos-anos-los-libros-de-historia-del-cine-le-dedicaban-solo-tres-paginas-a-la-epoca-del-peronismo/|url-status=live}}</ref> The last four Paramount productions with Gardel were his own productions that the studio agreed to finance, with full property rights for both creators after a first period of commercial exploitation.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Hacia el sonoro}}

===Development (1933–1956)===
====1933–1936: Birth and growth of the industry ====
{{multiple image|perrow = 2|total_width=300|direction=horizontal
 | align = right

 | image1 = Tango 1933 film poster.jpg
 | caption1 = 
 
 | image2 = Los tres berretines afiche.jpg
 | caption2 =

 | footer= The Argentine [[film industry]] took off in 1933 with the release of the first national [[optical sound]] films: ''[[¡Tango!]]'' ''(left)'' and ''[[Los tres berretines]]'' ''(right)'', produced by [[Argentina Sono Film]] and [[Lumiton]], respectively.
}}
The year 1933 meant the beginning of an industrial organization in Argentine cinema due to the emergence of [[Argentina Sono Film]] and [[Lumiton]]{{sfn|Mahieu|1966|p=15}} (the first two optical sound [[film studio]]s in Latin America){{sfn|Schumann|1987|p=xxxvi}} and the almost simultaneous release of their first productions ''[[¡Tango!]]'' (1933) and ''[[Los tres berretines]]'' (1933), respectively, the first feature films with optical sound in Argentine cinema.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=1933–1941}} Inspired by the Hollywood model, Argentina Sono Film founder {{ill|Ángel Mentasti|es|Ángel Mentasti}} introduced serial industrial production to local filmmaking,{{sfn|Manetti|Rodríguez Riva|2014|p=21}} and his plan consisted of "[forming] a company on the basis of three films and not release the first until the second had started and the third was announced."{{sfn|Di Núbila|1998|p=75}} The project started after [[Luis Moglia Barth]] contacted Mentasti with the idea of producing a film entirely starring the popular performers of revue theater, tango and radio.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=1933–1941}} The duo secured financing for Argentina Sono Film and conducted serial production to give them a better chance of negotiating with distributors.{{sfn|Di Núbila|1998|p=75}} The musical ''¡Tango!'' premiered on 27 April 1933 and attracted audiences for its select cast of popular performers, including [[Luis Sandrini]], [[Azucena Maizani]], [[Mercedes Simone]], [[Libertad Lamarque]], [[Pepe Arias]] and [[Tita Merello]], among others.{{sfn|Di Núbila|1998|pp=71–73}} While ''¡Tango!'' was being released, Argentina Sono Film was shooting its second film, ''[[Dancing (film)|Dancing]]'' (1933), which performed poorly at the box office,{{sfn|Di Núbila|1998|p=76}} while the great success of the third film, ''[[Riachuelo (film)|Riachuelo]]'' (1934), ensured the economic viability of the studio.{{sfn|Di Núbila|1998|p=88}}

[[File:Lumiton estudios.jpg|thumb|left|View of Lumiton in [[Munro, Buenos Aires|Munro]], [[Greater Buenos Aires]], {{circa|1930s}}.]]

Lumiton was founded by {{ill|César José Guerrico|es|César José Guerrico}}, [[Enrique Telémaco Susini]], Miguel Mugica and Luis Romero Carranza; they were a group of well-off entrepreneurs who introduced radio to the country in 1920.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=1933–1941}}{{sfn|Di Núbila|1998|p=76}} The group had traveled to Hollywood in 1931, where they studied the novelty of optical sound films and decided to bring the new technology to Argentina.{{sfn|Di Núbila|1998|p=77}} After purchasing complete film equipment at [[Bell & Howell]] in Chicago, they returned to Buenos Aires and began building a studio in [[Munro]], [[Buenos Aires Province]], replicating the [[sound stage]]s they had seen in Hollywood.{{sfn|Di Núbila|1998|p=77}} Thanks to the financial backing of its founding partners, Lumiton became a pioneer in the industrial and autonomous conceptualization of production.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Manuel Romero}} The company brought in experienced technicians (including cinematographer [[John Alton]]) and opened its first film gallery in December 1932, beginning production with an adaptation of the successful play ''Los tres berretines'',{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=1933–1941}} which was released on 19 May 1933.{{sfn|Di Núbila|1998|p=400}} Although ''¡Tango!'' is often considered the first success of classical Argentine cinema, research on the box-office records of the time indicates that ''Los tres berretines'' had an even greater impact on audiences.{{sfn|Kriger|2018|pp=181-182}} In both films, Sandrini plays an awkward, stuttering comic archetype that he had previously consecrated in the theatrical version of ''Los tres berretines''.{{sfn|Di Núbila|1998|p=72}} With some variations, Sandrini played this character in the rest of his films of the decade, which established him as a star of humorous cinema in the Spanish-speaking world during the 1930s and early 1940s.{{sfn|Di Núbila|1998|p=72}}

Several new production companies formed after the success of ''¡Tango!'' and ''Los tres berretines''.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Otras empresas}} The number of released films grew from 6 films in 1933 to 14 in 1935,{{sfn|Getino|2005|p=176}} half of which were directorial debuts.<ref name="ibermedia"/> Among them were Manuel Romero, [[Mario Soffici]], [[Daniel Tinayre]], [[Luis Saslavsky]] and [[Alberto de Zavalía]].{{sfn|Di Núbila|1998|p=114}} {{ill|Estudios Río de la Plata|lt=Río de la Plata|es|Estudios Río de la Plata}} was founded by musician [[Francisco Canaro]] in 1934, and had a studio in Buenos Aires.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Otras empresas}} Its first production was ''[[Idols of the Radio|Ídolos de la radio]]'' (1934), which sought to attract audiences with a star-studded cast of radio personalities, including singers (including the only film performance of [[tango]] star [[Ada Falcon]]), comedians, orchestras and announcers.{{sfn|Di Núbila|1998|p=90}} Daniel Tinayre's debut film {{ill|Bajo la Santa Federación|lt=''Bajo la Santa Federación''|es|Bajo la santa federación}} (1935) was produced by Productora Argentina de Filmes (PAF).{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Otras empresas}} Luis Saslavsky and Alberto de Zavalía presented in 1935 their first films, ''[[Crimen a las tres]]'' and ''[[Escala en la ciudad]]'', respectively, which were produced with family money disguised under the name of the Sifal production company.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Otras empresas}} Manuel Romero joined Lumiton after the commercial failure of the company's second film ''[[Ayer y Hoy (film)|Ayer y hoy]]'' (1934) and brought it a new box-office success with ''[[Noches de Buenos Aires]]'' (1935).{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Manuel Romero}} Romero would become one of the most prolific directors of classical Argentine cinema, known for the speed with which he shot and released his films, most of them with Lumiton.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Manuel Romero}}

In addition to new production companies, the demand for Argentine films prompted the emergence of [[Independent film|independent]] productions, that is, those that were made outside the studios.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Otras empresas}} However, Peña notes that the term "independent" for these films is actually a misnomer, as "in the early years of sound, Argentina Sono Film itself was not really a 'big studio' and could have disappeared like many other production companies of those years"; because all the production companies other than Lumiton lacked the financial resources to weather commercial failures, Peña says, "the mode of production remained, as in the silent period, atomized, adventurous, fragile."{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Otras empresas}} Alton temporarily stepped away from Lumiton to make his own film, {{ill|El hijo de papá|lt=''El hijo de papá''|es|El hijo de papá}} (1933) starring Sandrini, which was such a failure that it caused the latter to set the film's [[Negative (photography)|negatives]] on fire.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Otras empresas}} Moglia Barth also decided to try independent production, moving away from Mentasti to make {{ill|Picaflor (film)|lt=''Picaflor''|es|Picaflor (película)}} (1935), although the following year he returned to Argentina Sono Film.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Otras empresas}} Also in 1933, the film {{ill|El linyera|lt=''El linyera''|es|El linyera}} directed by [[Enrique Larreta]] was released, which is considered more of a filmed theatrical piece than a cinematographic work.{{sfn|Di Núbila|1998|p=82}} The director who had the greatest success in independent filmmaking was Ferreyra, with three films released between 1934 and 1935: ''[[Streets of Buenos Aires|Calles de Buenos Aires]]'', ''[[Puente Alsina (film)|Puente Alsina]]'' and {{ill|Mañana es domingo|lt=''Mañana es domingo''|es|Mañana es domingo}}, all of them made with "very few resources but recovering the poetics of his best silent period."{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Otras empresas}}

Argentina's film industry grew in the 1930s despite American studios having advantages against Argentinians, including greater capital, scale, and distribution leverage.{{sfn|Karush|2012|p=74}} The Argentine film studios were very small compared to powerful companies such as Paramount, [[Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer]], [[Warner Bros.]], [[Twentieth Century-Fox]], [[Columbia Pictures|Columbia]], [[Universal Pictures|Universal]] and [[United Artists]], all of which had offices in Buenos Aires and other cities in the country by 1935.{{sfn|Karush|2012|p=74}} Lacking the bargaining strength of foreign companies, Argentine producers could not secure a distribution system guaranteeing a share of gross receipts, thus resorting to flat fee sales.{{sfn|Karush|2012|p=74}} Despite financial challenges, Argentine studios did have some specific competitive advantages, including the country's long tradition of popular theater, especially the short comic plays called ''[[sainetes]]''; by offering similar entertainment at a more affordable admission price, local filmmakers could attract an audience that already existed.{{sfn|Karush|2012|p=76}} Additionally, a significant portion of this audience either could not or did not prefer to read subtitles that accompanied English-language films.{{sfn|Karush|2012|p=76}} The gradual consolidation of the film industry impacted other areas of the broader [[entertainment]] industry, as the interplay between cinema, radio, and music led to a unified commercial approach, supported by specialized publications, fostering a [[star system]] reminiscent of Hollywood but tailored to Argentina.<ref name="tesis"/> 

According to [[Octavio Getino]], the rapid growth of the nascent Argentine film industry was made possible by several factors, which include: the preceding industrial, technical, and commercial experience that, albeit limited, was unparalleled in Latin America; the temporary inability of the United States to retain Spanish-speaking audiences with their films; the popular style and themes of Argentine cinema, which were much more in tune with those of other Latin American countries; and the composition of the primary audience of Argentine cinema, comprising large groups of urban workers, either recently migrated from the country's interior or originating from European immigration.{{sfn|Getino|2005|p=17}}

====1936–1942: Rise to international influence====
The industrialization process was accompanied by [[standardization]] in production,{{sfn|Schumann|1987|p=19}} going from 6 films released in 1933, to 14 in 1935, 30 in 1937, 41 in 1938,{{sfn|Getino|2005|p=176}} and an average of 50 films per year in the following four years.{{sfn|Karush|2012|p=74}} Following Lumiton, the second company to have its own studios and an industrial production plan was Alfredo Murúa's SIDE, which began producing films at the end of 1935.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Alfredo Murúa, sonidista y productor}} Between 1936 and 1938, Ferreyra directed a trilogy of tango films for SIDE starring Libertad Lamarque and inspired by the work of Gardel.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Alfredo Murúa, sonidista y productor}} The first of these films was ''[[Ayúdame a vivir]]'' (1936), which marked a key moment in the economic history of Argentine cinema, since it "contributed enormously to its popularity throughout Latin America and was the key that finished opening the continental markets in which it expanded the most during its golden age."{{sfn|Di Núbila|1998|p=133}} Followed by ''[[Besos brujos]]'' (1937) and ''[[La ley que olvidaron]]'' (1938), Lamarque's films with Ferreyra were the first Argentinian productions to dominate the international Spanish-speaking market.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Alfredo Murúa, sonidista y productor}} Argentine productions dominated the Latin American market until being overtaken by the [[Mexican film industry]] in the mid-1940s.{{sfn|Karush|2012|p=83}} 

By the end of 1936, the profitability of the Argentine film industry attracted formerly hostile distributors and exhibitors.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Un nuevo estudio}} The initiator of this was the successful distributor of European films {{ill|Adolfo Z. Wilson|es|Adolfo Z. Wilson}}, who formed the company Porteña Films and built his own studios with the initial intent to rent them to other production companies.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Un nuevo estudio}} The following year, the distributor Julio Joly and the owner of movie theater chains {{ill|Clemente Lococo|es|Clemente Lococo}} joined the company, which was renamed {{ill|Establecimientos Filmadores Argentinos|es|Establecimientos Filmadores Argentinos}} (EFA).{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Un nuevo estudio}}

[[File:Rodaje de Puerto Nuevo (1936).jpg|thumb|left|View of the shooting of Argentina Sono Film's ''[[Puerto nuevo (film)|Puerto Nuevo]]'' (1936), directed by [[Mario Soffici]] and [[Luis César Amadori]], at {{ill|Sociedad Impresora de Discos Electrofónicos|lt=SIDE|es|Sociedad Impresora de Discos Electrofónicos}}'s studios.]]

{{ill|Domingo Di Núbila|es|Domingo Di Núbila}} noted 1937 as a time of great progress for Argentine cinema as it saw over 30 films released which featured Enrique Muiño, [[Elías Alippi]], [[Ángel Magaña]], [[Florencio Parravicini]], [[Hugo del Carril]], [[Mecha Ortiz]], [[León Zárate]], [[Orestes Caviglia]], [[Luis Arata]], [[José Olarra]], [[Camila Quiroga]], [[Enrique Santos Discépolo]], [[Santiago Gómez Cou]] and others.{{sfn|Di Núbila|1998|p=149}} Unlike the silent era, there were no female directors during the classical period, as industry leaders firmly prevented their emergence; and the first sound film directed by a woman did not come until 1960 with [[Vlasta Lah]]'s ''[[Las furias]]''.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Mujeres cineastas}} By 1937, there were 9 film studios and 30 production companies in Buenos Aires.{{sfn|Karush|2012|p=74}} One of these was Baires, which was born within the ''[[Crítica de la Argentina|Crítica]]'' newspaper, inspired by the [[William Randolph Hearst]] model.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Mirar para afuera}} Founder Eduardo Bedoya appointed Daniel Tinayre as his main advisor and he supervised the construction of Baires' studios in [[Don Torcuato]], Greater Buenos Aires.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Mirar para afuera}} Therefore, its first production, Tinayre's ''[[Mateo (1937 film)|Mateo]]'' (1937), had to be filmed at Lumiton, and Baires would concentrate on the construction of its studios until it produced another film.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Mirar para afuera}}

Unlike companies such as Lumiton and Baires, which advanced in the construction of studios before being sure of the economic dynamics of the business, Argentina Sono Film was more prudent.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=La evolución de Argentina Sono Film}} In 1937, the company built its own studios and produced eight films.{{sfn|Mahieu|1966|p=18}} After the success of ''Riachuelo'', Mentasti brought in [[Arturo S. Mom]], who directed films such as ''[[Monte Criollo|Monte criollo]]'' (1935), ''[[Loco lindo]]'' (1936), and ''[[Palermo (film)|Palermo]]'' (1937).{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=La evolución de Argentina Sono Film}} Moglia Barth returned to Argentina Sono Film after his failure with ''Picaflor'', directing films such as ''[[Amalia (1936 film)|Amalia]]'' (1936), ''[[¡Goal!]]'' (1936), ''[[Melgarejo]]'' (1937), ''[[Melodías porteñas]]'' (1937), and {{ill|La casa de Quirós (film)|lt=''La casa de Quirós''|es|La casa de Quirós (película)}} (1938), which inaugurated the long trend of Argentine cinema in adapting foreign works.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=La evolución de Argentina Sono Film}} Also in 1936, Argentina Sono Film released the successful ''[[Puerto nuevo (film)|Puerto Nuevo]]'', which marked the directorial debut of [[Luis César Amadori]] (co-credited with Mario Soffici), who would develop an extensive and successful career throughout the classical period.{{sfn|Di Núbila|1998|p=124}}

[[File:Técnicos rodaje Lumiton.jpg|thumb|left|Lumiton technicians during a shoot, {{circa|1930s}}.]]
The year 1938 continued to break production records after the previous year's developments increased the demand for Argentine films in the country and throughout the Spanish-speaking world.{{sfn|Di Núbila|1998|p=185}} In response to the expanding market, the industry intensified its production pace, imported new studio equipment, upgraded laboratories and brought in new filmmakers.{{sfn|Di Núbila|1998|p=185}} That year, 16 new directors debuted, most of them coming from the theater, including [[Orestes Caviglia]], [[Elías Isaac Alippi]], [[Ivo Pelay]], [[Ernesto Vilches]], {{ill|Edmundo Guibourg|es|Edmundo Guibourg}} and {{ill|Miguel Coronatto Paz|es|Miguel Coronatto Paz}}, among others.{{sfn|Mahieu|1966|p=45}} Manuel Romero emerged as the most prolific filmmaker of the period, strengthening Lumiton with the release of six films between March 1937 and March 1938, including important titles like ''[[The Boys Didn't Wear Hair Gel Before (1937 film)|Los muchachos de antes no usaban gomina]]'' (1937), ''[[Three Argentines in Paris|Tres anclados en París]]'' (1938) and ''[[La rubia del camino]]'' (1938).{{sfn|Di Núbila|1998|pp=185–186}} Although the initial idea was that EFA would not produce, in 1938 it released its first film, ''[[La vuelta al nido]]'', directed by Leopoldo Torres Ríos.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Un nuevo estudio}} Although it was a commercial failure, Torres Ríos' film was years later revalued as misunderstood by the commercial spirit of its time and a precursor of modern cinema, for its intimate and reflective style and for the naturalist performances of [[José Gola]] and [[Amelia Bence]].{{sfn|Di Núbila|1998|p=196}}<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.pagina12.com.ar/228560-desde-el-proximo-sabado-9-de-noviembre-vuelve-el-festival-de|language=es|accessdate=8 November 2022|title=Desde el próximo sábado 9 de noviembre vuelve el Festival de Mar del Plata|work=Radar. [[Página/12]]|last=Brodersen|first=Diego|date=3 November 2019|archive-date=8 November 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221108132725/https://www.pagina12.com.ar/228560-desde-el-proximo-sabado-9-de-noviembre-vuelve-el-festival-de|url-status=live}}</ref>

[[File:Ángel Magaña y Delia Garcés en Kilómetro 111.jpg|thumb|right|[[Ángel Magaña]] and [[Delia Garcés]] in ''[[Kilómetro 111]]'' (1938), directed by [[Mario Soffici]] and produced by Argentina Sono Film.]]
Soffici was an important filmmaker of this period and directed for Argentina Sono Film ''[[El alma del bandoneón]]'' (1935), ''[[La barra mendocina]]'' (1935), ''[[Cadets of St. Martin|Cadetes de San Martín]]'' (1937)—with which he experienced censorship for the first time after an army refusal to his original script—and ''[[Viento norte]]'' (1937).{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=La evolución de Argentina Sono Film}} 

In 1938, Soffici released social commentary films such as ''[[Kilómetro 111]]'' (1938), ''[[El viejo doctor]]'' (1939) and ''[[Héroes sin fama]]'' (1940), which gave him greater prestige.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=La evolución de Argentina Sono Film}} However, Soffici's most celebrated film, ''[[Prisioneros de la tierra]]'' (1939), was released under another production company: [[Pampa Film]].{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Pampa Film}}<ref name="criterion"/> Founded by Olegario Ferrando in 1936, the company's first film was ''[[La fuga (1937 film)|La fuga]]'' (1937) by Luis Saslavsky, who also directed {{ill|Nace un amor|lt=''Nace un amor''|es|Nace un amor}} (1938), films which sought to distance themselves from the popular cinema of Ferreyra and Romero.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Pampa Film}} Saslavsky also brought Alberto de Zavalía to the company, who directed the successful ''[[The Caranchos of Florida (film)|Los caranchos de la Florida]]'' (1938).{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Pampa Film}} Pampa Film also hired {{ill|Enrique de Rosas|es|Enrique de Rosas}} and {{ill|Enrique de Rosas Jr.|es|Enrique de Rosas (hijo)}}, who directed a series of commercial failures.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Pampa Film}} The company managed an improvement the following year with ''Prisioneros de la tierra'', which was hailed as a classic practically from its release.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Pampa Film}}

[[File:Niní Marshall en Cándida.jpg|thumb|left|upright|[[Niní Marshall]] as her popular character Cándida in the 1939 [[Cándida (1939 film)|eponymous film]] by [[Luis Bayón Herrera]].]]
In 1939, Argentina became the world's leading producer of Spanish-language films, with a new record of 50 feature films being made,{{sfn|Schumann|1987|p=xxxvi}} and had consolidated industrial production, an expanding market and its own system of stars, genres and popular authors.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Y llegó el dinero}} In this year, Laboratorios Alex acquired the first [[flatbed editor]] in Argentina, and the new system would be progressively adopted by the industry in the following years.{{sfn|Di Núbila|1998|pp=276–277}} The construction of the [[Estudios San Miguel]] in [[Bella Vista, Buenos Aires|Bella Vista]], Greater Buenos Aires, the largest studio in Argentina, was finished in 1939.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Los misterios de San Miguel}}

[[File:Mirtha Legrand en Los martes, orquideas.jpg|thumb|upright|[[Mirtha Legrand]] in ''[[Los martes, orquídeas]]'' (1941), directed by [[Francisco Mugica]] and produced by Lumiton.]]
The new prosperity of Argentine cinema brought about a strong change in the themes and atmospheres that had characterized it until then, appealing to middle-class audiences' taste for aspirational themes and wealthy settings.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Y llegó el dinero}}{{sfn|Mahieu|1966|p=24}} The major representative of this trend at Lumiton was [[Francisco Mugica]], who directed the successful and influential ''[[Such Is Life (1939 film)|Así es la vida]]'' (1939) and ''[[Los martes, orquídeas]]'' (1941), while at Argentina Sono Film it was Luis César Amadori, who manufactured successful [[star vehicle]]s for Pepe Arias, Libertad Lamarque, Luis Sandrini, Hugo del Carril, Niní Marshall and [[Mirtha Legrand]].{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Y llegó el dinero}} For its part, EFA cast all the biggest stars of the era by offering them more money than any other production company.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=EFA se despliega}} The studio's main director was [[Luis Bayón Herrera]], who imitated Manuel Romero's model of making low-cost, fast-production, star-driven films.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=EFA se despliega}} Examples include ''[[Cándida (1939 film)|Cándida]]'' (1939), ''[[Los celos de Cándida]]'' (1940) and ''[[Cándida millonaria]]'' (1941), all of them starring Marshall playing her popular comic character.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=EFA se despliega}} Also at EFA, director [[Carlos Schlieper]] had the first important period of his career, with a more refined style than Bayón Herrera.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=EFA se despliega}} At the end of the 1930s, with Soffici's departure from the company, Argentina Sono Film incorporated Saslavsky and [[Alberto de Zavalía]], who stood out for introducing a more cultured and refined take on commercial filmmaking with titles such as ''[[Puerta cerrada]]'' (1939), {{ill|El loco Serenata|lt=''El loco Serenata''|es|El Loco Serenata}} (1939) and ''[[Historia de una noche]]'' (1941) in the former, and ''[[La vida de Carlos Gardel]]'' (1939) in the latter.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Cultos y refinados}} The sophistication of these two directors in Argentina Sono Film had its counterpart in Lumiton with the incorporation of [[Carlos Hugo Christensen]], who directed films such as ''[[Los Chicos crecen (1942 film)|Los chicos crecen]]'' (1942), ''[[Safo, historia de una pasión]]'' (1943) and ''[[La pequeña señora de Pérez]]'' (1944).{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Cultos y refinados}}

[[File:El cura gaucho 1941.jpg|thumb|upright|left|Enrique Muiño and Graciliano Batista in ''[[El cura gaucho]]'' (1941), directed by Lucas Demare and produced by [[Pampa Film]].]]

The year 1941 was one of great progress for the Argentine film industry, despite some conflicts between exhibitors that began to monopolize domestic distribution.{{sfn|Di Núbila|1998|pp=342–343}} Several laboratories were modernized, such as Laboratorios Cristiani and Tecnofilm, incorporating automatic [[Film processing|film processors]], [[optical printers]], a [[microcinema]] for [[dailies]], among other innovations.{{sfn|Di Núbila|1998|p=350}} But the most notable advance was that of the Laboratorios Alex following the knowledge acquired by Connio Santini and Alfredo Rosiano in their chemistry university studies in the U.S.{{sfn|Di Núbila|1998|p=350}} This allowed Laboratorios Alex to achieve remarkable quality in their black and white films, and to begin to experiment with the possibility of color.{{sfn|Di Núbila|1998|p=351}} Gradually in the following years, Alex absorbed practically all the work of the Argentine professional film industry.{{sfn|Di Núbila|1998|p=351}} In 1941, the [[Argentine Academy of Cinematography Arts and Sciences (1941–1955)|Argentine Academy of Cinematography Arts and Sciences]] was created, which was inspired by the U.S. [[Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences]], included some of the most prominent names in the industry, and presented its own annual awards ceremony.{{sfn|Di Núbila|1998|pp=346–347}} The first film to receive the academy's Best Picture award was ''Los martes, orquídeas'', while Saslavsky received Best Director for ''[[Historia de una noche]]'' (1941), with [[Delia Garcés]] in {{ill|Veinte años y una noche|lt=''Veinte años y una noche''|es|Veinte años y una noche}} (1941) and Enrique Muiño in ''[[El cura gaucho]]'' (1941) receiving Best Actress and Actor, respectively.{{sfn|Di Núbila|1998|p=348}}

[[File:Premios de la Academia de Artes y Ciencias Cinematográficas de la Argentina, 1942.jpg|thumb|View of the first [[Argentine Academy of Cinematography Arts and Sciences (1941–1955)|Argentine Academy Awards]] in 1942, with [[Orson Welles]], [[Enrique Muiño]], Delia Garcés, [[María Duval (Argentine actress)|María Duval]], Mirtha Legrand, Mario Soffici, [[Luis Saslavsky]], Francisco Mugica and [[Sebastián Chiola]] in the crowd.]]

Also in 1941, [[Artistas Argentinos Asociados]] (English: "Associated Argentine Artists"; AAA) was established, a production company founded by director [[Lucas Demare]], actors [[Elías Alippi]], [[Ángel Magaña]], [[Enrique Muiño]] and [[Francisco Petrone]], and producer {{ill|Enrique Faustín|es|Enrique Faustín}}; while directors [[Homero Manzi]] and [[Ulyses Petit de Murat]], assistant director [[Hugo Fregonese]] and actor [[René Mugica]] also took part informally, among others.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Asociados}} According to Peña, they were united by the desire to "take the risks that other companies avoided in order to obtain a cinema of artistic quality that would also be commercial."{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Asociados}} In 1942, AAA released ''[[The Gaucho War|La guerra gaucha]]'',{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Asociados}} which was the highest-grossing Argentine film in history and represented the peak of the Golden Age according to Di Núbila.{{sfn|Di Núbila|1998|pp=391–392}} The early 1940s also saw a brief reappearance of the Baires studios, which released a series of box office bombs and soon halted production amid legal disputes.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Breve regreso de Baires}} On the other hand, Pampa Film continued its line of nationalist-themed films after ''Prisioneros de la tierra'' with titles such as [[Adelqui Migliar]]'s ''[[La carga de los valientes]]'' (1940) and {{ill|La quinta calumnia|lt=''La quinta calumnia''|es|La quinta calumnia}} (1941), and the great success of Demare's ''El cura gaucho'' (1941), a biopic of [[Cura Brochero|Priest Brochero]] that was "inserted in the context of a strong discussion on the identity of Argentine cinema."{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Pasión y muerte de Pampa}} However, in subsequent years the studio made a series of costly but unprofitable productions that would eventually lead to its dissolution.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Pasión y muerte de Pampa}}

====1942–1955: Industry crisis and state intervention ====
The Argentine film industry was affected by [[World War II]]. Several European immigrants who escaped the war joined the Argentine film industry, like musicians [[George Andreani]] and [[Paul Misraki]], screenwriter [[Jacques Rémy (writer)|Jacques Rémy]], and director [[Pierre Chenal]],{{sfn|Peña|2024|p=186}} who found success with the films ''[[Todo un hombre (1943 film)|Todo un hombre]]'' (1943), ''[[El muerto falta a la cita]]'' (1944), ''[[Se abre el abismo]]'' (1945) and ''[[Viaje sin regreso]]'' (1946).{{sfn|Peña|2024|pp=190–192}} Some Argentine films of the period even made reference to the war, although most of them in an allusive way, such as Jewish exile [[James Bauer]]'s ''[[Explosivo 008]]'' (1940), Saslavsky's ''[[Ceniza al viento]]'' (1942), Mugica's ''[[La guerra la gano yo]]'' (1943), [[Carlos Borcosque]]'s ''[[La verdadera victoria]]'' (1943), Alberto de Zavalía's ''[[Concierto de almas (film)|Concierto de almas]]'' (1942) and ''[[El fin de la noche]]'' (1944), Bayón Herrera's ''[[The Two Rivals (1944 film)|Los dos rivales]]'' (1944).{{sfn|Peña|2024|pp=193–195}} When World War II began, the magazine ''Cine argentino'' conducted anonymous interviews with industry figures and, although several had optimistic views, others anticipated the problems that the industry would soon face, like the following interviewee:
<blockquote>
—The materials used in film production, which we import almost exclusively from Germany, are also used in the war industry. And since Germany is at war, it does not take a fortune teller to predict that the price of celluloid will soon be skyrocketing. <br>
—And it can't be imported from North America? <br>
—Don't be naive! Do you think the Americans are going to provide us with the means to continue competing with them? They will take advantage of the situation. We will have to pay for celluloid at the price of gold. What remains to be seen is whether the price of raw film will rise to the point of forcing us to close the studios...{{sfn|Peña|2024|p=186}}
</blockquote>

{{Chart|definition=Argentine versus Mexican film production between 1933 and 1945.chart|data=Argentine versus Mexican film production between 1933 and 1945.tab
|width=500px|thumb=yes
|align=left
|caption=The evolution of Argentine and Mexican film production between 1933 and 1945, measured in number of [[feature film]]s released.{{sfn|Getino|2005|p=176}}<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/24312551|accessdate=19 November 2022|language=es|title=Medio siglo de cine mexicano|pages=1–19, 21–32|last1=García Riera|first1=Emilio|last2=Larralde|first2=Elsa|issue=31|year=1960|journal=Artes de México|location=Mexico City|jstor=24312551|archive-date=19 November 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221119174412/https://www.jstor.org/stable/24312551|url-status=live}}</ref> Since the emergence of [[industrialization]] in 1933, Argentine cinema grew exponentially and became the world leader for the production of films in [[Spanish language|Spanish]] by 1939.{{sfn|Schumann|1987|p=19}} This primacy ended abruptly in 1943, when the United States imposed a boycott on sales of film stock to the country and provided a series of benefits to the Mexican industry.{{sfn|Schumann|1987|p=21}}
}}

In the context of the war, Argentina's success in the Latin American film industry posed a challenge for American policymakers.{{sfn|Karush|2012|pp=181–182}} [[Argentina during World War II|Argentina's policy of neutrality]] was influenced by factors such as the [[Smoot–Hawley Act]] of 1930, which led to high U.S. tariffs on Argentine imports, fostering anti-American sentiment.{{sfn|Karush|2012|pp=181–182}} This was further exacerbated by the [[Lend-Lease Act]] of 1941, where the U.S. provided arms to Argentina's regional rival, Brazil.{{sfn|Karush|2012|pp=181–182}} Despite some right-wing nationalists' pro-Nazi inclinations, Argentina's neutral stance was initially supported by Britain, which relied on Argentine food imports and feared that abandoning neutrality would disrupt trade.{{sfn|Karush|2012|pp=181–182}} However, Argentina's refusal to join the Pan-American alliance and its occasional censorship of Hollywood films at the behest of Germany and Spain fueled U.S. suspicions about South American Fascism and led the [[Office of the Coordinator of Inter-American Affairs]] (OCIAA) to counteract by promoting Mexican films over Argentine ones.{{sfn|Karush|2012|pp=181–182}} The U.S. bolstered the Mexican film industry with investment, loans, equipment, and technical assistance, while restricting the export of raw film stock to Argentina, which resulted in severe shortages for national studios and forced them to rely on the more expensive black market.{{sfn|Karush|2012|pp=181–182}} Consequently, Argentine film production plummeted from 56 films in 1942 to only 36 in 1943, while Mexican production rose from 49 to 67 in the same period.{{sfn|Karush|2012|pp=181–182}}{{sfn|Getino|2005|p=176}} By the end of the war, Mexico had firmly supplanted Argentina as the leading producer of Spanish-language films in Latin America, with a significant increase in production.{{sfn|Karush|2012|pp=181–182}}{{sfn|Schumann|1987|p=21}} The boycott was beneficial for North American investors who had heavily invested in the Mexican film industry, ensuring that political and commercial interests were closely aligned.{{sfn|Karush|2012|pp=181–182}}

The decline experienced by the Argentine industry compared to the Mexican industry is not attributed only to U.S. intervention, but also to a series of defects in its commercial management.{{sfn|Di Núbila|1998|p=384}} The success of national cinema did not favor the industrial production sector so much as it did the commercial sector of distributors and exhibitors.{{sfn|Getino|2005|p=20}} {{ill|José Agustín Mahieu|es|Agustín Mahieu}} noted that the growth of the industry did not increase revenue for productions and that most revenue gains were accrued by the distributors.{{sfn|Mahieu|1966|p=26}} In 1942, director Luis Saslavsky denounced the business exploitation of filmmakers.{{sfn|Di Núbila|1998|p=384}} The cinema of Mexico, on the other hand, had begun to adopt a more favorable long-term policy for its development, through direct [[state management]] of production, distribution and exhibition companies, unlike the [[free market]] that reigned in Argentine cinema.{{sfn|Getino|2005|p=20}} For example, since 1942 the country had the National Film Bank (Spanish: ''Banco Nacional Cinematográfico''), which helped finance the productions.{{sfn|Di Núbila|1998|p=385}}

[[File:Orestes Caviglia - Enrique Muiño, Su mejor alumno.jpg|thumb|[[Orestes Caviglia]] and [[Enrique Muiño]] in ''[[Su mejor alumno]]'' (1944), directed by [[Lucas Demare]] and produced by Artistas Argentinos Asociados.]]

Throughout the 1930s, the Argentine state had remained largely on the sidelines of the development of the film industry.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=El Estado benefactor}} This situation began to change following the [[1943 Argentine coup d'état|1943 military coup]].{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=El Estado benefactor}} By ushering in a nationalist government that rejected liberal economic principles, the coup laid the groundwork for the state to protect the Argentine film industry.{{sfn|Karush|2012|p=183}} The new military government created the Undersecretariat of Information and Press of the Presidency, which included a General Directorate of Public Shows with three divisions: Cinema, Theater and Control.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=El Estado benefactor}} After the end of World War II, the United States still maintained its raw film stock restrictions on Argentina.{{sfn|Mahieu|1966|p=37}} Faced with a shortage of raw film stock, studios attempted negotiations with domestic theater chains for improved terms; when these negotiations faltered, the matter was escalated to [[Juan Domingo Perón]]'s {{ill|Secretaría de Trabajo y Previsión|lt=Secretariat of Labor and Welfare|es|Secretaría de Trabajo y Previsión (Argentina)}}.{{sfn|Karush|2012|p=183}} In response, Perón issued a decree favoring the studios, instituting a percentage rental system and mandating a quota of Argentine films to be shown in theaters.{{sfn|Karush|2012|p=183}} This decree, with slight modifications, would significantly shape the film industry following Perón's election to the presidency in 1946.{{sfn|Karush|2012|p=183}}

A 1947 law mandated that domestic films constitute 25% of screen time in first-run ''porteño'' theaters and 40% elsewhere in the country.{{sfn|Karush|2012|p=183}} Simultaneously, the Banco de Crédito Industrial initiated financing options for domestic film producers, while producers also received a substantial subsidy funded by a minor fee added to ticket prices.{{sfn|Karush|2012|p=184}} Through the implementation of this law, the established legal and official parameters for the development of the Argentine film industry were set.<ref name="manzano"/> Although these measures didn't restore international sales, they successfully revitalized film production levels: in 1950, the industry released 56 films, finally reaching the peak it had attained in 1942.{{sfn|Karush|2012|p=184}} 

According to Matthew B. Karush, there was a tendency to produce low-budget films due to limited capitalization and the idiosyncrasies of Argentina's protectionist framework.{{sfn|Karush|2012|p=184}} These films, reliant on subsidies, were assured screen time irrespective of their quality.{{sfn|Karush|2012|p=184}} The Peronist government actively pursued a moralizing and nationalistic agenda in the domestic cinema.{{sfn|Karush|2012|p=184}} Films deemed to be "of national interest" were granted privileged access to government credit, and the government centralized the distribution of raw film stock, favoring specific producers.{{sfn|Karush|2012|p=184}} By 1949, with the appointment of [[Raúl Alejandro Apold]], former press chief for Argentina Sono Film, as the undersecretary of information and press, the regime had effectively shaped a film industry where every artistic decision fell under political control.{{sfn|Karush|2012|p=184}} According to Clara Kriger, a researcher on the little-frequented subject of cinema and Peronism, there "was no written decalogue and there was no prior censorship", although "everyone knew that there were things that could not be said" and, in any case, what could happen was that the authorities would not give credit to certain screenplays.<ref name="kriger"/> It was a tacit but existing censorship, which occurred not only for political but also for religious or other reasons.<ref name="kriger"/>

Lumiton, which had been the country's first film studio, was also the first to succumb to the production crisis and was sold in 1949.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Se apaga Lumiton}} It continued operating under new ownership, though with reduced activity, until its bankruptcy in 1952.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Se apaga Lumiton}} The brand survived into the early 1960s, occasionally functioning as a distributor, while the studio facilities were mainly used for advertising productions before being leased to a trouser factory.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Se apaga Lumiton}} Estudios San Miguel reached its artistic peak shortly before its closure.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Estudios que cierran}} Under producer Manuel Alba it released {{ill|La barra de la esquina|lt=''La barra de la esquina''|es|La barra de la esquina}} (1950), directed by [[Julio Saraceni]] and remembered as one of [[Alberto Castillo (performer)|Alberto Castillo]]'s most notable films.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Estudios que cierran}} Lucas Demare followed with ''[[Los isleros]]'' (1951), based on a script by {{ill|Ernesto L. Castro|es|Ernesto L. Castro}}, which became a landmark in Tita Merello's career.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Estudios que cierran}} Around the same time, Carlos Hugo Christensen directed two acclaimed noir films adapted from [[William Irish]] stories, ''[[No abras nunca esa puerta]]'' (1952) and {{ill|Si muero antes de despertar|lt=''Si muero antes de despertar''|es|Si muero antes de despertar}} (1952).{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Estudios que cierran}} Despite these achievements, the studio went bankrupt in 1951.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Estudios que cierran}} Estudios EFA, by contrast, lacked consistent critical success, and most productions ranged from uneven to unsuccessful.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Estudios que cierran}} After the sale of the studio in 1951, its new owners continued sporadic production before operations ceased, and the original building was later adapted as the headquarters of [[El Trece|Canal 13]] television.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Estudios que cierran}}

===End and aftermath (1956–1962)===

In 1955, Perón was overthrown by the ''[[Revolución Libertadora]]'', which installed a military dictatorship. Contemporaries emphasize that the regime's impact on cinema was less a direct "mission" against film than a revelation and acceleration of a crisis that was already unfolding as the studio system unraveled.{{sfn|España|2005|p=19}} Under this new government, several exiled artists returned to Argentina, such as Francisco Petrone and María Rosa Gallo, while others remained abroad, such as Libertad Lamarque and Carlos Hugo Christensen.<ref name="ibermedia"/> Figures such as Luis César Amadori and Zully Moreno went into exile while Hugo del Carril faced reprisals for his links with Peronism.<ref name="ibermedia"/> The new government eliminated film subsidies, deregulated the sale of raw film stock and dissolved Peronist film policies without offering clear alternatives. In practice, this vacuum sharpened intra-sector conflicts: labor groupings and producers lobbied—sometimes through "independent" emissaries—over replacement mechanisms, and when the existing "social aid and film promotion" pact expired on 13 April 1956, exhibitors refused renewal, precipitating a production halt with only carryover releases reaching screens.{{sfn|España|2005|p=19}} This aggravated conflicts within the sector, where divisions arose between producers and directors.<ref name="ibermedia"/>

[[File:La casa del ángel still.jpg|thumb|left|[[Elsa Daniel]] and [[Lautaro Murúa]] in ''[[La casa del ángel]]'' (1957), directed by [[Leopoldo Torre Nilsson]] and produced by Argentina Sono Film.]]

By 1956, the economic measures introduced by the new dictatorship triggered a crisis that the film industry was unable to overcome, as major production companies closed, sold their studios, and much of their film archives were dispersed or lost.{{sfn|Peña|2024|p=251}} The only releases in 1956 were films made the previous year and there were only 15 national premieres in 1957.{{sfn|España|2005|p=66}} The end of the industrial era of Argentine cinema was foreseeable as before the coup, most of the "big studios" had already closed or stopped production, and the few that remained were still afloat thanks to state support.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=1956–1972}} Most films were made, as in the silent and early sound films, through isolated projects, where production companies were created to make one or two films, but these productions could not be considered "independent" because they only existed due to state support and did not represent a real alternative to the industrial model.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=1956–1972}} They were, in essence, products that imitated the industry, but lacked a real industrial infrastructure, and featured a variety of companies instead of the few that existed previously.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=1956–1972}}

[[File:El primer desnudo del cine argentino.png|thumb|[[Isabel Sarli]] in Armando Bó's ''[[El trueno entre las hojas]]'' (1958), starring in the first fully [[nude scene]] in Argentine cinema.]]

The market was mutating as early television experiments began to complicate theatrical windows, distributors probed co-productions with Europe and Latin America to extend reach with uneven results, and producers tested widescreen and color even as black-and-white and standard ratios remained preferred for personal or socially critical projects.{{sfn|España|2005|pp=65, 72, 77–79}} This transitional climate also fostered thematic ventures into the provinces, where cameras sought "authentic" landscapes in [[Catamarca Province|Catamarca]], [[Jujuy Province|Jujuy]] or [[Tucumán Province|Tucumán]].{{sfn|España|2005|p=67}} The period from 1957 to 1960 has been generally considered by Argentine film historians as one of passage between classical and modern cinema, often without going deeper into those conceptions.{{sfn|Manetti|Rodríguez Riva|2014|p=170}} A pervasive but ill-defined demand for "authenticity" dominated criticism and programming rhetoric, frequently used to censure industrial formulae without clear criteria; by 1960, recognition of the director's authorial mark (''[[auteur]]'') provided a new evaluative framework that helped steady the debate.{{sfn|España|2005|pp=19, 66–67}} According to film historian María Valdez, during that period local cinema appeared to "had fallen prey to a kind of generalized derangement, where anything could find a place."{{sfn|Manetti|Rodríguez Riva|2014|p=167}} Lucas Demare's ''[[Después del silencio]]'' (1956) and ''[[Detrás de un largo muro]]'' (1958) pursued social realism, while classic-era actor turned director [[Armando Bó]]'s ''[[El trueno entre las hojas]]'' (1958) introduced [[Isabel Sarli]] and inaugurated a cycle of erotic melodramas that would challenge censorship under the guise of morality.{{sfn|España|2005|pp=68–71}} In ''El trueno entre las hojas'', Sarli performed Latin America's first full-frontal [[nude scene]],<ref>{{cite book|page=317|title=Latin American Cinema: A Comparative History|last=Schroeder Rodríguez|first=Paul A.|year=2016|isbn=978-052-028-863-8|publisher=[[University of California Press]]}}</ref> launching her long partnership with Bó, whose internationally recognized [[sexploitation film]]s secured her lasting status as a national [[sex symbol]].<ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://time.com/archive/6911018/isabel-sarli-a-sex-bomb-at-lincoln-center/|title=Isabel Sarli: A Sex Bomb at Lincoln Center|magazine=[[Time (magazine)|Time]]|last=Corliss|first=Richard|date=7 August 2010|accessdate=8 December 2025|archive-date=10 February 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250210000042/https://time.com/archive/6911018/isabel-sarli-a-sex-bomb-at-lincoln-center/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cinemaretro.com/index.php?/archives/11953-Book-Review-Violated-Frames-Armando-Bo-and-Isabel-Sarlis-Sexploits-by-Victoria-Ruetalo.html|accessdate=8 December 2025|work=[[Cinema Retro]]|title=Book Review: 'Violated Frames: Armando Bó and Isabel Sarli's Sexploits by Victoria Ruétalo'|first=Adrian|last=Smith|date=20 October 2022|archive-date=20 October 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221020144934/http://www.cinemaretro.com/index.php?/archives/11953-Book-Review-Violated-Frames-Armando-Bo-and-Isabel-Sarlis-Sexploits-by-Victoria-Ruetalo.html|url-status=live}}</ref> 

Film historian Mariano Calistro proposed in 1984 an alternative periodization for the years immediately after the classical era, extending from 1957 to 1968, grounded in the historical trajectory of the period's filmmakers and the shifting affinities of their often loosely defined groups of belonging.{{sfn|Manetti|Rodríguez Riva|2014|p=167}} Some writers consider the premiere of [[Leopoldo Torre Nilsson]]'s ''[[La casa del ángel]]'' in 1957 as a turning point in Argentine cinema, marking the beginning of a new stage with a different proposal both in style and conception.<ref name="ibermedia"/> Nilsson's early cycle, scripted with [[Beatriz Guido]], including ''[[La caída]]'' (1959) and ''[[La mano en la trampa]]'' (1960), consolidated a fracture with the classical-industrial model by placing interior conflicts and adolescent subjectivities at the center of the narrative.{{sfn|España|2005|pp=74–75}} Parallel to this, [[Fernando Ayala]], often paired with [[Héctor Olivera (film director)|Héctor Olivera]], set up [[Aries Cinematográfica Argentina|Aries Cinematográfica]] to operate within the emerging regulatory framework.{{sfn|España|2005|p=76}} With ''[[El jefe (1958 film)|El jefe]]'' (1958) and ''[[The Candidate (1959 film)|El candidato]]'' (1959), Ayala modeled a sustainable production firm that balanced social allegory with industrial
