continuity.{{sfn|España|2005|p=76}} Such projects proved crucial to stabilizing the sector and to anchoring the broader passage into modern cinema.{{sfn|España|2005|p=76}} In 1957, the government enacted Decree Law 62/57, with measures to promote national cinematography as an industry, art and means of dissemination.<ref name="ibermedia"/> Passed after hard bargaining among guilds, producers and technicians, the decree created the National Institute of Cinematography (INC) to administer financing and regulation, equated cinematic freedom with press freedom, and earmarked a 10% levy on ticket sales to capitalize production credits, selective subsidies, promotion and an official film school.{{sfn|España|2005|pp=19, 73}} A later rule capping credits at one feature per company per year prompted larger firms to split into multiple labels to qualify, while "quality awards" tied to funding nudged average standards upward.{{sfn|España|2005|pp=80–81}}

In the early 1960s a new generation of filmmakers who opposed "commercial" cinema and experimented with unconventional cinematic techniques emerged.<ref name="cossalter"/><ref name="manzano14"/> The new trend, initially known as New Argentine Cinema (Spanish: "''nuevo cine argentino''") and later as the {{ill|Generation of '60|es|Generación del 60}} (Spanish: "''Generación del '60''"), was not a unified movement and included a series of directors who made their feature film debut between the late 1950s and early 1960s, including [[Enrique Dawi]] with ''[[Río abajo]]'' (1960), {{ill|Simón Feldman|es|Simón Feldman}} with {{ill|El negoción|lt=''El negoción''|es|El negoción}} (1959) and {{ill|Los de la mesa diez|lt=''Los de la mesa diez''|es|Los de la mesa diez}} (1960), {{ill|David Kohon|es|David Kohon}} with ''[[Prisioneros de una noche]]'' (1962) and {{ill|Tres veces Ana (film)|lt=''Tres veces Ana''|es|Tres veces Ana (película)}} (1961), [[José Martínez Suárez]] with ''[[El Crack (1960 film)|El crack]]'' (1960), {{ill|Dino Minitti|es|Dino Minitti}} with {{ill|Tiernas ilusiones|lt=''Tiernas ilusiones''|es|Tiernas ilusiones}} (1961), [[René Mugica]] with ''[[El centroforward murió al amanecer]]'' (1961), and [[Lautaro Murúa]] with ''[[Shunko]]'' (1960) and [[Alias Gardelito]] (1961).{{sfn|Feldman|1990|p=46}} By the mid-1960s, critics already spoke of the "end" of this first wave, yet its imprint was durable.{{sfn|España|2005|pp=83–84}} [[Film society|Cine-clubs]] such as {{ill|Cine Club Núcleo|lt=Núcleo|es|Cine Club Núcleo}} and journals like {{ill|Tiempo de Cine|lt=''Tiempo de Cine''|es|Tiempo de Cine}} elevated the debates around modern cinema, while INC subsidies, short-film grants from the 1958 [[Fondo Nacional de las Artes]], and project-based production models institutionalized many of the practices pioneered by the Generation of '60.{{sfn|España|2005|pp=73, 80–81, 83}} These legacies shaped subsequent directors and ensured that, even after the movement's critical exhaustion, its ethos remained embedded in Argentine film culture.{{sfn|España|2005|p=84}}

==Style and themes==
===1933–1939: Tango and working-class culture===
{{Multiple image|total_width = 400
|image1=Tagliacozzo, Troilo, Rizutti y Sandrini en Los tres berretines.jpg
|image2=El alma del bandoneón 1935.jpg
|footer=Musical numbers in ''Los tres berretines'' (1933) ''(left)'' and ''[[El alma del bandoneón]]'' (1935) ''(right)''. The early films of classical Argentine cinema were aimed at the ''porteño'' [[working class]]es, incorporating the popular [[tango music]] as one of its main attractions.<ref name="tesis"/>
}}
The Argentine cinema of the 1930s was characterized by a deliberate effort to portray the working classes, which, in turn, emerged as its main consumers.<ref name="tesis"/>

The first Argentine sound films were strongly linked to theatrical performances, which was reflected in their staging and [[List of acting techniques|acting style]].{{sfn|Berardi|2006|p=27}} As noted by Karush: "Domestic filmmakers benefited from the long tradition of popular theater in Argentina, particularly the short comic plays known as sainetes; by providing comparable entertainment at a lower admission price, they could capture an already existing audience."{{sfn|Karush|2012|p=76}} In early classical films like ''¡Tango!'' (1933), ''[[Radio Bar|Radio bar]]'' (1936) and {{ill|Por buen camino|lt=''Por buen camino''|es|Por buen camino}} (1935), the "actors speak, move and gesticulate as if they were on a theatrical stage. The camera was limited to capturing those gestures and attitudes (which today seem excessive or exaggerated), often in fixed general shots, so that the actors could move without risk of going out of frame."{{sfn|Berardi|2006|p=27}} Some critics, such as Domingo Di Núbila, identified these "narrative weaknesses" in terms of "backwardness" in relation to the cinema of other countries.{{sfn|Berardi|2006|p=27}} On the other hand, writer Mario Berardi suggests that it was actually a moment of "creative freedom", in which filmmakers "made use of the impunity of the 'no one knows' to freely appropriate the resources of the new medium. On the contrary, in the 40s and 50s, filmmakers submitted to the canons of the industry, giving rise to a homogeneous and strongly structured mode of representation."{{sfn|Berardi|2006|p=28}} According to {{ill|Ricardo García Oliveri|es|Ricardo García Oliveri}}, the directors of the early sound period "have in common the intuition, the enthusiasm and the sense of the popular. These directors generally come from the middle class and they all coincide, at this stage, in a naive cinema, considered ordinary by the upper classes and hardly costumbrist by the aesthetes, but with virtues that are not harmed by its eminently local content."<ref name="ibermedia"/>

[[File:Alicia Vignoli en Puerto Nuevo.jpg|thumb|upright|left|[[Alicia Vignoli]] in Soffici and Amadori's ''Puerto Nuevo'' (1936), a tango melodrama set in a ''[[villa miseria]]'' (i.e., [[shanty town]] or [[slum]]) at the [[port of Buenos Aires]].{{sfn|Di Núbila|1998|pp=128–132}}]]

Sound technology broadened cinema's appeal by making films accessible to immigrants and to audiences of varying levels of literacy.{{sfn|España|1999|p=233}} For many spectators, cinema became an arena for social integration, offering models of speech, behavior and social aspiration.{{sfn|España|1999|pp=233, 243, 253}} The early sound period thus drew heavily on the theater and radio, encouraging stage and radio performers to cross over into film.{{sfn|España|1999|pp=231, 233}} It required directors with an overarching vision, as well as scenographers and costume designers capable of imbuing productions with social prestige and period detail.{{sfn|España|1999|pp=233–234}} Music became an essential communicative element, while editing was conceived not only as a technical process but also as the arena where ideological frameworks and generic conventions were established.{{sfn|España|1999|p=234}} The institutionalization of narrative followed what film theorist [[Noël Burch]] has termed the "[[institutional mode of representation]]", privileging transparency and immersion.{{sfn|España|1999|pp=234–235}} Argentine classical cinema sought to present stories without noticeable mediation, allowing audiences to identify directly with characters and situations.{{sfn|España|1999|p=234}} Although later decades would expose fissures in this model, during the 1930s the dominant trend was to minimize the visible presence of the author and privilege collective identification.{{sfn|España|1999|pp=234–235}} The approach was aimed particularly at the urban middle and working-class audiences, who found in cinema both entertainment and a framework for imagining themselves as Argentines.{{sfn|España|1999|pp=233, 243}} The star system was central to this process, and by the late 1930s an extensive constellation of actors and actresses provided Argentine cinema with a distinctive repertoire of recognizable personas that embodied class, gender and ethnic archetypes.{{sfn|España|1999|pp=235–236, 238}}

[[File:Los muchachos de antes no usaban gomina, rodaje.jpg|thumb|Shooting of a scene of ''[[The Boys Didn't Wear Hair Gel Before (1937 film)|Los muchachos de antes no usaban gomina]]'' (1937), directed by Manuel Romero, a film centered on the lowly settings of Buenos Aires in the early 20th century where the tango emerged.{{sfn|Di Núbila|1998|p=154}}]]

Unlike American cinema, Argentine industrial cinema was slow to structure its production in the well-defined matrices of [[film genre]]s.{{sfn|Lusnich|2007|p=14}} Peña noted that, although in terms of production the Argentine industry wanted to resemble that of the US and [[Cinema of France|France]], it "owes less to these other cinematographies than to its strong links with tango, radio or revue, forms of popular art from which many of its main performers, directors and screenwriters came. These roots not only conditioned a certain aesthetic in a particular way, but also the configuration of the various genres, which are almost always hybrids."{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=Introducción}} Gardel's success with Paramount was also extremely influential, as it showed Argentine filmmakers that by focusing on local authenticity, settings, and dialects, they could effectively compete with Americans, taking advantage of actors "who were often recognizable to filmgoers from their previous careers in theater and radio".{{sfn|Karush|2012|p=76}} The first defined genre of Argentine cinema consisted of a "sentimental narrative structure originated in the tango",{{sfn|Lusnich|2007|p=13}} which has been called the "tango melodrama" (Spanish: ''melodrama tanguero'').{{sfn|Manetti|Rodríguez Riva|2014|p=28}}{{sfn|Lusnich|2007|p=13}} This style had its antecedents in the silent films of the 1920s, especially in the work of José A. Ferreyra, focused on portraying the world and characters associated with tango, a genre linked to the lower-class neighborhoods of Buenos Aires.{{sfn|Manetti|Rodríguez Riva|2014|p=26}} According to Karush, Argentine classical cinema, and national mass culture of the 1930s as a whole, was most significantly influenced by [[Melodrama (film genre)|melodrama]].{{sfn|Karush|2012|p=85}} This cultural mode not only shaped the aesthetic of media content but also reflected a society starkly divided by class.{{sfn|Karush|2012|p=86}} Local producers, while adopting styles from the United States, often portrayed an Argentina where class divides were insurmountable, even with hard work.{{sfn|Karush|2012|p=11}} Argentine films promoted consumerist dreams but simultaneously critiqued the moral failings of the wealthy.{{sfn|Karush|2012|p=11}} The authenticity of cultural products was tied to their roots in the lower-class neighborhoods, emphasizing a narrative of class struggle.{{sfn|Karush|2012|p=11}} Tango, a key element of this period's culture, often told tales of moral corruption and downfall linked to the opulence of the rich, contrasting with the purity and solidarity of the poor.{{sfn|Karush|2012|p=11}} Melodrama's conventions were not just limited to cinema; they permeated radio, poetry, theater, and even circus performances, highlighting emotional excess and a clear division between the rich and the poor.{{sfn|Karush|2012|p=86}} This portrayal of Argentina as a rigidly stratified society was a stark contrast to the more nuanced, fluid class interactions in Buenos Aires neighborhoods of the time.{{sfn|Karush|2012|p=85}}{{sfn|Karush|2012|p=86}}

[[File:José Gola y Amelia Bence.jpg|thumb|left|[[José Gola]] and [[Amelia Bence]] in ''[[La vuelta al nido]]'' (1938), directed by Leopoldo Torres Ríos. Initially withheld from release and a commercial failure, it was later celebrated for its unconventional narrative.<ref>{{cite book|editor-first=Lautaro|editor-last=García Candela|editor-last2=Granero|editor-first2=Lucas|editor-first3=Lucía|editor-last3=Salas|editor-last4=Sonzini|editor-first4=Ramiro|title=La vida útil|issue=6|issn=2618-5318|location=Córdoba|year=2023|language=es|chapter=Dossier: Cine clásico argentino|pages=67–68|publisher=Ramiro Sonzini}}</ref>]]

[[Immigration to Argentina|Immigration]] was a recurrent theme in early sound films, reflecting both optimism and ambivalence about Argentina's social composition.{{sfn|España|1999|p=238}} Portrayals of foreigners oscillated between affirmations of immigrant contribution to the middle class and tragic or grotesque depictions of failure.{{sfn|España|1999|p=238}} Urban nightlife was another important motif, with cabarets, theaters and brothels serving as settings for moral lessons and melodramatic conflicts.{{sfn|España|1999|pp=238, 244}} At the same time, the home was consistently depicted as the guarantor of virtue, education, and stability, often contrasted with the corruption or frivolity of the upper classes.{{sfn|España|1999|p=238}} Literary and theatrical adaptations were abundant, ranging from local authors such as [[Florencio Sánchez]] and [[Enrique Larreta]] to international figures including [[Ibsen]], [[Balzac]] and [[García Lorca]].{{sfn|España|1999|p=239}} Theater provided not only source material but also a steady flow of performers.{{sfn|España|1999|p=239}} Tango, however, was the cultural form most central to Argentine sound cinema, linking the worlds of stage, radio, record, and film.{{sfn|España|1999|p=239}} Films like ''El alma del bandoneón'' (1935) and ''Besos brujos'' (1937) combined musical performance with melodrama, reinforcing tango's association with lower-class neighborhoods and narratives of moral corruption and downfall.{{sfn|España|1999|pp=239, 243, 251–252}} By the late 1930s, filmmakers such as Mario Soffici and Luis Saslavsky pushed stylistic and thematic boundaries.{{sfn|España|1999|pp=246–247}} ''Prisioneros de la tierra'' (1939), based on stories by [[Horacio Quiroga]], combined realism with poetic imagery in its depiction of exploited [[yerba mate]] workers, while ''[[Puerta cerrada]]'' (1939) introduced sophisticated use of flashbacks to narrate the tragic trajectory of a tango singer, [[Nina Miranda (Uruguayan singer)|Nina Miranda]], played by Lamarque.{{sfn|España|1999|p=246}} Leopoldo Torres Ríos' ''La vuelta al nido'' (1938) anticipated [[Modernist film|modernist]] sensibilities with its restrained tone and depiction of urban alienation.{{sfn|España|1999|p=247}} These works signaled that, even within a studio-driven system, directors could assert individual styles.{{sfn|España|1999|p=247}}

[[File:Camila Quiroga y Ángel Magaña en Viento norte.jpg|thumb|[[Camila Quiroga]] and Ángel Magaña in Mario Soffici's ''[[North Wind (film)|Viento norte]]'' (1937), a [[historical epic]] that helped establish the "social-folkloric drama" style.{{sfn|Lusnich|2007|pp=27–31}}]]

Over time, the rural–urban divide that had characterized silent cinema gave way to depictions of the countryside as either a site of retreat for urban dwellers or the stage for historical epics.{{sfn|España|1999|p=239}} Aside from tango-based films, film scholars, notably Ana Laura Lusnich, have also identified another important genre of the classical era of Argentine cinema, the so-called ''drama social-folclórico'' (English: "social-folkloric drama"),<ref name="krigerhistoria"/>{{sfn|Lusnich|2007|p=19}} a local variant of the [[epic film]] that was prevalent between 1933 and 1956.{{sfn|Lusnich|2007|p=16}} The social-folkloric drama emerged as a distinctive style that weaved together influences from established cinematic traditions and local artistic expressions, such as literature, theater, and visual arts.{{sfn|Lusnich|2007|pp=23–24}} It is defined by straightforward narratives that progress through a defined temporal and spatial journey, featuring protagonists whose lives are deeply intertwined with their social surroundings.{{sfn|Lusnich|2007|pp=23–24}} The visual and auditory elements are crafted to heighten the storytelling and emotional impact, while the narrative structure often incorporates framed tales that create a unified whole.{{sfn|Lusnich|2007|pp=23–24}} This model frequently delves into cultural tensions like civilization versus barbarism and rural versus urban life, reflecting broader societal themes.{{sfn|Lusnich|2007|pp=23–24}} Within this framework, two main variants stand out: [[biographical films]], which portray either historical figures or popular heroes, and [[historical drama]]s, encompassing stories of independence struggles, social and economic conflicts, or romantic intrigues, showcasing the versatility of this cinematic approach.{{sfn|Lusnich|2007|pp=23–24}} Examples include biographical films such as ''[[Su mejor alumno]]'' (1944) and ''[[Santos Vega vuelve]]'' (1947); films set during the Independence era such as ''[[North Wind (film)|Viento norte]]'' (1937), ''La guerra gaucha'' (1942) and ''[[Savage Pampas (1945 film)|Pampa bárbara]]'' (1945); and films focused on socioeconomic conflict such as ''[[Kilómetro 111]]'' (1938), ''Prisioneros de la tierra'' (1939), ''El cura gaucho'' (1941) and ''[[Dark River (1952 film)|Las aguas bajan turbias]]'' (1952), among others.{{sfn|Lusnich|2007|p=27}}

===1939–1945: Turn to bourgeois topics===
[[File:Así es la vida 1939 lobby card crop.jpg|thumb|A scene from [[Francisco Mugica]]'s ''[[Such Is Life (1939 film)|Así es la vida]]'' (1939), which marked a turning point in the adoption of [[Bourgeoisie|bourgeois]] settings.]]

By the early 1940s, audiences had shifted significantly: the majority of cinema-goers were women and children, and studios increasingly tailored films to domestic, family-oriented consumption.{{sfn|España|1999|p=246}} Argentina Sono Film promoted itself as "a family that makes films for families", while Lumiton emphasized its orientation toward more cosmopolitan themes.{{sfn|España|1999|p=246}} 

The release of ''Así es la vida'' (1939) is regarded as a turning point for the themes, stars, directors and representation universes in Argentine cinema.<ref name="tesis"/> For the first time, the ascending middle class and the bourgeoisie emerged as protagonists who elicited empathy and identification from the audience, in contrast to previous cinema that criticized and portrayed the upper classes as villains.<ref name="tesis"/> Unlike the ruling classes depicted in Manuel Romero's films, associated with the imagery of an elite land-owning oligarchy, the protagonists of ''Así es la vida'' belong to an industrial and professional bourgeoisie, something that promoted ideas of social ascent and appealed to the middle classes, through its celebration of hard work and family unity.<ref name="tesis"/> The film did not target differentiated audiences but encompassed both lower and middle to upper-class sectors, allowing identification for the latter while also shaping specific imaginations and aspirations; by integrating modernity into the national reality, it reconciled both factors through the exaltation of the family as a point of balance.<ref name="tesis"/>

The box-office and critical success of ''Así es la vida'' led to the proliferation of films that sought to imitate its style, such as Alberto de Zavalía's {{ill|Dama de compañía|lt=''Dama de compañía''|es|Dama de compañía (película)}}, Luis Bayón Herrera's {{ill|Mi fortuna por un nieto|lt=''Mi fortuna por un nieto''|es|Mi fortuna por un nieto}} and Mugica's ''[[Medio millón por una mujer]]'', all of them premiering in 1940.<ref name="tesis"/> However, none of these productions managed to replicate the success of ''Así es la vida'', and debates persisted in the specialized press regarding the need to renew Argentine cinema without alienating the working classes.<ref name="tesis"/> These debates and problems seemed to be settled with the release of ''[[Los martes, orquídeas]]'' (1941), which was a success with both audiences and critics, and even had an American remake the following year, titled ''[[You Were Never Lovelier]]''.<ref name="tesis"/> The film opened the doors to a new style that would enjoy great success during the 1940s: that of the so-called "bourgeois comedy" (Spanish: ''comedia burguesa'').<ref name="tesis"/> In particular, ''Los martes, orquídeas'' was the initiator and main exponent of the so-called ''cine de ingenuas'' (which may be translated to "ingénue cinema" or "cinema of naive women"), the first dominant model adopted by the bourgeois comedy in Argentine cinema.<ref name="tesis"/> The ''cine de ingenuas'' introduced new themes, scenarios and imagery for the local film industry, largely thanks to the incorporation of teenage girl debutantes in leading roles.<ref name="tesis"/> The new genre was based on the already internationally known "[[ingénue]]" type, defined as a "beautiful, pure, generous and virginal adolescent girl, who has not yet come into contact with the world."<ref name="tesis"/> In Italy, it had its greatest exponent with the so-called ''[[Telefoni Bianchi]]'' films (Italian for "white telephones"), while American actress [[Deanna Durbin]] became a paradigmatic example of international presence.<ref name="tesis"/> Beyond the central figure of the ingénue, the innovation of the ''cine de ingenuas'' was to radically alter the development of stories and imaginaries in local cinema, as the 1930s trend of criticizing the upper classes was abandoned in favor of depicting them as an idyllic space, where the bourgeois family served as a moral beacon for tradition in the face of the dangers of modernity.<ref name="tesis"/>

''Los martes, orquídeas'' was followed by other productions that introduced young female actresses, including [[Nury Montsé]] in ''[[Canción de cuna (1941 film)|Canción de cuna]]'' (1941), {{ill|Nelly Hering|es|Nelly Hering}} in ''[[Sensational Kidnapping|Secuestro sensacional!!!]]'' (1942) or {{ill|Mariana Martí|es|Mariana Martí}} in {{ill|Dieciséis años|lt=''Dieciséis años''|es|Dieciséis años}} (1943).<ref name="tesis"/> One of the main strategies in the search for new attractions were the contests promoted by magazines or companies, from which the main figures of the genre emerged: Mirtha Legrand (a main reference point after her debut in ''Los martes, orquídeas'') and [[María Duval (Argentine actress)|María Duval]], the two actresses who most frequently embodied the ingénue role under the process of [[typecasting]] and were also incorporated into the star system.<ref name="tesis"/> Unlike these two, the other actresses who were pigeonholed as ''ingenuas'' took part in films with more varied narrative and ideological proposals.<ref name="tesis"/> Within the ''cine de ingenuas'', Duval became the main star associated with the "family comedy" genre, starring in titles such as {{ill|Cada hogar, un mundo|lt=''Cada hogar, un mundo''|es|Cada hogar, un mundo}} (1942), {{ill|Su primer baile|lt=''Su primer baile''|es|Su primer baile}} (1942) and {{ill|Casi un sueño|lt=''Casi un sueño''|es|Casi un sueño}} (1943); while Legrand was the leading figure in romantic comedy, starring in titles written specifically for her ingénue figure, such as ''[[The Journey (1942 film)|El viaje]]'' (1942), {{ill|Claro de luna (film)|lt=''Claro de luna''|es|Claro de luna (película)}} (1942) or ''[[Adolescencia]]'' (1942).<ref name="tesis"/> 

Although it has often been underestimated by historians, the ''cine de ingenuas'' was a genre of great relevance in Argentine cinema between 1941 and 1945, reaching 20% of national film production in 1942.<ref name="tesis"/> However, it soon declined due to several factors, such as the increasing age of the genre's stars, the overexploitation of the same themes, and its evasion of the modern world at a time of transition for Argentine society.<ref name="tesis"/> In response to this, the developers of the genre decided to turn to urban melodramas with a central sexual component, or to zany comedies with modern rather than naive girls.<ref name="tesis"/> The pioneer in this sense was Carlos Hugo Christensen, with titles such as ''[[Safo, historia de una pasión]]'' (1943), ''Dieciséis años'' (1943) and ''La pequeña señora de Pérez'' (1944).<ref name="tesis"/>

===1945–1956: International aspirations and Peronism===
[[File:La señora de Pérez se divorcia.jpeg|thumb|Mirtha Legrand and Juan Carlos Thorry in {{ill|La señora de Pérez se divorcia|lt=''La señora de Pérez se divorcia''|es|La señora de Pérez se divorcia}} (1945), directed by Carlos Hugo Christensen. Films like this overcame the ingénue model and opened the way to the more modern and cosmopolitan ''cine de fiesta''.<ref name="tesis"/>]]
The exhaustion of the ''comedia de ingenuas'' model around 1945 gave way to the second model of bourgeois comedy in Argentine cinema, the so-called ''cine de fiesta'' (literally "party cinema"), which was characterized by its celebration of urban life and focus on young, bourgeois couples who revel in leisure and entertainment while defying traditional social expectations.<ref name="tesis"/> This subgenre signified a marked departure from the earlier ''cine de ingenuas'', not only through its thematic content but also in its stylistic approach to filmmaking.<ref name="tesis"/> The narrative and thematic elements of the ''cine de fiesta'' explicitly challenged the established norms of romantic love, the sanctity of monogamy, and the rigidity of social institutions.<ref name="tesis"/> Instead, it celebrated a more liberated, joyful existence marked by the exuberance of youth and the excitement of modernity.<ref name="tesis"/>

The directors Schlieper and Christensen were central to this genre.<ref name="tesis"/> Their work captured a society in flux during the mid-20th century in Argentina—a time of significant social mobility, the rise of the middle class, and the political upheaval with the advent of Peronism in 1945.<ref name="tesis"/>

This period was also marked by a surge in consumer culture and urban modernization, where comfort and access to entertainment became not just luxuries but necessities of a modern lifestyle.<ref name="tesis"/> The ''cine de fiesta'' thus provided a cinematic mirror to these societal shifts, showcasing a world where the pursuit of pleasure and immediate gratification was celebrated.<ref name="tesis"/> Initially, the genre was critiqued for its perceived superficiality or triviality.<ref name="tesis"/> However, over time, there has been a reevaluation of the ''cine de fiesta''{{'}}s contribution to the evolution of comedy in Argentine cinema and connection to the [[screwball comedies]] of the United States, yet with unique influences from directors like [[Preston Sturges]] and [[Ernst Lubitsch]].<ref name="tesis"/> Some examples of party films include Christensen's ''[[Adán y la serpiente]]'' (1946) and ''[[Con el diablo en el cuerpo]]'' (1947), and Schlieper's ''[[Arroz con leche (1950 film)|Arroz con leche]]'' (1950), ''[[Cuando besa mi marido]]'' (1950), ''[[Esposa último modelo]]'' (1950) and ''[[Cosas de mujer]]'' (1951), all of them theatrical adaptations.<ref name="tesis"/> At the same time, comedians such as Niní Marshall and Luis Sandrini sustained mass appeal with [[grotesque]] and popular humor, while Mirtha Legrand consolidated her screen persona in comedies directed by Daniel Tinayre and Luis César Amadori, which mixed genre conventions with touches of glamour and melodrama.{{sfn|España|2005|pp=26–28, 31, 34, 52, 56–58}}

[[File:Enrique Alvarez Diosdado - Delia Garcés - La dama duende (1944).jpg|thumb|left|[[Enrique Diosdado]] and Delia Garcés in ''[[La dama duende]]'' (1945), directed by Luis Saslavsky, an example of the growing tendency of Argentine cinema to adapt foreign works.]]
As the 1940s progressed, the style of Argentine cinema became increasingly "internationalist" as a strategy to gain markets.<ref name="ibermedia"/> This was reflected in an increasing interest in adapting foreign literary works, the disuse of Argentine Spanish and the elimination of other local or costumbrist references.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=El afán internacional}}<ref name="ibermedia"/> Examples of this trend include Saraceni's ''[[The Three Musketeers (1946 film)|Los tres mosqueteros]]'' (1946), Soffici's ''[[El pecado de Julia]]'' (1946), Schlieper's ''[[Madame Bovary (1947 film)|Madame Bovary]]'' (1947), and Saslavsky's ''[[Story of a Bad Woman|Historia de una mala mujer]]'' (1948), among others.{{sfn|Peña|2012|loc=El afán internacional}} The purported elimination of Argentine identity that characterized the last stage of classical Argentine cinema was harshly evaluated by traditional Argentine historiography. Mahieu described the period as the "rise of the falsely international, hybrid cinema, the pink comedy, the hollow melodrama", although he commended the "isolated exceptions" of {{ill|Pelota de trapo|lt=''Pelota de trapo''|es|Pelota de trapo (película)}} (1948), ''[[El crimen de Oribe]]'' (1950), ''[[Días de odio]]'' (1954) and ''Las aguas bajan turbias'' (1952).{{sfn|Mahieu|1966|p=73}} This "prestige cinema" was reinforced by star-centered melodramas.{{sfn|España|2005|pp=43–44}} [[Zully Moreno]], often directed by Amadori or Arancibia, became the archetypal diva in ''[[The Lady of the Camellias (1953 Argentine film)|La mujer de las camelias]]'' (1953), [[La Dama del mar|''La dama del mar'']] (1954) or ''[[El barro humano]]'' (1955), where elaborate décor and tragic heroines displaced ''[[costumbrismo]]'' in favor of a cosmopolitan ''mise-en-scène''.{{sfn|España|2005|p=44}} [[Laura Hidalgo]] offered a darker variant in ''El túnel'' (1952) and ''[[Armiño negro]]'' (1953), where [[existentialist]] overtones and fractured flashbacks revealed the cracks in classical narrative.{{sfn|España|2005|pp=45–46, 64}} The widespread use of [[Flashback (narrative)|flashback]] as a narrative device, fashionable both locally and internationally, fractured linearity and allowed more complex temporal structures, even if audiences sometimes complained of its overuse.{{sfn|España|2005|pp=32–33, 43}}

[[File:Zully Moreno y Arturo de Córdova.jpg|thumb|[[Zully Moreno]] and [[Arturo de Córdova]] in ''[[Dios se lo pague]]'' (1948), directed by [[Luis César Amadori]].]]

During the Peronist era, Argentine cinema continued the comedic trends of the early 1940s,<ref name="manzano"/> with films often reflecting elements of official discourse despite the absence of explicit propaganda.<ref name="kriger"/> According to Clara Kriger, one of the greatest examples of this is the successful melodrama ''[[Dios se lo pague]]'' (1948), which, despite being labeled a typical "hybrid" film of the 1940s and early 1950s for its perceived lack of clear contextual grounding, embodies Peronism's emphasis on social reconciliation by portraying harmony between rich and poor, aligning with the movement's ideological rhetoric, while highlighting the centrality of public institutions like hospitals, reflecting the Peronist advocacy for state-driven [[social welfare]].<ref name="kriger"/> Additionally, the film's commercial logic capitalized on the prevailing Peronist discourse, incorporating characters like factory workers and working women in prominent roles, which echoed the social mobility and visibility of these groups under Perón's policies.<ref name="kriger"/>

Unlike countries of the region like Mexico and Brazil, Argentina's cinematic engagement with state ideology was relatively late, emerging prominently under Perón.<ref name="kriger"/> Globally, the era's cinema shared similarities with state-influenced filmmaking, such as American [[New Deal]] documentaries or British wartime propaganda, where governments leveraged film to communicate with citizens.<ref name="kriger"/> However, Argentina's classical cinema stood out for its integration of Peronist themes into mainstream melodramas rather than relying solely on documentaries, blending entertainment with ideological messaging in a way that felt organic to audiences.<ref name="kriger"/> The lack of archival records complicates understanding the production context of these films, as unlike studies of in the United States or Mexican films during [[Lázaro Cárdenas]]' rule, where detailed documentation exists, Argentina's Peronist-era archives were destroyed, leaving researchers to rely on the films themselves.<ref name="kriger"/> Films such as ''Los isleros'' (1951) or ''Las aguas bajan turbias'' (1952) gave melodrama a socially committed dimension, linking collective labor and female sacrifice to Peronist values, while ''[[Mercado de abasto|Mercado de Abasto]]'' (1955) turned a Buenos Aires market into a showcase of official anti-speculation discourse.{{sfn|España|2005|pp=47, 63–65}} These narratives often blended [[Italian neorealism|neorealist]] influence with heightened melodramatic codes, using ''[[chiaroscuro]]'' cinematography and voice-over to emphasize moral struggle.{{sfn|España|2005|pp=48, 63–64}}

[[File:El grito sagrado 1954.jpg|thumb|left|[[Fanny Navarro]] and [[Carlos Cores]] in the [[Mariquita Sánchez]] biopic ''[[El grito sagrado]]'' (1954), directed by Luis César Amadori. The film represents the heroine as a figure similar to [[Eva Perón]], portrayed as a fighter for the poor and disadvantaged.<ref>{{cite book|via=[[Google Books]]|accessdate=11 November 2023|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xwQOEAAAQBAJ|type=eBook|chapter=El militar: San Martín y el poder por la fuerza (del Padre de la Patria al paternalismo criollo)|location=Buenos Aires|publisher=Biblos|title=Biopics: historia y poética en el cine argentino reciente|year=2020|first1=Alfredo|last1=Dillon|first2=María Teresa|last2=Téramo|isbn=978-987-691-893-0|language=es}}</ref>]]

According to Valeria Manzano, the Peronist government supported "highly moral films, which exalted values such as solidarity, the maintenance of family unity, and patriotism, and pointed out binary oppositions that were typical of the Peronist public discourse, such as 'people-oligarchy' or 'luxury-austerity'."<ref name="manzano"/> The emergence of the industrial ''[[nouveau riche]]'' was portrayed in contrast with old elites, often through parody, as seen in Carlos Schlieper's ''[[Esposa último modelo]]'' (1950).<ref name="manzano"/> Manzano highlights the exaggerated style of these films: "Everything appears exaggerated, even ridiculed: exuberant costumes, overloaded sets, and the chaos that reigns in these new 'disordered' houses. (...) In this chaos, marital entanglements take place (...) the resolution of these conflicts leads to a rarely disguised moral: any 'male mischief' will be forgiven, as long as it does not endanger the security of the home."<ref name="manzano"/>

Manzano also examines the comedies of Niní Marshall and Luis Sandrini, where "conflicts are resolved by tapping into a kind of 'popular common sense'."<ref name="manzano"/> These films frequently depicted low-skilled workers striving for middle-class stability and highlighted the acceptance of class boundaries, like in Manuel Romero's ''[[Navidad de los pobres]]'' (1947), where "the class society of Peronism coexists (...) the classes share a code and a conflict, the relationships are friendly and pleasant, but the assigned places are never, ever subverted."<ref name="manzano"/> Another recurring theme was a work ethic opposed to "corruption" and "idleness", exemplified by Pepe Arias' roles, where his character "usually begins by dreaming of being able to escape the harshness of work and takes on a thousand characters to achieve it."<ref name="manzano"/> [[Sports film|Sports dramas]] such as ''[[Escuela de campeones]]'' (1950) or ''[[El cura Lorenzo]]'' (1954) reinforced this ethos of discipline and sacrifice, while musical comedies starring [[Lolita Torres]] or [[Amelia Vargas|Amelita Vargas]] integrated popular rhythms like tango, [[bolero]] and [[Mambo (music)|mambo]] into optimistic narratives of family, youth and nation.{{sfn|España|2005|pp=53–54, 56}} The cycle of "quickie" films by the {{ill|Productora General Belgrano|es|Productora General Belgrano}} studio exploited radio and revue stars such as [[Pepe Iglesias|Pepe "El Zorro" Iglesias]] or Los Cinco Grandes del Buen Humor, demonstrating how comic parody and music offered escapist entertainment within the moral boundaries promoted by the regime.{{sfn|España|2005|pp=35, 53–55}}

The 1940s and 1950s marked the peak of Argentine noir, with directors like Carlos Hugo Christensen, [[Román Viñoly Barreto]], Hugo Fregonese, [[Don Napy]], Daniel Tinayre and Mario Soffici producing some of the era's most celebrated titles.<ref name="noir">{{cite web|url=https://www.pagina12.com.ar/diario/suplementos/radar/9-8438-2012-12-09.html|work=Radar. [[Página/12]]|language=es|accessdate=26 December 2022|title=El aluvión noir|date=9 December 2012|first=Paula|last=Vazquez Prieto|archive-date=26 December 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221226134940/https://www.pagina12.com.ar/diario/suplementos/radar/9-8438-2012-12-09.html|url-status=live}}</ref>{{sfn|Peña|2024|pp=241–251}} Argentine cinema developed a distinctive form of [[film noir]], shaped by both American and French influences while drawing on local cultural elements such as tango and popular literature.{{sfn|Peña|2024|pp=241–251}} French critics coined the term film noir in the postwar era to describe 1940s American [[crime film]]s which blurred the boundaries between good and evil and emphasized moral ambiguity, nocturnal atmospheres, and feelings of paranoia and fatalism.{{sfn|Peña|2024|pp=241–251}} In Argentina, these traits appeared early on, with silent films like {{ill|Bajo la mirada de Dios|lt=''Bajo la mirada de Dios''|es|Bajo la mirada de Dios}} (1925) and the first sound-era crime successes such as Arturo S. Mom's ''Monte criollo'' (1935) and ''Palermo'' (1937), which merged crime plots with popular music and tango.{{sfn|Peña|2024|pp=241–251}} Directors like Manuel Romero and Daniel Tinayre later expanded on this formula with films like ''[[Ven... mi corazón te llama]]'' (1942) and ''[[Vidas marcadas]]'' (1942), respectively, incorporating the archetype of the [[femme fatale]].{{sfn|Peña|2024|pp=241–251}} Christensen's ''No abras nunca esa puerta'' (1952) and Viñoly Barreto's ''[[La bestia debe morir]]'' (1952) showcased atmospheric visuals, psychological tension and morally complex characters.<ref name="noir"/>{{sfn|Peña|2024|pp=241–251}} Meanwhile, ''[[Apenas un delincuente]]'' (1948) reflected Italian neorealist influences, while ''[[Los tallos amargos]]'' (1956) captured the essence of classic noir with its subjective narrative and bleak tone.{{sfn|Peña|2024|pp=241–251}} The portrayal of law enforcement was often reverential due to political pressures, leading some filmmakers to create "police-less" noirs, as seen in ''Los tallos amargos''.{{sfn|Peña|2024|pp=241–251}} Complementary cycles like ''[[El vampiro negro]]'' (1953), ''[[Barrio gris]]'' (1954) or ''[[Deshonra]]'' (1952) broadened noir toward carceral melodrama and social tableaux of Buenos Aires' underworld, while adaptations from the ''Séptimo Círculo'' detective series underscored the period's interplay between literary prestige and [[Pulp magazine|pulp suspense]].{{sfn|España|2005|pp=50, 58–60, 64}} These films exploited ''chiaroscuro'' lighting, fractured temporality and grotesque villains such as [[Nathán Pinzón]]'s child predator in ''El vampiro negro'', pushing the classical codes toward darker, more disturbing registers.{{sfn|España|2005|pp=48, 60, 62, 65}}

==Historiography==
===1959–1966: Foundational works===
The first [[historiographic]] proposals on national cinema appeared in a very fragmentary manner and in specialized magazines shortly after the emergence of the Argentine film industry.<ref name="krigerhistoria">{{cite journal|url=http://www.adversus.org/indice/nro-26/dossier/XI2609.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200717212254/https://www.adversus.org/indice/nro-26/dossier/XI2609.pdf|archive-date=17 July 2020|accessdate=27 August 2024|year=2014|first=Clara|last=Kriger|journal=AdVersuS|language=es|location=Buenos Aires|issue=XI|pages=133–150|issn=1669-7588|publisher=Istituto Italo-argentino di Ricerca Sociale|title=Estudios sobre cine clásico en Argentina: de la perspectiva nacional a la comparada}}</ref> In the mid-1940s, there was a publishing boom in the United States and Europe of books on film history, which ignored Latin American industries such as Argentina's, beyond a few brief mentions.<ref name="krigerhistoria"/> An exception was the publication in 1944 of the Spanish version of ''The Cinema To-day'' by Douglas Arthur Spencer and Hubert D. Waley, whose translator [[Francisco Madrid]] included an epilogue focused on Argentina, becoming the earliest antecedent of the study of Argentine classical cinema.<ref name="krigerhistoria"/> 

The first proper book dedicated to the history of Argentine cinema was journalist Domingo Di Núbila's ''Historia del cine argentino'', published between 1959 and 1960.<ref name="historiografia"/><ref name="krigerhistoria"/> Di Núbila's work emerged at a time in which the idea of writing the history of the different regional cinemas arose in Latin America, inspired by the growing publishing of books focused on the history and making of cinema in general.<ref name="historiografia"/> Around the same time, histories of national cinema were published in Brazil by {{ill|Alex Viany|pt|Alex Viany}} and in Mexico by [[Emilio García Riera]].<ref name="krigerhistoria"/> These works were the first to deal with the history of cinema in the Latin American context, and it is fitting that they emerged in the only three countries that had managed to develop a local industry.<ref name="krigerhistoria"/> In addition, García Riera's book on Mexican cinema had the novelty of being the first to historicize cinema from the Latin American academic framework.<ref name="krigerhistoria"/>

Di Núbila's book—which introduced the concept of the "Golden Age"—<ref name="manzano"/> became a foundational work and an unavoidable point of reference for Argentine film studies of the classical period, established concepts and assessments that were highly influential in the following decades, although questioned and reinterpreted from the late 20th century onwards.<ref name="historiografia"/><ref name="krigerhistoria"/> His book was published in a context of great uncertainty for local cinema, in which classical forms were disappearing and new modernizing forms were beginning to emerge.<ref name="krigerhistoria"/> In this context, he advocated a less regulated industry that would be revitalized through the [[Law of supply and demand|laws of supply and demand]].<ref name="krigerhistoria"/> In order to propose the new objectives that Argentine cinema should adopt in the following years, Di Núbila necessarily established a narrative of the past.<ref name="krigerhistoria"/> His book revolves around a selection of releases that he distinguishes by their popularity, technical elements, or his own personal tastes.<ref name="krigerhistoria"/> For Di Núbila, the problems of Argentine cinema revolved around four central elements: lack of investment to update technology, mismanagement of the business, an inadequate relationship between industry and state, and the weakening of authentically national themes and narrative forms.<ref name="krigerhistoria"/> Another important element of Di Núbila's text is that it highlights national elements in local cinema, especially those linked to popular or urban traditions (such as tango), in order to demonstrate an independence with respect to film histories linked to traditional countries.<ref name="krigerhistoria"/> Although it allowed to establish its own parameters to analyze Argentine cinema, this perspective had the counterpart of excluding it from comparisons with the cinema of other Latin American countries and the rest of the world.<ref name="krigerhistoria"/>

In 1966, José Agustín Mahieu published ''Breve historia del cine argentino'' which, in addition to Di Núbila's book, became a foundational reference text for subsequent historical studies of Argentine classical cinema.<ref name="historiografia">{{cite journal |last=Pardo |first=Soledad |year=2016 |title=Los estudios sobre el cine argentino del período clásico industrial: un panorama histórico |trans-title=Studies on Argentine cinema from the classic industrial period: a historical overview |url=https://ri.conicet.gov.ar/bitstream/handle/11336/90762/CONICET_Digital_Nro.500317f7-f9a5-46b6-9d0a-6db783ff3f9d_A.pdf?sequence=2&isAllowed=y |journal=Questión |language=es |location=La Plata |publisher=[[Universidad Nacional de La Plata]] |volume=1 |issue=49 |pages=352–367 |issn=1669-6581 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241207232737/https://ri.conicet.gov.ar/bitstream/handle/11336/90762/CONICET_Digital_Nro.500317f7-f9a5-46b6-9d0a-6db783ff3f9d_A.pdf?sequence=2&isAllowed=y |archive-date=7 December 2024 |via=[[CONICET]] |accessdate=5 January 2025}}</ref> Like Di Núbila, Mahieu proposed a history of Argentine cinema in evolutionary terms and with a focus on the opposition between the national and the foreign.<ref name="historiografia"/> Both authors gave special value to the films of the 1930s for their "authentically Argentine" themes and undervalued those of the 1940s for having fewer local references.<ref name="historiografia"/> In the case of Mahieu's work, there is a defense of the new cinema that was emerging in the 1960s, considering the classical-industrial period (in particular the 1940s) as a lower step and modern cinema as a final stage of maturity.<ref name="historiografia"/> This approach had a great impact and longevity in the historiography of Argentine and Latin American cinema.<ref name="historiografia"/>

===1969–1990: Modern criticism and minimization===
[[File:Afiche de La hora de los hornos.jpg|thumb|upright|Poster for the political film ''[[La hora de los hornos]]'' (1968), directed by [[Octavio Getino]] and [[Fernando Solanas]] of [[Grupo Cine Liberación]], a [[Third Cinema]] movement that openly rejected classical cinema and influenced the subsequent lack of interest of film historians in the period.<ref name="historiografia"/>]]

In 1969, the left-wing collective [[Grupo Cine Liberación]], formed by Octavio Getino and [[Pino Solanas|Fernando "Pino" Solanas]], elaborated its manifesto "[[Third Cinema|Towards a Third Cinema]]", which strongly condemned classical-industrial films.<ref name="historiografia"/> In the 1970s, books were published by Estela Dos Santos (who again focused on the mimicry between classical Argentine cinema and Hollywood), Getino and Solanas (maintaining their views of the late 1960s), and Abel Posadas, who distanced himself from the positions of his time for his criticism of the validity of Di Núbila's work, the rescue of traditionally underrated films and directors of the classical period, and his opposition to leftist intellectuals.<ref name="historiografia"/>

In the 1980s, the historiography of Argentine cinema was renewed with the appearance of new works that broadened the analysis by focusing on Latin America as a whole, at a time when the conceptualization of Latin American cinema was in vogue, focused on the region's political cinema.<ref name="historiografia"/><ref name="krigerhistoria"/> As noted by Kriger, the texts that "had the greatest impact on the incipient group of Argentine scholars and researchers [were those which] based their hypotheses on the [[dependency theory]]—a consideration in terms of [[Core countries|core]]-[[Periphery countries|periphery]] of the functioning of the productive structures and of the aesthetic results obtained."<ref name="krigerhistoria"/> The most important books of this trend were ''O cinema na América Latina'' (1985) by Paulo Antonio Paranaguá and ''Historia del cine latinoamericano'' (1987) by Peter Schumann.<ref name="krigerhistoria"/> Although useful for the analysis of modern cinema, these approaches concentrated on the aspects in common in the cinema of the different countries of the region, giving very little presence to classical cinema.<ref name="krigerhistoria"/> As noted by Soledad Pardo: "The position was very clear: in the face of a classical cinema considered conservative and heir to foreign forms that were always harmful, modern cinema burst in with its revolutionary and authentically Latin American vocation. The immediate consequence of the disqualification of [Argentine classical cinema] was the lack of interest and, therefore, the scarcity of exhaustive studies on it."<ref name="historiografia"/>

===1990–present: Renewal and growth===
[[File:Homero Cárpena en Los tres berretines.png|thumb|left|[[Homero Cárpena]] as Pocholo in ''Los tres berretines'' (1933), identified by film historian Adrián Melo as the first [[Media portrayal of LGBTQ people|portrayal of a queer character]] in Argentine cinema.<ref>{{cite journal|location=Buenos Aires|accessdate=12 January 2025|language=es|url=https://www.asaeca.org/imagofagia/index.php/imagofagia/article/view/782/759|issn=1852-9550|publisher=Asociación Argentina de Estudios de Cine y Audiovisual (ASAECA)|journal=Imagofagia|issue=2|year=2010|first=Willie|last=Méndez|title=Sobre Adrián Melo (compilador). Otras historias de amor. Gays, lesbianas y travestis en el cine argentino. Buenos Aires, Editorial LEA, 2008. La teoría cinematográfica argentina sale del clóset|archive-date=12 January 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250112174935/https://www.asaeca.org/imagofagia/index.php/imagofagia/article/view/782/759|url-status=live}}</ref> Research like Melo's were part of a renewal of Argentine [[film studies]] in the 2000s.<ref name="krigerhistoria"/>]]
A turning point in classical Argentine film studies came in the 1990s, when much new scholarship on Argentine cinema began to appear, and although the classical period did not appear as the most studied, the texts still multiplied exponentially.<ref name="krigerhistoria"/> These new texts avoided the stance of classical historiography, which viewed the history of Argentine cinema as a succession of notable films and events.<ref name="krigerhistoria"/> They also introduced [[Film semiotics|semiotic]] or [[Structuralist film theory|structuralist]] tools to the analysis of films, which until then had been based on summarizing their plots.<ref name="krigerhistoria"/> The publication in 1992 of the book ''Cine argentino. La otra historia'', compiled by {{ill|Sergio Wolf|es|Sergio Wolf}}, was pivotal and inaugurated this new renovating stage, with texts deliberately questioning the traditional narratives of Argentine cinema.<ref name="historiografia"/><ref name="krigerhistoria"/> The studies from this period were characterized by not being all-encompassing but rather by focusing on specific themes selected based on different theoretical or methodological criteria.<ref name="krigerhistoria"/> With the arrival of the 21st century came the publication of ''Cine argentino, industria y clasicismo'' (2000), a comprehensive two-volume work edited by {{ill|Claudio España|es|Claudio España}}. This influential collective research delved deeply into the classical era of Argentine film production from 1933 to 1956.<ref name="historiografia"/>

Since the early 2000s, studies on classical Argentine cinema have undergone a significant transformation, as the longstanding disregard or indifference toward this era gave way to renewed interest from scholars who have approached it with an unprecedented level of theoretical and methodological rigor.<ref name="historiografia"/> These texts demonstrate different levels of focus on specific topics from the period, emphasizing the importance of introducing new questions and perspectives that were overlooked in traditional accounts, rather than simply rewriting the classical past.<ref name="krigerhistoria"/> Examples include Horacio Campodónico's political-economic analysis (2005), Ana Laura Lusnich's study of the "social-folkloric drama" genre (2005), and Adrián Melo's research on [[LGBT representation in media|LGBT representations]] in Argentine cinema (2009).<ref name="krigerhistoria"/> The fields of [[cultural studies]] and [[Transnationalism|transnational]] studies further enriched the exploration of classical Argentine cinema. In the realm of the former, Matthew B. Karush published a book in 2012 that examined classical Argentine cinema as part of the "mass cultural commodities", understanding the convergence of media industries as a phenomenon of meaning within the films themselves.<ref name="krigerhistoria"/> Transnational studies, on the other hand, opened up new problems in the comparative study of the Argentine classical era with that of other countries, notably Mexico.<ref name="krigerhistoria"/> Most recently, several historians identified with the [[New Cinema History]] movement—which analyzes cinema as a [[social phenomenon]]—have studied the audiences and filmgoing experiences of classical Argentine cinema, aspects until then unexplored by national film scholarship.{{sfn|Kriger|2018|p=191}}

==Legacy==
===Conservation===
{{Quote box
| quote = "A combination of a total lack of knowledge about the best conditions for [[Film preservation|preserving the material]] and the high cost of preserving it led to a situation in which most of the Argentine cinema preserved to this day is preserved 'by chance'. The State never became truly aware of how important it is to preserve national cinema, as if indefinite production would replace the successive loss of material."
| source = — Film historian Martín Miguel Pereira, 2015.<ref name="conservacion"/>
| width = 25%
}}
Due to a long history of neglect in the [[film preservation|preservation]] of Argentine films, much of the country's classical era cinema is considered [[Lost film|lost]]. It is estimated that half of Argentine sound films are lost, a figure that rises to 90% in the case of silent films.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.clarin.com/sociedad/argentina-perdio-gran-parte-archivo-cinematografico_0_ByV-TegeAYg.html?srsltid=AfmBOooviblwt51iTVUPZXz6lhIprboPGX3igFeiPnMT5UCaewRynTxe|title=La Argentina perdió gran parte de su archivo cinematográfico|date=27 September 2003|accessdate=23 July 2025|work=[[Clarín (Argentine newspaper)|Clarín]]|language=es|archive-date=26 September 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250926214414/https://www.clarin.com/sociedad/argentina-perdio-gran-parte-archivo-cinematografico_0_ByV-TegeAYg.html?srsltid=AfmBOooviblwt51iTVUPZXz6lhIprboPGX3igFeiPnMT5UCaewRynTxe|url-status=live}}</ref> Unlike most countries, Argentina has not adopted public policies that preserve the national film heritage.<ref name="cinemateca">{{cite web|url=https://www.lacapital.com.ar/argentina-es-el-unico-pais-que-no-tiene-cinemateca-n2691635.html/amp|language=es|accessdate=26 November 2022|title="Argentina es el único país que no tiene cinemateca"|work=[[La Capital]]|first=Fernando G.|last=Varea|date=3 October 2022|archive-date=25 November 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221125131800/https://www.lacapital.com.ar/argentina-es-el-unico-pais-que-no-tiene-cinemateca-n2691635.html/amp|url-status=live}}</ref> This has led to the loss of a large amount of material and to the fact that of many films only a single copy survives in a poor condition, even some that are considered among the most important in Argentine cinema by critics and specialists.<ref name="conservacion">{{cite journal|url=http://www.asaeca.org/imagofagia/index.php/imagofagia/article/view/446|last=Pereira|first=Martín Miguel|language=es|accessdate=26 November 2022|journal=Imagofagia|issn=1852-9550|location=Buenos Aires|publisher=Asociación Argentina de Estudios de Cine y Audiovisual|issue=11|year=2015|title=La conservación del cine nacional: La larga agonía del patrimonio fílmico argentino|archive-date=26 November 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221126174431/http://www.asaeca.org/imagofagia/index.php/imagofagia/article/view/446|url-status=live}}</ref> Many films survive but through incomplete copies, missing scenes, entire acts or musical numbers.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.lanacion.com.ar/espectaculos/cronica-de-la-destruccion-del-cine-argentino-nid100003/|accessdate=12 December 2022|date=14 June 1998|work=[[La Nación]]|title=Crónica de la destrucción del cine argentino|language=es|archive-date=12 December 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221212040134/https://www.lanacion.com.ar/espectaculos/cronica-de-la-destruccion-del-cine-argentino-nid100003/|url-status=live}}</ref> 

Between the late 1930s and mid-1940s, there were some measures for the conservation of film material, although they were interested in the documentary record rather than fiction films.<ref name="conservacion"/> In 1949, the [[nonprofit]] cinematheque Fundación Cinemateca Argentina was created as a result of the merging of two film clubs, with the objective of preserving and disseminating cinema.<ref name="conservacion"/> The relationship between the Fundación Cinemateca Argentina and the state and its financial support is complex and spans decades.<ref name="conservacion"/> In the early 1990s, the Argentine government subsidized the Fundación Cinemateca Argentina, funding the purchase of its current building in [[Constitución, Buenos Aires|Constitución]] and acquiring around 400 national films from the U.S. to prevent their disposal due to the video boom.<ref name="conservacion"/> Further acquisitions of Argentine films abroad occurred between 1996 and 1997.<ref name="conservacion"/> Legal issues have kept around 300 films in the [[National Autonomous University of Mexico]]'s cinematheque since 2002, unable to return.<ref name="conservacion"/> Senator [[Luis Falcó]] from [[Río Negro Province|Río Negro]] attempted in 2006 to legislate their duty-free import, but his proposal failed, and he died the following year. The initiative lapsed in 2008, leaving 700 Argentine films (of an estimated 3,000) still abroad.<ref name="conservacion"/>

[[File:Museo del Cine, Buenos Aires.jpg|thumb|left|Established in 1971, the [[Museo del Cine Pablo Ducrós Hicken]], dependent of the city of [[Buenos Aires]], exhibits and preserves a large number of films and diverse materials from Argentine classical cinema.]]

The law that created the National Institute of Cinematography in 1957, decreed by the military government after the overthrow of Perón, provided for the creation of the National Cinematheque, where producers reportedly had to deliver a copy of every film made with credit or subsidy from the organization.<ref name="conservacion"/> Nevertheless, these film copies were of poor quality, either being the initial, worst "A copy" or ones heavily used in national screenings, representing the only surviving copies in most cases.<ref name="conservacion"/> Additionally, many have been lost overseas or through careless lending.<ref name="conservacion"/> In 1968, a new law established that films of special interest should be given a copy to the [[General Archive of the Nation (Argentina)|General Archive of the Nation]], in addition to that of the new [[National Institute of Cinema and Audiovisual Arts]] (INCAA).<ref name="conservacion"/> The law also ordered the creation of a National Cinematheque dependent on the INCAA, which casts doubt as to whether what was stipulated in 1957 was ever fulfilled, and made its prerogatives explicit, making it perhaps the first action of the state in terms of film preservation.<ref name="conservacion"/> In addition, in 1971 the [[Museo del Cine Pablo Ducrós Hicken]] was created, which among its functions includes the conservation of a large film archive and is administered by the government of the city of Buenos Aires.<ref name="conservacion"/> Currently located in [[La Boca]], the museum exhibits a large number of objects, artifacts and audiovisual material from the history of Argentine cinema, including the Golden Age.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.clarin.com/cultura/museo-cine-celebra-pasado-apuesta-futuro_0_Hya7DI7Jz.html|location=Buenos Aires|language=es|work=[[Clarín (Argentine newspaper)|Clarín]]|title=El Museo del Cine celebra el pasado y apuesta al futuro|first=Ezequiel|last=Viéitez|date=10 November 2017|accessdate=15 January 2025|archive-date=21 January 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250121080316/https://www.clarin.com/cultura/museo-cine-celebra-pasado-apuesta-futuro_0_Hya7DI7Jz.html|url-status=live}}</ref> The abandoned Lumiton studios in Munro were rescued from demolition in the 1990s and converted into a museum run by the municipality of [[Vicente López Partido|Vicente López]], with a permanent collection of Lumiton's history, a screening room, and an extensive archive.<ref>{{cite web |title=Los 90 años de Lumiton |access-date=15 January 2025 |work=[[Página/12]] |location=Buenos Aires |date=7 January 2023 |first=Lucía |last=Requejo |url=https://www.pagina12.com.ar/513970-los-90-anos-de-lumiton |archive-date=25 July 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250725182608/https://www.pagina12.com.ar/513970-los-90-anos-de-lumiton |url-status=live }}</ref>

In the 1990s, Fernando "Pino" Solanas presented a national law for the creation of the Cinematheque and Archive of the National Image (Spanish: ''Cinemateca y Archivo de la Imagen Nacional'', CINAIN), in order to unify all the scattered and poorly preserved national film heritage in a single place.<ref name="conservacion"/> After being approved by the [[Argentine National Congress|National Congress]] and then vetoed by President [[Carlos Menem]], the law was finally approved in 1999, although it was not regulated until 2010.<ref name="conservacion"/> Since then, no government has ensured that the CINAIN began to operate under the terms established by law or to fulfill the functions that correspond to it, and the demand for the need of a National Cinematheque continues to be reiterated by the country's film community.<ref name="cinematecanacional">{{cite web|url=https://www.clarin.com/revista-n/escenarios/cinemateca-nacional-23-anos-larga-espera_0_n96cLfjFqa.html|work=Revista Ñ. [[Clarín (Argentine newspaper)|Clarín]]|accessdate=12 January 2025|date=18 November 2022|title=Cinemateca Nacional: 23 años de una larga espera|language=es|last=Kozak|first=Daniela|archive-date=18 November 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221118210453/https://www.clarin.com/revista-n/escenarios/cinemateca-nacional-23-anos-larga-espera_0_n96cLfjFqa.html|url-status=live}}</ref> According to a study conducted by filmmaker Hernán Gaffet and film collectors Fernando Martín Peña and Octavio Fabiano, 50% of national sound films have been lost forever.<ref name="cinematecanacional"/> In addition to the INCAA film archive (which is different from the CINAIN), the General Archive of the Nation and the Museo del Cine Pablo Ducrós Hicken, there are also films in other public organizations such as the [[Televisión Pública]] and the [[National Library of Argentina|National Library]]; storage conditions vary by institution, but none prioritize preservation, restoration, and dissemination, often due to prohibitively high costs.<ref name="cinematecanacional"/> There are also several private collections of various kinds, although they cannot afford the costs of their proper conservation.<ref name="cinematecanacional"/> The most important of these collectors is Peña, who is also a popular film historian and communicator, individually undertaking the safeguarding of a large part of the surviving Argentine cinema at the same time that he continues the demand for a National Cinematheque.<ref name="oscuras">{{cite web|url=https://www.lanacion.com.ar/espectaculos/cine/la-vida-a-oscuras-un-documental-que-advierte-sobre-el-serio-riesgo-que-corre-el-patrimonio-filmico-nid11072023/|title=La vida a oscuras: un documental que advierte sobre el serio riesgo que corre el patrimonio fílmico argentino|first=Alejandro|last=Lingenti|location=Buenos Aires|language=es|accessdate=12 January 2025|work=[[La Nación]]|date=11 July 2023|archive-date=21 January 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250121075659/https://www.lanacion.com.ar/espectaculos/cine/la-vida-a-oscuras-un-documental-que-advierte-sobre-el-serio-riesgo-que-corre-el-patrimonio-filmico-nid11072023/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.pausa.com.ar/2024/07/perdimos-el-50-de-nuestro-cine/|title=Perdimos el 50% de nuestro cine|accessdate=12 January 2025|language=es|date=31 July 2024|first=Marcelo|last=Przylucki|work=Pausa|location=Santa Fe|archive-date=21 January 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250121075559/https://www.pausa.com.ar/2024/07/perdimos-el-50-de-nuestro-cine/|url-status=live}}</ref>

===Critics' lists===
[[File:Prisioneros de la tierra.jpg|thumb|A [[film still]] of ''[[Prisioneros de la tierra]]'' (1939) by [[Mario Soffici]], which has been considered the greatest Argentine film of all time on several occasions.]]
Several films from the classical period have been listed among the best in the history of Argentine cinema. The [[Museo del Cine Pablo Ducrós Hicken]] carried out [[The 100 Greatest Films of Argentine Cinema|polls to determine the greatest Argentine films of all time]] in the years 1977, 1984, 1991 and 2000.<ref name="editorial">{{cite web|url=https://encuestadecineargentino.com/editorial/|title=Editorial|accessdate=13 November 2022|date=11 November 2022|publisher=[[The 100 Greatest Films of Argentine Cinema|Encuesta de cine argentino 2022]]|language=es|archive-date=13 November 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221113034628/https://encuestadecineargentino.com/editorial/|url-status=live}}</ref> In the 1977 list, 8 of the top 10 results were films released before 1957, including ''Prisioneros de la tierra'' (1st place), ''La guerra gaucha'' (3rd place), ''Así es la vida'' (4th place), ''La vuelta al nido'' (5th place), ''Las aguas bajan turbias'' (6th place), ''[[La dama duende]]'' (7th place), ''[[Malambo (1942 film)|Malambo]]'' (8th place) and ''[[Outside the Law (1937 film)|Fuera de la ley]]'' (10th place).<ref name="lamiradacautiva">{{cite journal|url=https://drive.google.com/file/d/1ITZbOc_XZnbJ1W2a9Lq9Zk8xJRrWrzPg/view|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221121182959/https://drive.google.com/file/d/1ITZbOc_XZnbJ1W2a9Lq9Zk8xJRrWrzPg/view|archive-date=21 November 2022|accessdate=21 November 2022|year=2000|issue=3|journal=La Mirada Cautiva|location=Buenos Aires|publisher=[[Museo del Cine Pablo Ducrós Hicken]]|via=[[The 100 Greatest Films of Argentine Cinema|Encuesta de cine argentino 2022]] on [[Google Drive]]|pages=6–14|title=Las 100 mejores del periodo 1933–1999 del Cine Argentino}}</ref> In the 1984 list, ''Prisioneros de la tierra'' was again selected as the greatest film of Argentine cinema, although only three other pre-1957 films reached the top 10: ''La guerra gaucha'', ''Las aguas bajan turbias'' and ''Los isleros''.<ref name="lamiradacautiva"/> Due to the coincidences in the number of votes, the top 100 list of the 2000 poll resulted in 43 positions comprising 101 films, of which 29 were released before 1957; these are:<ref name="lamiradacautiva"/>

[[File:Hugo del carril 1952.jpg|thumb|[[Hugo del Carril]] in a still of ''[[Dark River (1952 film)|Las aguas bajan turbias]]'' (1952), the highest-rated classical-era film in a 2022 [[The 100 Greatest Films of Argentine Cinema|survey of the 100 greatest Argentine films of all time]].]]

In 2022, the film magazines ''La vida útil'', ''Taipei'' and ''La tierra quema'' carried out a new top 100 list inspired by the previous ones, which was presented at the Mar del Plata International Film Festival.<ref>{{cite web|language=es|url=https://www.lanacion.com.ar/espectaculos/cine/festival-de-mar-del-plata-2022-se-eligieron-las-100-mejores-peliculas-de-la-historia-del-cine-nid11112022/|work=[[La Nación]]|date=11 November 2022|first=Astrid|last=Riehn|title=Festival de Mar del Plata 2022: se eligieron las 100 mejores películas de la historia del cine argentino|accessdate=13 November 2022|archive-date=13 November 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221113034624/https://www.lanacion.com.ar/espectaculos/cine/festival-de-mar-del-plata-2022-se-eligieron-las-100-mejores-peliculas-de-la-historia-del-cine-nid11112022/|url-status=live}}</ref> Due to the coincidences in the number of votes, the total list includes 812 titles and 62 ranking positions,<ref name="editorial"/> while the "top 100" includes places from 1 to 52 and comprises 103 films.<ref name="top100">{{cite web|url=https://encuestadecineargentino.com/top-100/|title=Top 100|accessdate=13 November 2022|date=11 November 2022|publisher=[[The 100 Greatest Films of Argentine Cinema|Encuesta de cine argentino 2022]]|language=es|archive-date=30 May 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230530153727/https://encuestadecineargentino.com/top-100/|url-status=live}}</ref> For the first time, no pre-1960s film appeared in the top 10,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.clarin.com/revista-enie/escenarios/encuesta-cine-argentino-cifrar-mirada_0_ANitr9rf7N.html|work=Revista Ñ. [[Clarín (Argentine newspaper)|Clarín]]|accessdate=22 November 2022|language=es|title=Encuesta de Cine Argentino: para cifrar la mirada|date=18 November 2022|archive-date=22 November 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221122015702/https://www.clarin.com/revista-enie/escenarios/encuesta-cine-argentino-cifrar-mirada_0_ANitr9rf7N.html|url-status=live}}</ref> and classical-era films were among those that decreased the most compared to the previous poll.<ref name="editorial"/> The fact that more than a third of the list corresponds to films released in 2000 onwards has been interpreted as a consequence of the absence of conservation policies for the country's film heritage.<ref name="editorial"/><ref>{{cite web|last=Prividera|first=Nicolás|accessdate=21 November 2022|title=Lo que (no) dice la 'Encuesta de cine argentino'|date=15 November 2022|work=Con los ojos abiertos|location=Buenos poll fueled the long-standing claim for the need for a national cinematheque.<ref name="mesaredonda">{{cite web|url=http://www.incaa.gov.ar/mesa-redonda-la-preservacion-cinematografica-y-los-espacios-de-exhibicion-en-el-37o-festival-internacional-de-cine-de-mar-del-plata|location=Buenos Aires|language=es|accessdate=25 November 2022|date=11 November 2022|publisher=[[INCAA]]|title=Mesa redonda 'La preservación cinematográfica y los espacios de exhibición' en el 37º Festival Internacional de Cine de Mar del Plata|archive-date=25 November The films prior to 1957 that reached the top 100 of 2022 were:<ref name="top100"/>

In 2000, ''[[American Cinematographer]]''—the magazine of the [[American Society of Cinematographers]]—listed ''[[Los tallos amargos]]'' (1956) as one of the "50 Best Photographed Films of All-Time", the work of cinematographer Ricardo Younis.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.clarin.com/espectaculos/mejor-fotografiadas-siglo_0_BJEUx2xCte.html|language=es|title=Las mejor fotografiadas del siglo|accessdate=4 December 2022|date=4 January 2000|work=[[Clarín (Argentine newspaper)|Clarín]]|archive-date=4 December 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221204034814/https://www.clarin.com/espectaculos/mejor-fotografiadas-siglo_0_BJEUx2xCte.html|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.moma.org/calendar/events/1773?locale=en|title=Los Tallos amargos (The Bitter Stems). 1956. Argentina. Directed by Fernando Ayala|publisher=[[MoMA]]|accessdate=4 December 2022|year=2016|archive-date=4 December 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221204045118/https://www.moma.org/calendar/events/1773?locale=en|url-status=live}}</ref> In 2022, the Spanish magazine ''[[Fotogramas]]'' included ''Los tres berretines'' (1933), ''Los martes, orquídeas'' (1941) and ''Dios se lo pague'' (1948) in its list of the "20 best Argentine films in history".<ref>{{cite
